A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watch

BBC News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 13:49:19 GMT

Millions of Americans are about to decide the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.

A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.

Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.

There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report.

Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.

In a nutshell:

This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.

Story of the race:

The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.

Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner.

Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race.

The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge.

Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.

How they got here:

Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.

In a nutshell:

One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the survivors of US politics.

Story of the race:

Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections.

Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump.

Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election.

But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate.

Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).

How they got here:

Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.

In a nutshell:

James Talarico aims to end a decades-long electoral drought for the Democrats in Texas - and show that one of the Republicans' main strongholds could be in play for the 2028 presidential election. His match-up with Ken Paxton has become the most expensive Senate race ever.

Story of the race:

Republican Paxton knows his party has been winning statewide races in Texas for more than 30 years.

Texas State Representative James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminary student, is the latest Democrat hoping to break his party's long losing streak.

Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. It is a challenging national political environment for conservatives and there are several state issues like data centre construction and aggressive immigration enforcement that have cut against their party. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.

The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".

Supported by more than $170m in funds from tech mogul Elon Musk, Paxton has attempted to paint Talarico as a liberal who is out of touch with Texans on issues like transgender rights, law enforcement, immigration and energy policy.

A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.

How they got here:

Before he entered public service, Paxton spent 14 years launching and building his own law firm. He served in the state House and Senate before becoming the chief legal officer in Texas.

Talarico taught at a middle school in San Antonio, in a neighbourhood he has described as one of the poorest in the state. He has studied theology and names Pope Leo as a "spiritual hero".

In a nutshell:

This is one of the most bitter contests, with left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed aiming to keep this crucial seat in Democratic hands. He is up against Mike Rogers, a Republican former FBI agent who received a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's defeated Democratic rival, only adding to the acrimony that has characterised this race from the start.

Story of the race:

A doctor and public health official, El-Sayed is one of the most left-wing Senate nominees this election cycle.

He supports a government-run health insurance system and the abolition of ICE. His strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension in the party.

Rogers, who emphasises his military and intelligence background, has managed to maintain Trump's support despite decrying his Canada tariffs and his Russia diesel deal.

He has also diverged from the president by calling for a quick end to the war with Iran. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate.

As well as attacking him for his politics, Trump and Rogers have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood; El-Sayed has denounced the organisation.

The president has also invoked 9/11 and even called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

How they got here:

El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in Michigan before his medical studies in the US and UK and subsequent work in the sector. Rogers, 63, served in the US Army and in the FBI before entering Congress and emerging as a key advocate of US surveillance policies.

In a nutshell:

Trump made the trip to Iowa on his final day of campaign rallies, such is its importance. Polls have it as a toss-up between Republican and former TV news host Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, who won gold at basketball at two Paralympic Games.

Story of the race:

Farms, tariffs and Trump have all emerged as key issues in the closely-watched race.

Hinson has slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.

Meanwhile, Turek argues that Trump's tariffs have led to "farmageddon" in the largely rural state. He has also sought to convince voters that the war in Iran has led to rising fuel and fertiliser costs.

Hinson has cast Turek as a candidate who would vote as an "East Coast liberal".

The two have also clashed on issues ranging from taxes and social security to immigration. The last time a Democrat won a federal election in Iowa was nearly 20 years ago.

How they got here:

Hinson, 43, is a former local news reporter who says her journalistic background helps her understand the issues faced by the state's farmers and small businesses. Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida, going through multiple surgeries before representing the USA at wheelchair basketball at four Paralympic Games, twice triumphantly.

In a nutshell:

A Democratic victory in Kansas would upend 94 years of history - the last time this Midwestern state elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Senator Roger Marshall is the Republican trying to avoid a humbling defeat, while first-time candidate and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton is the Democrat trying to break records.

Story of the race:

Marshall has closely aligned himself as a Trump-aligned, pro-farmer candidate.

Hamilton, who once considered running as an independent, has pitched himself as a candidate that can bridge the partisan divide. He has largely campaigned on a message of lower costs and protecting healthcare access.

Marshall has sought to attack Hamilton's record as a pastor, describing him as "too woke" for the conservative state.

Marshall, meanwhile, has been under scrutiny ever since reports emerged that he sued patients unable to pay their medical bills. He told Fox News the story was a hit job by the left media and senior Democrats.

The tight race is broadly seen as a potentially ominous sign for Republicans.

A Hamilton victory would be seen as a sign of increasing dissatisfaction with Trump's policies - particularly on economics - in territory that was once considered safe for the party.

How they got here:

Both Marshall, 66, and Hamilton, 62, highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans who are in close touch with local issues. Marshall worked for 25 years as an obstetrician, delivering some 5,000 babies, while his rival Hamilton founded a church which became the centre of the largest United Methodist congregation in America.

In a nutshell:

Trump won this state with ease in 2024 and no-one a year ago considered it in play for the midterms. But Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown who is running to get his old job back, having represented Ohio in the Senate for many years before losing his seat.

Story of the race:

Husted was appointed in 2025 to the Senate seat vacated by Vice-President JD Vance, and is now running to serve the rest of Vance's term.

He promises to use his business experience to bring jobs and growth to Ohio.

In a different election cycle he would probably be the favourite to win this onetime swing state that has become reliably red in the Trump era.

But Husted is facing a formidable challenge from Brown, who has high name recognition from three decades representing Ohio in Congress.

Brown is known as a champion of workers and was advocating economic populist policies long before others in his party.

The race is a referendum on Trump's economic policies, in particular his trade wars that have impacted the manufacturing and auto industries that underpin Ohio's economy.

How they got here:

Husted, 59, began life in a foster home and was in the world of business before politics; he was an elite American football player at college and his physique has been repeatedly praised by President Trump at rallies. Brown, 73, was introduced to political activism from a young age and was recruited into local politics even before graduating from Yale.

By Bernd Debusmann, Daniel Bush and Anthony Zurcher in Washington, and James FitzGerald and Tom Geoghegan in London.

Man caught in car with £14k of drugs as a lamb ate chips in the back seat avoids jail

BBC News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 13:05:15 GMT

A man who was caught in a car with £14,000 of drugs, while a lamb ate from a bag of chips in the back seat, has avoided jail.

John McNeil, 56, was a passenger in Lindsey Sangster's vehicle which was stopped by police on the M74 in Glasgow on 22 April 2023.

Bags of heroin and cocaine were later recovered by a police dog underneath the front passenger seat of the Volkswagen Golf.

When quizzed about the animal - called Pablo - a sergeant claimed Sangster's partner McNeil told him she was a "trainee shepherdess." The duo were found guilty in September of possession of cocaine and diamorphine with intent to supply.

The pair claimed they had tried to save the lamb - named after Colombian drug lord Pablo Escobar - from a "dangerous position" on the middle of the road.

The court previously heard Pablo belonged to North Lanrigg Farm in Motherwell, which is owned by farmer Kirsty Mair.

A joint minute of agreed evidence said Mair had not given them permission to have the lamb.

Sgt Nick Twigg, 42, told jurors that he had reason to stop Sangster's car on the motorway, with Sangster, McNeil and another man in the vehicle.

An initial search found a glass pipe in the driver's door pocket while others were seized from McNeil and the man.

He said: "I asked Sangster where it [the lamb] came from and McNeil said that she was a trainee shepherdess."

Prosecutor Julianna Keenan asked the officer if there was evidence of this and he replied: "No, the lamb at the time was eating a bag of chips left on the back seat. There were no bottles."

A police dog named Billy later found £4,640 of cocaine and £10,050 of heroin under the front passenger seat within two bags.

The purity of the cocaine was stated to be no less than 76%.

In a joint minute of agreed evidence, Keenan said: "Officers were of the opinion that the circumstances of this case indicate the supply of cocaine and heroin due to the amount recovered being excessive for personal use."

Pablo was taken to a farm in Ayrshire where it was held for 48 to 72 hours before being returned to Mair.

A charge of resetting the lamb was dropped by the Crown mid-trial as there was "no reported theft" at the time.

McNeil told jurors in his evidence that he had experience with animals, having worked in the past with his father, who is a retired agricultural contractor.

He stated they came across Pablo on the middle of the road on the way home to Ayrshire after a journey to Edinburgh for the other man to purchase a car.

McNeil claimed that Pablo was "dehydrated" and appeared not have been fed for a couple of hours.

He told the court that the plan was to "take him back to the owner" as Pablo had identity markings on his ears.

McNeil denied any knowledge of the drugs in the car, as did Sangster.

Jurors were told that Sangster was under the influence of drugs at the time when she was behind the wheel and pleaded guilty at separate proceedings.

She was disqualified from driving for 18 months and ordered to do 100 hours of unpaid work.

Bronwyn Moore, defending McNeil at the sentencing, said her client was now a team leader at a construction company and that he was "at the height of his addiction" when arrested.

McNeil, of Fairlie, North Ayrshire, was back in the dock to be sentenced while Sangster, of Kilbirnie, did not appear and a warrant was granted for her arrest.

Sheriff Tony Kelly ordered McNeil to do 300 hours of unpaid work and tagged him for six months, meaning he must stay indoors between 20:00 and 05:00.

The sheriff said he had been advised the risk of McNeil offending again was low.

After the lamb was returned to Mair, she said he was in fine health and happy with "his new pet lamb pals".

How Antonelli 'blew everyone away' to make F1 history

BBC News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 01:47:30 GMT

Twelve world titles on one podium - Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton hold Kimi Antonelli aloft

Just after Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were united in their assessment of the 20-year-old's achievement.

"Incredible," they both said. Coming from the two most successful champions on the current grid, the men who are first and third in the all-time list of F1 race-winners, it meant something.

That Antonelli shared the Mexico City Grand Prix podium with these two titans meant something, too.

To Antonelli, firstly, who said: "I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it's just an incredible moment.

"And as well to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special and a moment that will live and will always be remembered."

So, too, though, for its symbolism. Antonelli seems destined to join them among the list of all-time greats of the sport, judging by the scale of his achievement this year.

"There are going to be others," said 1996 world champion Damon Hill, commentating for BBC Radio 5 live.

"I don't see anything else other than him getting better and better. He's going to have to go through hard times as well, but no-one is going to doubt his incredible talent."

No-one indeed. Not any more, anyway.

This video can not be played

Antonelli title win 'beginning of something special'

Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who became world champion

Antonelli heads list of F1's youngest champions

How much do you know about F1 champion Antonelli?

Antonelli's first title comes at the end of only his second season in F1. When he was drafted into Mercedes last year - to replace Hamilton, no less - there were those who said he was too inexperienced.

For some of last year, he looked it. There were flashes of promise, but by and large it was a shaky debut season, one that did not live up to Antonelli's billing as potentially the next generational talent.

So when it became clear that Mercedes would start this season with the best car, it was his team-mate George Russell, who had comfortably beaten him in 2025, who was favourite for the championship.

But that was without reckoning on the remarkable step forward Antonelli made in his development over last winter.

He finished the first race on Russell's tail. He took his maiden victory in the second, the first of five consecutive wins with which he took control of the championship. Since then, he has never looked like losing it.

Even when Mercedes' early season advantage was wiped out by their rivals, Antonelli was always there, always a factor. Which is more than can be said for Russell.

In that sense, it is important to see his achievement in context. Had the comparative performance between Russell and Antonelli carried on as it did last year, this championship may well have had a different complexion.

It could have been a season during which Russell and Hamilton were neck and neck in the title fight for most of the year - indeed, Russell has now slipped behind both Verstappen and Hamilton in the points table.

Instead, it has been a story of one driver's domination. His performances have been so strong that he has removed pretty much all jeopardy from the title fight.

That has not made it the most exciting season to watch, but it speaks volumes for the level at which Antonelli has performed. All because of the progress he has made - and his remarkable consistency.

This video can not be played

How a boy from Bologna became a world champion

"At his age," said Verstappen, "to be so solid, not make big mistakes, and of course also beat your experienced team-mate, he's just driven incredible, and I'm very proud of him, how he has handled himself this whole season."

Lando Norris, the outgoing world champion, was also effusive in his praise.

"It couldn't have gone to a better person," he said. "He's a genuine guy, very, very kind, and he has driven unbelievably well this year, better that what everyone was expecting of him.

"He's certainly not had an easy season in terms of his competition being incredibly high. He has gone up against the best drivers in the world, all in very good cars, and he's blown everyone away.

"I hope everyone gives him enough credit for what he's achieved this year. He's made everyone else look silly. He's driven that well and he's been able to click with his car, he's worked hard to understand how to drive this car and he's exploited it better than anyone else.

"So he should be very proud. He has achieved history and I am very, very happy for him."

For Antonelli, the difficulties of last year were formative, and critical in what he has been able to achieve this.

"The fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to F1," he said, "or I wasn't ready for it - which at some point last year I probably looked like I wasn't - being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year.

"Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver, as a person.

"Still this year I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better, so it's just a constant learning process.

"Last year being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."

One of those moments was this weekend.

He admitted after qualifying that he had been "tight", not driving as well as he could have, a result of the pressure of the moment.

"Austin, I was much more aggressive, much more present in the moment," said Antonelli, "while in Mexico, yesterday in qualifying, I was a bit more tense in a way because I also wasn't as intense in the way I was driving.

"So definitely, it hasn't been easy on that side. But now finally, we clinched it and now we can just enjoy the rest of the season."

The potency of the moment was clear to see after the race.

Antonelli admitted he was so emotional on the last lap as he followed Verstappen and Hamilton home that he was struggling to see.

"I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying basically and I couldn't see clearly ahead," he said. "I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.

"It was very special and a lot of memories went through my mind in that moment."

Then his father Marco and mother Veronica, who have been so important in his rise to F1, were there to greet him at the end.

Marco has been virtually ever-present this season, providing quiet support for his son whenever needed.

"To have my dad during the whole season was very important," said Antonelli, "because, first of all, he was the one keeping me grounded, especially after very high moments, but as well he was the one that was always there when I was facing a difficult situation or I wasn't feeling the best ahead of a session."

Then, in the champions' news conference, he became so emotional at one point as he remembered his late grandfather that he could not talk, and had to take a minute to compose himself.

"Oh my god," he said, after he had collected himself. "I cried way too much today. But it's good."

'We've got big problems' - Hamilton says Ferrari need 'serious talks'

BBC News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 00:28:28 GMT

This video can not be played

'Utter chaos at Ferrari right now'

Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari "have to have some serious talks behind closed doors" after fighting between their two drivers cost them victory in the Mexico City Grand Prix.

Leclerc cut a chicane on the first lap to take the lead from Hamilton, who then lost second place to Max Verstappen as a consequence of his team-mate's attack.

Verstappen went on to win the race with Hamilton second, as Kimi Antonelli finished third to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history.

"Ultimately, that lost us the win today," said Hamilton. "We have to have some serious talks behind closed doors."

During a red-flag period in the race caused by a crash for Valtteri Bottas' Cadillac, Hamilton had said over team radio: "We've got big problems. Big, big problems."

When informed Hamilton was unhappy, Leclerc said: "I will speak with Lewis. We both didn't make the corner. I don't know if Lewis' point was for me to get P3 but having the Red Bull second I felt it was worth it to keep the position and see what happened. That's what I did.

"I could be also unhappy with how much he pushed me off track out of Turn One, but it is racing. When you are fighting for a win it is the way it should be."

Hamilton's point is that if the Ferraris had worked together on the first lap, they would have been running one-two and could have controlled the race from there and likely finished in those positions.

He said: "We could have easily had a one-two today. We had the pace to do so.

"We're going into Turn Four first and second. If we just held position, I think anything can happen in the race. But when your team-mate works against you and then you lose positions like that, it's definitely tough.

"So we'll just talk about it offline and it's not really worth saying too much more. We don't have rules of engagement. And whether or not that would change anything from Charles' side, I don't know. We've just got to figure out. But something needs to change for sure."

Antonelli becomes world champion as Verstappen wins in Mexico

Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who became world champion

The rules said Leclerc should have given the place back to Hamilton for overtaking off track.

But because Hamilton was also passed by Verstappen, Leclerc decided to carry on in the lead and try to build a gap that would enable him to overcome the five-second penalty he was given by officials.

He was not quite able to extend his lead sufficiently and, when he pitted for new tyres, Verstappen followed him in to do the same and overtook him.

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur said he was "frustrated" at the way the incident played out.

"It's a lot of frustration for me but I'm not the most important," he said. "It's a lot of frustration for the 2,000 people working for the project. And this I will need time to digest."

The Frenchman added: "We'll discuss tonight, we'll fix it tomorrow and then we'll be focused on the cycle."

Hamilton added: "Fred's doing his best. Fred came and spoke to me before the race and I think he was nervous and I think he just wanted us, of course, he wants these two drivers to do well.

"From my side, if I'm coming from behind and I'm taking all the risk and it ends up we lose as a team, then I think I'd have some answering to do, because it impacts a lot of people.

"But the other way around, I'm in the lead and it was just unnecessary.

"The core thing to remember, which maybe that comes with age, but every decision you make in the car impacts all the people that work in the background for the whole team.

"So working as a team, part of our job and part of our contract is we have to work as a team, which we could have easily done today. So it's a shame to see us lose as we did. It will continue unless action is taken."

On Leclerc, Hamilton said: "The guy's 28 years old, so I don't think it's an age thing. I think it's a mentality thing. It's like do or die, either I win or none of us do, and it shouldn't be that."

The incident was the latest and arguably most serious of a series of tensions between Hamilton and Leclerc this season.

It follows Leclerc pushing Hamilton off track at the first corner of the Italian Grand Prix.

The race before that, Leclerc ignored a team order to let Hamilton by when they were on different strategies.

In Singapore last month, there was another incident when Hamilton felt he should have been let by when they were on different tyres, but Ferrari refused to make the call.

Verstappen, who capitalised on this latest battle in Mexico, said: "Ferrari were really fast, I do think they made it a little bit difficult for themselves fighting each other and that's why I was able to capitalise on that. I mean, I take it, right?"

Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?

BBC News Mon, 02 Nov 2026 00:25:12 GMT

The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.

A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.

Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.

A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.

But are the polls accurate?

Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.

Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.

According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.

"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."

If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.

That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.

One explanation for why Trump overperformed in previous presidential elections is that his supporters – many of whom were not regular voters – flocked to the polls in higher-than-expected numbers.

That unpredictability is one of the main contributing factors to those notable recent polling misses, even if the margins in most reputable polls were only off by a few percentage points.

In a close race, those few points can make the difference between victory and defeat for a candidate. And this year, many of the key Senate races are within those narrow margins.

In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.

In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.

While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.

While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.

It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.

One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.

It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.

The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.

Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.

Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.

Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.

There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.

Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.

Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.

At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.

The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.

There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.

Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.

In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.

"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."

Fish pay attention to one influential neighbour in virtual reality

New Scientist November 01, 2026

A virtual reality tailored to fish reveals that each animal may be paying attention to only a single, most influential neighbour. This finding may shed light on how animals move as groups without becoming overwhelmed by all the activity and interactions around them.

Fish form schools, milling about seamlessly and acting as a collective. But how does a single fish know what to do? Guy Theraulaz at the University of Toulouse in France and his colleagues attempted to answer the question by using virtual reality (VR) to better study interactions between five rummy-nose tetra fish (Hemigrammus rhodostomus).

“A fish in a group can perceive, simultaneously, many, many individuals, but perception is not equivalent to influence,” he says. “Does a real fish use all this information at once, or does it just focus on a few neighbours?”

Advertisement

Swimming in a school may help fish hear dolphins’ ultrasound clicks

The researchers put a single tetra fish in a hemispherical bowl and tracked its swimming with a camera while projecting four virtual tetra fish onto the bowl’s interior in such a way that they appeared real to the tetra. The projections and the camera were connected into a feedback loop, allowing the virtual tetras to react and adjust to the real fish. Theraulaz says that he and his colleagues previously studied tetras in observational experiments and developed a mathematical model for how they might interact. The virtual reality setup allowed them to test that model.

Specifically, they tested three hypotheses: that a single fish would have the most influence on the real tetra’s behaviour; that two tetras would jointly be the most influential fish; and that the real tetra would pay attention to all four virtual fish. The team found clear evidence favouring the first case: as far as the real tetra was concerned, there was only one most influential fish at a time. This may be the case simply because it is easier on the fish, says Theraulaz. “By focusing on just one neighbour, the fish reduce their sensory and cognitive demand,” he says.

Researchers trained a hawk outfitted with microphones to fly through a swarm of 600,000 bats, revealing how they can hear their own voice in a crowd

Iain Couzin at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany says that the new study confirms past ideas about tetra behaviour, which were largely pioneered by Theraulaz and his colleagues. It also underscores how powerful VR could be for eventually getting into the heads of animals as they make decisions, he says.

Studies of collective animal behaviour are difficult to perform because an individual animal in a group can’t be isolated without disturbing group behaviours that the researchers want to study, which makes it tricky to test specific hypotheses. But making some animals virtual and fully under researchers’ control sidesteps this problem. Overall, VR leads to endless opportunities for experimenting, says Guy Amichay at Northwestern University in Illinois.“You could technically design any virtual world you want,” he says. Couzin says that it would be exciting to apply the new method to other species of fish for whom no mathematical models exist.

Theraulaz and his colleagues now want to advance their experiment by making some of the virtual fish act stressed, as if they were facing a predator, and then see whether this would affect the real tetra through their interactions.

The best new science-fiction novels of November 2026

New Scientist November 01, 2026

I am currently deeply engrossed in the November read for the New Scientist Book Club, a piece of classic science fiction (well, from 2012) from Chris Beckett, Dark Eden. But I’m also in the mood for some fresh writing, and the new sci-fi on offer this month is an exciting and eclectic range. I’m keen to check out Benjamin Percy’s audio drama Exoplanet, produced by none other than Andy Weir, as well as books from some old favourites: Michael Moorcock, Carole Hailey, John Scalzi and Andrew Hunter Murray. And for all those still in the mood for scares after Halloween, there’s some space horror from SA Barnes in the deliciously named Cold Eternity.

The best new science-fiction books of October 2026

This is something a little different – produced by Andy Weir, author of The Martian and Project Hail Mary, and written by Benjamin Percy, this sci-fi thriller is a full-cast audio drama from Audible, and it sounds really exciting. It follows the fallout when a quantum anomaly tears a starship apart, leaving its crew in different eras on the same deadly exoplanet – one in a machine-ruled future, for example, another in a past peopled by hostile aliens. I’m a recent (only this year) audiobook adopter, and this sounds right up my street.

I really enjoyed Andrew Hunter Murray’s speculative novel The Last Day, in which the world stops turning, leaving half the planet in scorching sunlight and the other half permanently dark. This latest book sounds equally interesting. A young woman, Esme, escapes her dull job by taking tiny potions known as The Elsewheres, which allow her to visit alternate versions of herself. But then an “incident” turns her into the most important person in this, or possibly any, universe. How will she handle it?

Advertisement

Sci-fi legend John Scalzi’s latest speculative adventure has a Lovecraftian tinge, as the locals in Richland, Ohio, take offence to the actions of a predatory private-equity firm – and develop some unexpected tentacles. The local police chief, and former resident Mike, get entangled in what’s going on and in events that are likely to change humanity forever.

I always appreciate a good “asteroid hitting Earth” story (my recent-ish reads include Larry Niven and Jerry Pournelle’s Lucifer’s Hammer, a classic from 1977, and Not With A Bang by Temi Oh, a twist on the tale). Carole Hailey’s previous book, The Silence Project, was great, so I’m looking forward to her take on this story. It follows Cassie, who grew up with a father obsessed with an impending apocalypse. Now she’s middle-aged and discovers that his teachings might have some use after all when an asteroid is found in the solar system, heading for northern Europe.

There aren’t many names in science fiction and fantasy bigger than Michael Moorcock, and this is the final part of his “fictional autobiography”. It sees, if I understand the blurb correctly, the author tell the story of both his real life (from the impact of his science fiction to the music of the sixties) and of a fantasy world only he can see (the example given: “the Carmelite Monks must protect their latest multiverse-spanning invention”). Intriguingly weird, as you’d expect from this wonderful writer – I’m keen to see how, as we’re promised, “Moorcock meets ‘Moorcock’ and together they produce a remedy for the world’s pain!”.

If I were SA Barnes, I would be pretty pleased with the moniker laid on me by my publisher: she is, apparently, “the queen of space horror”. In this latest, Halley Zwick (who is on the run) boards the spaceship Elysian Fields. This was sold to the super-rich as a place to enter cryo-sleep until their immortality could be assured, but it has been silent and dark for decades… although is it really?

Free newsletter

My colleague Gerardo loved previous instalments in this series, which follows a protagonist living the same day on repeat. Tara has now spent 12 years reliving 18 November, while her partner Thomas, to whom she has returned, repeats his own identical day. Tara sets off with her friends for a community where other time-stranded people have come together and begins to see a life beyond Thomas on the horizon.

This is a graphic novel in which four thieves travel to an abandoned colony planet (Bridge Planet Nine) with plans to rob one of the uncrewed freighter ships that land there. But it turns out this apparently deserted outpost isn’t as empty as they thought…

This speculative crime novel was shortlisted for the Icelandic Crime Book of the Year award. It’s set in Reykjavík in 2052, where an artificial intelligence manages society and ensures it is almost crime-free. Sabína discovers that her brother, a dissident who lives outside the controlling AI’s reach, has been murdered, and she begins investigating his final days. I’ve enjoyed Sigurdardóttir’s straight crime novels, so will definitely be exploring this one.

Ex-con Z is asked to help locate the tomb of Ikanto, which is hurtling through space towards a black hole. It’s a strange job offer – especially when it’s made by a floating brain in a jar. But Z is desperate and up for the challenge. This is an irreverent sort of caper, according to its publisher, and comparable to Guardians of the Galaxy – no bad thing in my eyes.

Humans have moved to virtual reality to escape a world that is falling apart, in the second dystopian novel in The Strangeloom Trilogy. We follow those working against megacorporation NileCorp to bring it down. Sounds like some cyberpunky, futuristic fun.

Allergic reactions after sex should be listed as an antibiotic risk, experts say

New Scientist October 31, 2026

Clinicians are calling for patient information leaflets to be updated after a woman had a life-threatening allergic reaction to an antibiotic in her partner’s semen. They also want healthcare workers to be made aware of such risks during their medical training.

“If you read any drug leaflet, they list a whole bunch of super-rare risks, so it’s not unreasonable to also include this risk on those leaflets to boost awareness,” says Cassim Akhoon at King’s College Hospital in London.

Slashing sugar intake before antibiotics may save your microbiome

The woman developed anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, due to probable exposure to the antibiotic amoxicillin via her partner’s semen. He took the drug to treat a sinus infection 6 hours before they had penetrative vaginal sex without a condom.

Advertisement

The partner of the woman asked his doctor whether it was safe for the couple to have unprotected sex because she had a history of allergic reactions to penicillins, a group of antibiotics, of which amoxicillin is one of the most commonly prescribed. “He was explicitly reassured by his doctor that she would not be at risk of allergic reactions,” says Akhoon, who is part of a team that examined the case after the event.

But 5 minutes after ejaculation, the woman developed symptoms of anaphylaxis. “Everything started to swell. I couldn’t breathe,” she told New Scientist. “Obviously, nearly dying is quite a terrifying experience.”

Free newsletter

The woman self-administered an EpiPen, a device that injects a shot of the hormone adrenaline into the body to halt anaphylaxis. Paramedics then arrived and treated her with further adrenaline. She was taken to hospital and was discharged 6 hours later.

The healthcare workers who treated her seemed to be unaware that exposure to amoxicillin via semen is possible, the woman says, and some of them assumed she must have taken the drug. “I wasn’t taught about this in medical school,” says Akhoon. “I definitely think we should make this part of formal medical training.”

About a year after the incident, Akhoon and his colleagues confirmed the woman’s allergy to amoxicillin via a skin test. This has led them to conclude that exposure via semen was the most likely cause. Around 1 per cent of people have allergies to penicillins, as confirmed via skin-prick tests, but anaphylaxis as a result of exposure to these drugs is extremely rare.

Antibiotics enter the bloodstream and can then reach the prostate and the seminal vesicles, a pair of pouch-like glands situated behind the bladder, which produce most of the fluid that makes up semen, says Akhoon. Prior studies have also found that amoxicillin is excreted in urine, suggesting it can persist in the urethra – a thin tube that transports urine and semen – until it is flushed out during ejaculation, he says.

Neisseria gonorrhoeae, the microbe responsible for gonorrhoea, is developing resistance to most antibiotics, which means we need new drugs to treat the condition. An antibiotic called zoliflodacin might be part of a solution

Earlier case reports have described similar incidences, with one woman developing anaphylaxis after exposure to amoxicillin during oral sex. The team thinks the evidence that such transmission routes are a risk is strong enough to list it on the patient information leaflets provided alongside medications.

Amoxicillin’s leaflet already lists a rare side effect called aseptic meningitis, says Akhoon, which occurs when tissue around the brain and spinal cord become inflamed. “We don’t have any mechanistic proof that amoxicillin was absolutely, definitely the cause [of related meningitis cases], yet because of [the] high likelihood of causality, it’s mentioned on the leaflet.”

There isn’t sufficient evidence to list a risk of transmission via semen for other antibiotics or drugs, but this may emerge in future case reports, says Ahkoon. “As people consider this route of transmission more, we might start to get a bigger collection of cases to determine which drug classes are implicated.” There is also no evidence that transfer of antibiotics via vaginal fluid could lead to allergic reactions in sexual partners, he says.

As the world warms, antibiotic-resistant bacteria are escaping from frozen sediments. But with new monitoring tools, we can identify problem genes and develop treatments before our pathogens acquire them

The team has submitted the findings to the UK’s Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency, which will decide whether updates to amoxicillin leaflets are needed. It couldn’t respond to a request for comment before this article was published.

Once informed, “people can then wear condoms or avoid sex until the antibiotics course is over”, says Patrick Yong at Frimley Park Hospital in Surrey, UK, who also examined the case.

Consultant allergist Chris Rutkowski in London thinks the most effective way of avoiding such transmissions is for the risk to taught during medical training. “Not because it’s common, but because the cost of missing it is high,” he says.

BMJ Case Reports DOI: 10.1136/bcr-2025-271777

Dinosaur red blood cells recovered from 115-million-year-old fossil

New Scientist November 02, 2026

A nondescript 115-million-year-old fragment of leg bone has yielded spectacularly preserved red blood cells, which may be the earliest ever found in dinosaurs.

Red blood cells have previously been found in dinosaur remains, including 75-million-year-old bone fragments collected in Canada in 2015 and the femur of a Tyrannosaurus rex that died 68 million years ago, found in Montana in 2005.

Exquisite 66-million-year-old bird feather preserved in dinosaur dropping

Now, Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Perth, Australia, and her colleagues say they have isolated the oldest-ever dinosaur red blood cells from the hind-limb of a theropod dinosaur, Aratasaurus museunacionali, found in Brazil in 2008.

Advertisement

The Aratasaurus individual studied by the team wasn’t yet fully grown, with an estimated body length of just over 3 metres, and weighed about 34 kilograms.

“The fossils we worked on are not display specimens by any means, so they don’t look very interesting,” says Grice. “If you look at them, you think there’s just a bunch of bones and there’s probably not much in there.”

However, when she etched out part of the fossils, using hydrochloric acid to dissolve surrounding rock, she was shocked at what she saw.

“I was jumping up and down,” says Grice. “I ran up to my head of school’s office and was so excited that he gave me a whisky to calm me down. No one has ever seen dinosaur red blood cells in high resolution before.”

The cells she found were abundant: in a single slide, just a fifth of a millimetre wide, there were 20 blood cells. All of the cells were within fossilised blood vessels, providing further evidence that they really were red blood cells.

Liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry analysis revealed the presence of haem B, a constituent of haemoglobin that binds to oxygen, adding molecular evidence of the type of cell.

The team also had to rule out the possibility of any contamination, especially from the sediments in which the fossil was preserved, which were dominated by algae.

The cells found outside the bone were dominated by chlorophyll-derived compounds, whereas those inside contained haem-derived molecules, which strongly suggests that the latter cells weren’t a result of contamination.

The researchers also compared the blood cells to those of the closest living relatives of the dinosaur fossil, birds and crocodiles. The Aratasaurus red blood cells are significantly larger. This could indicate that the cells swelled during fossilisation, or that the species grew much bigger than the fossilised specimen.

Grice says the discovery may mean that other nondescript dinosaur fossils that have been locked away in museum collections may hold profound secrets. “There’s drawers and drawers of fossil material, which don’t look very nice,” she says. “This kind of work opens up a whole new opportunity to unlock those collections and bring modern technology and molecular techniques to these specimens.”

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2614248123

Zapping part of the brain makes you think harder – at a cost

New Scientist November 02, 2026

Struggling with a difficult mental task? Zapping the brain region linked to our motivation to make a mental effort might help – for a while. People who had this part of their brain stimulated by electrical currents excelled at a difficult task, but also became more mentally fatigued afterwards.

“Their performance is much better; however, this good performance comes with lower motivation in the end,” says Hongmei Xia at the University of Munich, Germany.

Your brain’s unexpected ability to regenerate and how to harness it

Xia and her colleagues put electrodes on the heads of 31 volunteers with no known health conditions. During a half-hour session in an MRI scanner, the volunteers spent 20 minutes doing the 3-back memory test, where you have to remember and identify the third item back as an ongoing sequence is presented to you – a very demanding mental task. They were then offered €1 for doing an easy test or €2 for a harder one.

Advertisement

During the 3-back memory test, the electrodes delivered transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to a region of the brain called the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to randomly chosen volunteers, who were unaware they were receiving it.

Other studies have shown the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex is involved in controlling the cognitive effort we make. “Our dorsolateral prefrontal cortex helps us to work hard,” says Xia.

The volunteers who had tDCS reacted faster and more accurately than those who didn’t receive this stimulation. For instance, their average reaction time was 0.98 seconds, compared with 1.12 seconds with sham stimulation.

Free newsletter

Xia thinks stimulating the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex will boost brain performance generally. “I can imagine any cognitive task will be better, but afterwards you will feel more fatigued,” she says.

After the tests, the volunteers who got tDCS had higher levels of the neurotransmitter glutamate in their dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, according to a non-invasive technique called magnetic resonance spectroscopy. The higher their glutamate levels, the more likely they were to choose the €1 task over the €2 one.

Some researchers think mental fatigue is a result of the buildup of glutamate, which can harm cells at high levels. Xia thinks her team’s findings are the strongest evidence of this yet. The findings suggest it is important to take a break when you feel mentally tired, she says.

Xia thinks future studies should also look at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in people with conditions such as depression, which can affect motivation.

We often think that our ability to be curious stems from our complex, human brain – but what if curiosity shapes that complexity?

“I think the claim that the stimulation made people ‘work harder’ is well substantiated,” says neuroscientist Emile Radyte at Samphire Neuroscience, a UK-based company exploring the use of tDCS to treat conditions such as premenstrual syndrome. But the study doesn’t prove that higher glutamate levels were the cause of the greater mental fatigue, she says.

Radyte says her trials have shown that if productivity is hindered by conditions such as premenstrual syndrome, applying tDCS over the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex can restore it. But she isn’t sure about using it to boost mental performance. “A 20-minute laboratory task does not establish a net productivity benefit over a working day,” says Radyte.

It is a good study, says Nilli Lavie at University College London, but the greater mental fatigue could be a result of using more neural energy, rather than the buildup of glutamate. It’s also hard to precisely target the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex with tDCS without an MRI scanner to guide you, says Lavie. “Drink coffee instead,” she says.

PNAS DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2534136123

We are finally pinning down what makes dyslexic brains different

New Scientist November 02, 2026

I used to be stupid. It was a long time ago and I was very young – too young to question teachers who said I was a bit dim. Besides, wasn’t there proof? I had been slow to learn to read, my spelling was atrocious and my aptitude for climbing trees wasn’t fooling anyone. So, I believed them. Then, aged 7, everything changed. For the first time, I had a teacher who saw beyond my literary ineptitude. She told me I was smart – and, suddenly, I was. Thank you, Mrs Kennedy!

That was more than 50 years ago. Back then, dyslexia already had a long history, but news of it hadn’t reached the classroom – at least none I found myself in. Children like me usually weren’t given a diagnosis or special help. Far from it. At the convent school I attended next, spelling tests were a ritual humiliation, where the nuns lined us up against a wall in the order of our results and shamed those who failed to perform.

Things have changed since then. Teachers are fully aware of dyslexia. Children with this, the most common of learning disabilities, are no longer labelled “stupid” or “lazy”. Huge volumes of research have been published. Yet, fierce disagreements have also raged about what causes dyslexia and how best to diagnose and treat it.

Advertisement

Now, finally, we are pinning down what makes dyslexic brains different. We may even have found the key neural pathway that drives the condition. Better yet, this research is pointing to novel, practical and fairer ways to help all children who struggle to read.

What if the idea of the autism spectrum is completely wrong?

Humans invented writing around 5000 years ago – far too recently to have evolved an adaptation for deciphering the written word. Besides, for most of our history, the vast majority of humanity has been illiterate. So, when we learn to read, our brains must co-opt areas specialised for other functions. That this isn’t straightforward for everyone has long been recognised. The word dyslexia (from the Greek for “disordered words”) was coined in 1883 to describe a curious condition in which experiencing a stroke had left a person unable to read or spell. But, within a few years, it was being used for a far larger group – children who find it hard to acquire these skills.

Developmental dyslexia is often described as a significant and persistent difficulty with reading and spelling. Traditionally, the definition has also included the idea that these difficulties are unexpected given the child’s other cognitive abilities – although the recently updated definition issued by the International Dyslexia Association has finally dropped this controversial “discrepancy” idea. We know that both genes and environment play a role, that dyslexia is a spectrum and that it can manifest in different ways, such as spelling difficulties (a particular problem in alphabetic language systems), slow reading and writing speeds, or both.

All this makes its prevalence hard to quantify. Most estimates put it at around 10 per cent of people globally; some say twice that. What’s more certain is that dyslexia is a universal human condition found in all languages and writing systems.

Reading is cognitively complicated. It entails three key components: understanding how sounds relate to squiggles on a page (phonology); mastering the patterns of written words and the rules of spelling (orthography); and making sense of what you see (semantics). To do this, your brain recruits networks evolved to process vision and speech and links them into a new “reading circuit”. This is located primarily in the brain’s left hemisphere and also comprises three main components. The occipitotemporal region, located low in the back of the brain, instantly recognises those squiggles as words, hence its common name: the “visual word form area”. Word shapes are matched to sounds in the temporoparietal junction, above and behind your left ear. And further forward, the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca’s area) handles speech production and meaning.

The underlying circuitry is the same, regardless of the language or script – even for writing systems that don’t look anything alike, such as those for English and Chinese.

Clearly, there is a lot that can go wrong, not just in the reading circuit, but in other aspects of reading such as attention, memory, processing speed, logical thinking and knowledge of vocabulary. So perhaps it shouldn’t surprise us that, over the years, researchers have come up with a wide range of ideas to explain the condition.

One of the most prominent is the phonological deficit theory, which asserts that the problem lies in poor awareness of speech sounds and difficulty relating these to written symbols. “This is now considered to be a primary deficit,” says Maggie Snowling, a psychologist at the University of Oxford who has long been a proponent of the idea. Phonological deficit and a second problem known as rapid automatised naming (RAN) – slowness in identifying letters, numbers and even pictures – constitute the “double-deficit hypothesis”.

A long-overlooked writing system from 5000 years ago is still largely undeciphered, but could mark the moment humans first represented their speech with written words

Then there are explanations that focus on the brain itself. Temporal processing theory, for instance, points to an underlying problem of timing in the way the auditory system processes sounds, which has profound knock-on effects for reading and writing. The magnocellular hypothesis, in contrast, places an emphasis on visual attention. It stems from findings that magnocellular neurons, which process fast-moving visual information, are less active and less numerous in people with dyslexia.

In short, decades of research have generated plenty of ideas, but not much consensus. A major roadblock has been that studies were small and not easily compared. This is now being addressed thanks to the availability of large-scale longitudinal datasets and improved methods. That may not sound dramatic, but it has been a game changer.

Take genetics. Clearly, dyslexia runs in families: I have my father to thank for mine. “The heritability you see in twin studies is about 70 per cent,” says Michelle Luciano, who studies behavioural genetics at the University of Edinburgh in the UK. That’s massive – but comes with a big caveat. “It’s not just the genes; it’s the gene-environment correlation that’s really important,” says Snowling. The idea is that factors such as low birth weight and whether literacy is encouraged at home play a key part in shaping the chances of developing dyslexia in those with a genetic susceptibility.

There is also no single dyslexia gene – many tiny genetic changes interact to generate the condition in all its guises. And tracking them down is fiendishly difficult. Traditional methods of genetic analysis identified several “candidate” genes that people with dyslexia appear to share. Now, geneticists can scan full genomes looking for variants linked with complex traits – and do this at scale. The first such genome-wide association study (GWAS) on dyslexia was published in 2022.

Using information from the 23andMe genetic database, a team led by Luciano analysed the genomes of 51,800 people with a dyslexia diagnosis and over 1 million controls. This revealed something surprising about those previously identified candidate genes. “A lot of these actually haven’t turned out to be that important,” says Luciano. The analysis did, however, identify 42 genetic variants linked with a risk of dyslexia. “Many of these genes had already been reported as being associated with either general cognitive ability or educational attainment,” she says. “But we also found several novel ones that may be more specific to language and reading.”

We’re finally pinning down the mechanisms that drive obsessive-compulsive disorder, revealing a complex combination of imbalanced brain networks, the immune system and even gut microbes

The study highlights the genetic complexity of dyslexia. It also confirms observed links with some neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD – but not others. “For autism, for instance, we found no genetic overlap,” says Luciano. She and her colleagues have since worked on an even larger dataset of more than 1.2 million people, identifying a further 13 genes related to dyslexia that implicate early brain developmental processes in the biological underpinning of reading. “Genetic studies give us a possibility to bridge the gap between cognitive theories and neuroscience,” she says.

In fact, these genetic findings have already provided a springboard for a giant leap in revealing the neuroanatomy of dyslexia. A team led by Clyde Francks at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, used them to calculate the genetic predisposition to dyslexia of 35,231 people in the UK Biobank database. They then identified brain regions that differed in people whose genes put them at risk of dyslexia. (I must now declare an interest: I have been in the UK Biobank project from the start, done all the tests and had my genome sequenced and my brain scanned, so one of those 35,231 people is me.)

Francks and his colleagues found that the genetic risk of dyslexia was associated with widespread reduction in brain volume compared with people not at genetic risk, especially in language-related and motor areas. (Yikes!) Again, there were correlations with ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions – although reductions in the motor cortex were specifically linked with dyslexia. That might seem strange, but motor control could affect reading in a variety of ways, says Francks. “For example, infants with better motor skills might be able to learn language-related skills more quickly through better coordination when producing speech sounds, pointing to track letters and words or keeping time during chants and songs.”

Meanwhile, earlier this year, another impressive large-scale study finally nailed a long-standing debate in the field over the contribution of visual difficulties, not just phonological ones, to reading problems. “We and others have long held the view that dyslexia is quite heterogenous, and phonological problems are only one part of the story,” says Jason Yeatman, who specialises in the neurobiology of reading at Stanford University.

He and his colleagues carried out tests on 400 children in kindergarten and first grade (typically aged 5-7) at California schools, measuring how quickly they processed visual information such as identifying the direction of dots moving on a computer screen. This revealed that around 15 per cent of the children had problems with visual-spatial attention, and these were associated with reading difficulties a year later. “These kids aren’t picked up by any of the conventional screening processes,” says Yeatman. What’s more, the research identified a hidden subgroup whose weak visual processing was masked by strong phonological skills.

But for many people with dyslexia, the primary problem is with phonology and, over the years, researchers have pinpointed a key neurological mechanism underlying these difficulties. It boils down to the way the brain processes the rhythm patterns of speech, in particular the rates of change in loudness that mark the beginning of syllables – a cue that the brain uses to make sense of the stream of information it receives by chunking it into meaningful units. This is the basis of the temporal sampling theory devised by Usha Goswami at the University of Cambridge, which combines phonology with what is happening in the brain.

Neurons in the brain fire automatically in response to these sounds, which can be measured using EEG to visualise the brainwaves in the auditory cortex – even in infants who are just learning to speak. “You can think of word representations in the brain almost like auditory objects, like 3D mountains,” says Goswami. However, she and her colleagues have found that children with dyslexia have a subtle mismatch between speech sounds and these mental representations due to problems discerning rhythm and pitch, especially at low frequencies.

This doesn’t cause obvious issues with speech, but can have a profound impact on reading and writing, because these skills utilise speech-processing pathways to decode written words. “This really only hits when a child is learning to read,” says Goswami. “The whole shape of the mountain range will be a bit different, but they’re trying to learn to read and spell in a system made for children with another type of mountain range.”

For instance, a 2024 study by Goswami and her colleagues of more than 100 English-speaking children in Australia and the UK used EEG to measure their brain responses to speech, and found that issues with temporal sampling were strongly associated with dyslexia. What’s more, this technique could be used as the basis of a ‘classifier’ tool to identify children with the condition. “If we randomly select one child with dyslexia and one without dyslexia, the classifier has a 77 per cent chance of correctly identifying which child is more likely to have dyslexia, based on their brain responses to speech,” says auditory neuroscientist Mahmoud Keshavarzi at the University of Cambridge.

Indeed, Goswami thinks that difficulties with temporal sampling are the primary cause of dyslexia, and that the other problems associated with the condition arise during a child’s development. However, other researchers think that the condition is too heterogeneous to be driven by a single underlying factor. “The more recently accepted understanding is that dyslexia is a consequence of multiple biological and environmental risk factors,” says Julian Elliott at Durham University, UK, who researches dyslexia in children.

Still, there is clear evidence that boosting the ability of young children to process rhythms can improve their language skills – as demonstrated in a study by Goswami and her colleagues involving 120 children under the age of 11, which added activities such as drumming, chanting and marching to a beat into their classrooms. “These all help stamp in the rhythmic patterns which are so fundamental,” she says.

The team is also developing technologies specifically to help those with dyslexia. “We’ve found a neural characteristic called the theta-delta ratio, which is too high in children with dyslexia when they’re listening to natural speech,” says Goswami. One intervention allows children to visualise what is happening in their brain while listening to a story, via the movement of a little spaceship on a screen. “When they’re keeping the spaceship up, it means they’ve reduced their theta-delta ratio,” she says. This feedback leads to improvements in phonology and reading.

Fewer people are reading for pleasure, but getting lost in a good book has repeatedly been linked to substantial cognitive benefits

She isn’t alone in believing we can do more to help children who struggle with reading and spelling. Decades of tinkering make it clear that the key is a focus on phonics – specifically, training on phonemes, letters and single-sound associations, says Snowling. “But it’s also not everything,” says Yeatman. In addition, young readers require help tailored to their particular needs. For those with visual-processing problems, there is no reliable evidence that coloured lenses or special fonts work. But Yeatman’s team has found that this subset of children read faster when the spacing between letters is increased. He also thinks there is potential to train the visual system to work better through specially designed computer games. “This area is ripe for investigation,” he says.

Perhaps the biggest thing we can do is identify dyslexia early, as evidence shows that intensive interventions have significant effects on struggling readers, with the greatest influence if these are implemented in a child’s early school years. “I think it’s incredibly important,” says Snowling.

Another much-debated area is the best way to test for dyslexia. Assessments typically entail detailed tests, including whether there was a discrepancy between general level of cognitive ability and reading and writing attainment. However, the updated guidelines issued by the International Dyslexia Association have dropped this criterion, not least because it is biased against children from lower socioeconomic groups and those learning to read in a second language.

People with ADHD are unusually sensitive to hormone shifts. Psychiatrists have started to pay attention, creating strategies to address the intense emotions and cognitive challenges caused by these changes

Elliott thinks there is further to go. For years he has been arguing that the terms “dyslexia” be replaced by “reading disability”, so that all children who need help get it. “There are no clear criteria that would enable an assessor to make a determination between a poor reader who gets a dyslexia diagnosis and one who doesn’t,” he says. “Neither is there any intervention suitable for a diagnosed reader that is not equally valuable for any other struggling reader.” His view is controversial, but perhaps that’s not surprising. “It threatens vested interests – a dyslexia industry that is worth billions of dollars,” he says.

There are undoubtedly still problems, but progress is being made. “I’m an optimist,” says Yeatman. Me, too. After all, my (admittedly mild) dyslexia hasn’t held me back as a journalist. Today, I have my spellchecker, and eagle-eyed subeditors to pick me up on more subtle slips like “wonton destruction”, which I once used in a quote from an ecologist (and, yes, he was Chinese). But I do think there is still a stigma associated with dyslexia. Otherwise, why would 85 per cent of people diagnosed with the condition not reveal this to their employer?

Times have changed, and so should attitudes. So, I’m admitting it here for the first time in my career: My name is Kate Douglas, and I am dyslexic.
