COP31: Will this year’s climate summit be the most underwhelming ever?

New Scientist November 02, 2026

The Mediterranean beachside haven of Antalya in Turkey is more used to hosting well-fed tourists than stressed climate negotiators. But for two weeks starting on 9 November, the city will become the climate change capital of the world, welcoming tens of thousands of delegates to the UN COP31 summit.

COP31 is the latest instalment of the annual climate summits where countries come together with the aim of tackling climate change. The meetings were responsible for ushering in the Paris Agreement in 2015, the climate treaty under which nations have promised to hold warming to “well below” 2°C and as close to 1.5°C as possible.

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

But in recent years, the summits have had a less impressive track record. Critics argue the meetings are no longer fit for purpose, undermined by the need for unanimous consensus in all decisions and struggling to find direction now that the work of agreeing a legal climate treaty is completed.

Advertisement

Delegates left last year’s COP30 summit in Belém, Brazil, having agreed the bare minimum – that they remain united behind the Paris Agreement. But after a fortnight of tortuous negotiations, they were unable to agree on fresh commitments to move away from fossil fuel use or end deforestation.

And although the world is now on course for lower levels of warming than looked likely before the Paris Agreement was struck, global emissions are still not falling and the world is on track for 2.8°C of warming by the end of the century – nowhere near the goals laid out under Paris.

Free newsletter

So can this upcoming summit, COP31, change the game?

This year’s brutal weather should provide plenty of motivation. From devastating glacier collapses to severe heatwaves and raging wildfires, there has been no shortage of reminders that planet Earth is teetering on the brink of crisis. And that all came ahead of a super-sized El Niño now under way in the Pacific, a timely demonstration of what warming beyond 1.5°C will feel like in the real world – hot and dangerous, in short.

But don’t expect fireworks from this COP. So far, the mood music from the hosts – a joint gig between Turkey and Australia – is setting the tone for a business-as-usual summit.

As with recent summits, there’s no big declaration or new treaty pegged for Antalya. Instead, the main task negotiators face will be to grapple with a series of hangover decisions from Belém.

At COP30, countries agreed to create a “just transition mechanism”, which has alternatively been described as a “platform”, a “hub” and a “work programme”. The idea is to provide a support structure for those affected by the shift to a cleaner economy. For example, countries need to work out how best to support and retrain workers in the fossil fuel economy as energy grids transition to cleaner fuels. But the process of identifying how this just transition mechanism will work in practice has barely begun.

Nations also agreed to triple adaptation finance for lower-income countries – in short, helping them cope with the impacts of climate change – by 2035. But the commitment was vague, with no baseline year and no agreement on who should contribute or what types of finance would count. Delegates in Antalya will continue to hammer out the details.

“These are all big, kind of chunky areas where you know there will be strong expectation from developing countries and civil society that there is progress made,” says Gareth Redmond-King at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a UK climate and energy think tank.

One of the biggest disappointments from COP30 was that countries failed to commit to developing “road maps” away from fossil fuels. This would involve drawing up plans for moving their economies away from oil, gas and coal use. Although the idea had backing from more than 80 nations in Brazil, the final text from the summit failed to mention fossil fuels at all.

Countries that still backed the idea gathered in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April this year and jointly promised to draw up transition plans. However, to date, only France has produced anything like a fully fledged road map away from fossil fuels. Some countries are expected to announce their road maps on the sidelines of COP31, but it is unclear whether any major fossil fuel economies will come forward.

And despite a global oil crisis triggered by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz that makes the case for clean energy ever more obvious, it is unlikely the road map idea will make it into the formal COP agenda this year.

Europe faces incredibly harsh winters and unrelenting droughts if the vital AMOC ocean current fails – but when disaster will strike and how bad it will be remains uncertain. Now there is an ambitious plan to give us a warning

Instead, the summit’s hosts are pushing electrification as a route away from fossil fuels. The more you can electrify cars, home heating and the like, the faster the clean transition, the thinking goes. Turkey has launched a new “electrification target” that would see countries commit to electrifying 35 per cent of their annual energy consumption by 2035, up from the current rate of about 23 per cent.

We don’t yet know whether this would be a voluntary pledge countries would sign up to, or something that the hosts will push to be universally agreed under the main negotiations. Questions also remain over whether the target will include any directive for countries to decarbonise their power grids. Turkey and Australia “are talking about electrification in isolation, [and] rarely talking about electrification linked to ramping up renewables and decarbonising”, says Redmond-King.

Meanwhile, there are some serious headwinds facing the summit. In the face of rising fuel prices triggered by the Russia-Ukraine war and the US-Iran conflict, wealthy nations are tightening their belts. International aid has been cut significantly from many national budgets, including in the UK, where spending is set to fall by £6.5 billion to a historical low in 2027/2028. That leaves less money for funding climate action in lower-income countries, who in turn say they can’t take action to cut emissions without more cash. Arguments over funding risk souring the atmosphere of the summit.

Then there’s the awkward issue of the hosts. Both Turkey and Australia wanted to host COP31 and neither would back down, so the UN awarded them joint hosting responsibilities. Turkey is responsible for the location and logistics, as well as the so-called Action Agenda, which includes the pledges, commitments and announcements outside of the negotiations. Australia, meanwhile, will run the formal talks. But running a successful COP is a major challenge even for one country. With two countries in charge, there’s a real risk of things drifting into confusion and infighting. Questions over their commitment to the cause linger over both countries, who have each been slow to embrace the energy transition and still rely heavily on fossil fuels.

There has been a sudden increase in the rate of sea level rise

But there are a few spots of hope too. In Brazil, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a historic fourth term as president last month, defying expectations to beat right-wing populist candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Lula’s victory means Brazil’s delegation will be in Turkey pushing for more progress on deforestation and fossil fuel transition road maps.

Meanwhile, Democrats may take control of the US Congress in midterm elections on 3 November, just before COP31 kicks off. A win for the Democrats in both houses could lead to renewed incentives for clean energy development and electric vehicles.

The US withdrew from both the Paris Agreement and the UN climate convention after Donald Trump took office in 2025, a move that has substantially worsened warming projections for 2100. Any sense that the US is returning to climate action will bolster morale among delegates.

In the formal negotiations track, there will be further talks on how the different “implementation” programmes on cutting emissions and ensuring a fair transition will work in practice. But these are unlikely to produce any big headlines.

“What we are going to see… in Antalya are many very important discussions, but they are less grand, big decisions,” Ana Toni, executive director of COP30, told journalists on a briefing call on 22 October.

A cover decision, which can summarise key decisions or include new pledges, could offer the opportunity for nations to present a new headline-grabbing commitment. Australia and Turkey have said ahead of the summit that they will work on developing a cover text, which could acknowledge the inevitability that the world will overshoot 1.5°C of warming and call on countries to go faster on cutting emissions.

Negotiations over the wording of the cover decisions often provide the dramatic finale for a COP summit. But it can become a trap for ministers running the event, says Paul Watkinson, a highly experienced climate negotiator who has led both the French and European Union delegations at COPs.

Ministerial teams come into a COP thinking, “how do I get a result that doesn’t look dreadful?” says Watkinson. “Particularly the ministers in charge; they want to get a boost to their career, and the country wants to say it’s done something important for the world.” It means COPs often end up “focused on yet another decision where we change the adverb”, he says.

Cutting back on our use of energy and materials so that we live within Earth’s means can seem like an insurmountable challenge. But after a decade grappling with these problems, a historic Portuguese city is beginning to walk this tightrope

Watkinson wants to see COP summits focus much less on headlines generated by cover texts, and more on the backroom work to get countries to collaborate and communicate with each other. “If we seek the big decision each year, we’re using a huge amount of energy to get it, and we’re not focusing on the real challenge, which is how do we overcome the barriers that are holding us back,” he says.

That might mean changing the process to focus less on a consensus outcome with all parties, with action instead delivered by smaller groups of willing participants who work together to concentrate on delivering emissions cuts, he says.

It looks likely that the Antalya summit, despite its postcard-worthy setting, will be an unglamourous mix of long nights and bitter quarrels, reluctant compromises and underwhelming outcomes.

But for meeting insiders, the hope is that change will come in time for COP33 in two years’ time, when countries are due to conclude a global assessment of their progress to decarbonisation. The pressure will be even greater on that COP to deliver a meaningful response to the stocktake’s findings. The question is, can these summits reinvent themselves in time? As Watkinson puts it: “Practically everybody I speak to says, of course, we need to change it. We can’t carry on as we do.”

Curiosity may be what drives our brains to become so complex

New Scientist November 02, 2026

How did our brains evolve to be so complex? The answer may boil down to curiosity. Researchers who trained thousands of artificial neural networks with different learning styles found that the most curious ones not only had more sophisticated and flexible cognitive abilities, they also spontaneously organised into structures that resemble human brains.

The networks formed interconnected modules and followed a human-like developmental trajectory, for example, with dense neural connections forming early on before being pruned away. Curiosity is usually seen as a consequence of having a complex brain, says Francesco Poli at the University of Cambridge. “What if it’s actually helping to shape how the brain is?”

How curiosity can supercharge your brain and boost your success

To model how infants learn, Poli and his colleagues collected eye-tracking data from 275 babies who were between 8 and 15 months old. The infants were shown sequences of colourful shapes on a screen, which provided varying amounts of information about where the next shape was likely to be displayed. “The positions weren’t random, and every different shape had a sequence that could be learned,” says Poli.

Advertisement

The babies proved to be highly sensitive to how much information the different stimuli provided. Whenever their rate of learning dropped below average, they disengaged and looked for something new, says Poli.

The team used this principle to design artificial neural networks with different levels of intrinsic curiosity, then trained them on 20 tasks. The high-curiosity models were designed to immediately switch task if their rate of learning dropped below a certain threshold, whereas the low-curiosity models switched randomly.

All the networks, curious or not, became experts at the tasks they were trained on. But after the training, the curious models performed significantly better at tests they hadn’t seen before. This ability to put together different things in flexible ways is seen as a hallmark of complex human cognition, says Poli.

Free newsletter

The curious models also developed physical characteristics resembling those of complex brains. The researchers embedded the artificial networks into a virtual three-dimensional space, modelled on the anatomy of the human brain. They then forced the networks to wire themselves efficiently by penalising long-distance connections, in order to mimic the cost of long-range wiring in real brains.

On its own, this wasn’t enough to produce complexity, but when the researchers added curiosity on top, a range of brain-like features emerged. For example, the curious networks developed a hierarchical “modular” structure with highly-interconnected areas that were in turn connected to each other.

Poli was also surprised to see a particular trajectory in the curious networks: the density of their connections rose, then fell. “I thought that was weird,” he says.

But this is similar to what happens in human brains, says Poli, where the number of synapses – the junctions through which neurons communicate – rises steeply during the first year of life, followed by a pruning phase where unhelpful connections are lost. He speculates that curiosity, the drive to seek out tasks that yield the most information, could be “related to this selection process of what to keep and what not to keep”.

The controversial discovery that our brains can generate new neurons surprisingly late in life is now prompting a rethink of adult brain health, pointing the way to better treatments for stroke, dementia and depression

To estimate a biological age for each network, the researchers mapped the rise and fall of the neural networks’ densities against a typical human profile. They found that the most curious, human-like ones were at a more mature phase in the developmental arc, with an age of around 20 years, whereas those that didn’t have the combination of curiosity and the correct wiring were stuck at an earlier point, with an age of around 9 years.

It is unsurprising that curiosity makes learning more efficient, says Alireza Modirshanechi at the University of Göttingen in Germany, because it ensures we don’t waste time on tasks that are too easy or too hard. “You try to learn those that are most learnable,” he says.

But the finding that this enables the emergence of human-like brain architecture is “very surprising”, says Modirshanechi. “If true, it’s a very strong claim.” He says it will be important to check that the non-curious networks don’t eventually develop similar characteristics, albeit more slowly, if they are given enough training time.

Poli argues that the non-curious networks performed just as well as the curious ones on the basic training tasks, so their lack of complex cognition and brain-like features probably isn’t simply a question of learning slower. “I think that, even with more training time, they would have stayed pretty much the same,” he says. “Curiosity really changed how the networks learned.”

Dedicating time and money to inquire about aspects of our physiology that appear to serve little purpose might seem a little strange, but it turns out to be a great route to breakthroughs in biology

Regardless, Poli says the findings emphasise the role of curiosity in education. Environments that force children to do one particular activity for a length of time “might be counterproductive, especially early on”, he says. “It depends on what we want. If we value the ability to stay still and work on one thing for a long amount of time, then we have to train that in kids.” Whereas if we value curiosity and cognition, we may need to prioritise giving children a choice of activities, “then letting them free within the space”, he says.

The results also feed into debates around the development of flexible, human-like artificial intelligence. The vast majority of AI research “is just building bigger systems”, says Poli, that consume ever-greater data and resources. He argues that, for complex cognition, it might be fruitful to build curious AIs that learn more like people. The fact that evolution doesn’t have endless resources can be what drives clever solutions, he says. “Sometimes, these constraints are also what help us to excel.”

Modirshanechi isn’t convinced that AI developers should necessarily switch tack. Large language models such as ChatGPT show that scaling works, he says. But incorporating principles of curiosity might lead to more human-compatible systems, he says, for example models that would ask enough questions to figure out users’ intentions before providing lengthy answers.

The best new popular-science books of November 2026

New Scientist November 02, 2026

As seasonal storms take many of us by surprise, it’s time to head for the certainty of indoors, and a decent book (or two). We have some really intriguing titles this month, including a profoundly odd-sounding book by a forest that shares author rights with humans, and some terrifying night terrors that may teach us a lot about our brains. Oh, and if you want to stop trying to control everything around you, try surrendering to a higher power – of your choice, naturally.

In a complex world, the pressure to control your life is immense: from removing annoying noises around you to slavishly avoiding missing out on living your best life, to keeping your relationship, children and health on track in every way imaginable. It’s overwhelming. Surely we can’t keep it up? According to Anna Lembke’s new book, Radical Surrender: Letting go in a world addicted to change, there is a way out. The word ”addicted” in the subtitle offers a clue here: this is the author of the bestselling book Dopamine Nation, in which she looked at pleasure and pain – and the critical task of finding a delicate balance between them, especially in an age of unprecedented high-reward, high-dopamine stimuli, mostly delivered digitally.

In this new book, we are promised tools to help us let go of our desire for control, but we have to follow Lembke’s advice and acknowledge a “power greater than ourselves, however we define it, and give our will over to that power: less mastery and more a return to mystery”. As an addiction medicine psychiatrist and head of Stanford University’s Addiction Medicine Dual Diagnosis Clinic in California, this “radical surrender” should be scientifically argued. Watch out for our review on 5 November.

Advertisement

Free newsletter

Let’s face it: our every move, from our next Google search to our latest Netflix selection, is utterly dependent on numbers, and AI is now an everyday reality. We have no choice but to face up to the overwhelming presence of mathematics, small, medium – or big. In Big Math: The hidden codes that run our world, Steven Strogatz and Alex Townsend (both leading mathematicians at Cornell University, New York) set out to show how relatively familiar concepts such as matrices, vectors, Markov chains, linear algebra and the like lie at the heart of computer science and quantum computing – essential for us all to know, say its publishers, if we’re to “comprehend the changes sweeping the world”.

Dive into new titles from major names including Carlo Rovelli, Maggie Aderin, Xand van Tulleken and Jim Al-Khalili, as well as a new biography of Stephen Hawking

For some while now, we’ve known that the story of invasive species is complex, but just how complex is the stuff of Amy Crawford’s Undesirable: Invasive species, humans, and where we all belong. Blundering all over the world, we have accidentally (as well as deliberately) carried species with us on our adventures – and often created great incidental damage to the recipient environments, ranging from destroyed habitats to changes in the climate. Then there is the accidental introduction of blow-in species over relatively short stretches of water, or those dropped by migrating birds. After hundreds of years, it’s still not entirely clear where the gains or losses to local biodiversity really land.

“Whether it’s garlic mustard spreading through American forests or brushtail possums allegedly decimating the flightless birds of New Zealand,” Undesirable is a “multi-faceted story”, say its publishers. On top of that, exactly how to hold ourselves to account remains an open question. And apparently, the young field of “invasion biology” has been “wracked by controversy and haunted by ethical quandaries as it has sought to destroy some species for the benefit of others”. Crawford, a freelance writer and long-time contributor to Smithsonian magazine, looks set to give us plenty to chew on here.

Look closely at the list of creators on the cover of this book, aimed at a 5+ age group, about a cloud forest within the Intac valley in northwestern Ecuador, and along with nature writer Robert Macfarlane and other experts, you’ll spot a more unusual contributor: Los Cedros Cloud Forest itself. As the publishers (probably correctly) point out, this is the first time a forest has been included in the creation of a book. To celebrate that fact – and the anniversary of a court decision recognising Los Cedros’s right to exist and flourish in the future – this is apparently “more than a book”, in that by making it, “we are recognising the forest’s moral rights as the co-creator of a literary work”. When you open Song of the Cedars, the flora, fauna and fungi of Los Cedros Cloud Forest jump off the page in a panoramic scene, which can be read or displayed as you wish. All the royalties from sales of the book, the publishers say, will be used to support the protection of Los Cedros. Fighting talk!

What’s it like to make your money as a content creator? Angèle Christin, a digital studies scholar at Stanford University, California, takes us inside that world in her new book. The things these influencers post on social media range “from dance routines to political commentary, makeup tutorials to carpentry DIY”. She looks far and wide to explore what she calls their “golden dreams of passion, autonomy, and monetary returns”. No spoiler alert needed: the outcome for these creators and their followers shows how this digital work tends to fuel precarity, inequality – and much more. Christin’s bottom line: it’s more than time to rethink the economic structure of social media.

Ocean water is nearly four times saltier than human blood, yet it has been central to our evolution – the “amniotic fluid of life itself”, as the publishers of Saltwater: A natural history of the sea describe it. In this book, author Ashley Ward, a marine biologist, will bring readers face to face with the deep secrets of marine life. There will be jousting rival humpback whales, and claustrophobic journeys in a submersible to 600 metres deep to see an aurora of bioluminescence. We will also apparently encounter the complex seabird cities that develop along coasts, where auk fathers train their chicks to become skilful divers. And there’s mention of the ethereal song of a pod of belugas carrying across a fjord in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard. Ward could hardly be better placed to deliver all this and more, given his background as a biologist at the University of Sydney, Australia, and as head of its Animal Behaviour Lab.

A sneak peek at the introduction of Baland Jalal’s The Phantom Mind: Insights from the borderlands of sleep shows what we can expect from a researcher often billed as the leading expert in sleep paralysis. “One morning in my teenage years, I awoke gripped by terror… In horror, I realized a demon was on my bed. It grabbed my legs and began tossing them up and down in the air, while crushing my chest and squeezing my neck. While being strangled to death, I could somehow telepathically read the mind of the monster. It had one – and only one agenda: to destroy me.”

This terrifying no man’s land between REM sleep and wakefulness became the territory of his research for the next decade or so. There are plenty more great stories in this highly accessible book, including one featuring Jalal’s mentor, the eminent neuroscientist V. S. Ramachandran, who appears as a sleep-paralysis ghost to Jalal – and leads him off on a new train of thought about exactly how the ghostly figures people see in sleep paralysis are formed. The borderlands of sleep turn out to be a rich seam to mine for those hoping to discover more about the waking mind. And watch out for our interview with Jalal, in our 14 November issue.

This is the latest in the Chicago University Press’s Day series. Earlier in the year, we enjoyed marine biologist Helen Scales’s Shell Day and behavioural ecologist Marty Crump’s Snake Day. Insect Day: A story of 24 hours and 24 hexapod lives follows the same pattern, acting as an hourly guide, this time following insects as they hunt for food, mates or just plain safety from predators. Author Erica McAlister is a curator at London’s Natural History Museum who studies flies. She starts at midnight in Africa with a female mosquito, Anopheles gambiae, which is out for the blood of any unwitting sleeper and may unintentionally transfer malaria. Who knew, by the way, that the males have no taste for blood?

By 7am, we’ve moved on to the Arctic circle, where a queen of Bombus polaris, the Arctic bumblebee, is basking within the flowers of the Arctic poppy. She can also keep warm simply by vibrating. Throughout the day, we meet the yellow-legged saddle casemaker (Agapetus ochripes), the blue-winged helicopter (Megaloprepus caerulatus), the Peruvian shield mantis (Choeradodis rhombicollis), the ferocious water bug (Abedus herberti) and Grote’s bertholdia (Bertholdia trigona). In its closing pages, Insect Day delivers a final punch: we’ve just toured insects, but there may be as many as 30 million more yet to describe.

A new Richard Dawkins book is always a bit of a treat, and 42 Tales from Life: A modern bestiary looks set to be no exception. This is a collection of animal tales, explaining how they evolved into the extraordinary, intriguing and often beautiful forms they have, with a colourful backdrop of illustrations by 19th-century naturalist, morphologist and artist Ernst Haeckel. According to the publisher, Dawkins reveals “the fundamental truths behind even the most unfathomable animal behaviours”, such as the galloping of fish, the shape of the rhinoceros’ horn, the surprising similarities between horses and lizards, and why hummingbirds glow so brilliantly. The book starts with “The Cephalopod’s Tale” and “The Hummingbird’s Tale”, ending with “The Bat’s Tale” and “The Frog’s Tale”. They are accompanied by Haeckel’s art, whose depictions of plants, sea creatures and other animals turn out to have fascinated Dawkins all his life.

The scientific truth about collagen supplements

New Scientist November 02, 2026

While I was writing my forthcoming book on the science of the skin, the number one thing that friends asked me to look into was collagen supplements. Do they really reduce wrinkles as promised? As a 40-year-old with increasingly crinkly skin, I wanted to know the answer to this, too, so I spent a long time poring over the evidence and interviewing skin scientists and doctors.

Collagen is the major structural protein in our skin, forming a woven network of fibres that is strong but flexible, a bit like a trampoline mat. As we age, our skin produces less collagen to maintain this structure, leading to sagging and wrinkling.

Red-light therapy does have health benefits but not the ones you think

The logical solution to declining collagen levels is to top them back up, which is the basis for taking collagen supplements. However, I discovered that it isn’t that simple, because taking in collagen through your mouth doesn’t magically transport it to your skin.

Advertisement

Collagen for supplements is usually sourced from the skin of cattle, pigs or fish left over from meat and seafood processing. It is treated with chemicals to chop the collagen proteins into smaller bits that are easier to process into pills and powders. Whole collagen is made of three protein chains of more than 1000 amino acids each, arranged as a triple helix, whereas processed collagen that is used in supplements, called hydrolysed collagen, contains single chains of 40 or fewer amino acids.

When we ingest hydrolysed collagen, our digestive systems break it into even smaller fragments of just one to three amino acids. The same thing occurs when we eat whole collagen in foods like salmon skin, or sip bone broth, which contains gelatine, a heat-degraded form of collagen.

These tiny fragments add to a pool of amino acids that we get from other proteins in foods like meat, dairy and legumes. The skin uses these amino acids as building blocks to make new collagen. James Varani, a pathologist at the University of Michigan who has been studying skin collagen for decades, told me there’s no difference between taking a collagen supplement and eating “a good steak”, because they both provide the amino acids needed for making new collagen.

Notably, Varani and his colleagues found that the reason our skin loses collagen with age isn’t because it lacks the ingredients for making it. Instead, its cellular machinery for assembling these ingredients into collagen becomes less efficient. That means that taking collagen supplements to fix wrinkles is like buying more sugar to fix a broken assembly line at a chocolate factory.

Plenty of studies claim to show that collagen supplements smooth away wrinkles, but they need to be taken with a grain of salt. Some, for example, report significant reductions in wrinkle depth in participants taking collagen supplements compared with those taking a placebo, but if you look at their actual numbers, the difference is a fraction of a millimetre. This is unlikely to make a meaningful difference to skin appearance, and you have to wonder about the accuracy of measurements on such a tiny scale anyway.

In September, dermatologist Anjali Mahto at clinic Self London and biostatistician David Grimes at Trinity College Dublin published a paper highlighting “substantial methodological concerns” in existing studies of collagen supplements that “temper [their] optimistic conclusions”. They also noted that “an overwhelming proportion of studies are industry-funded or involve authors with commercial ties to collagen manufacturers, raising concerns about selective reporting and bias”.

What should we eat to give us better, healthier skin

It’s disappointing that collagen supplements don’t live up to the hype, but there are some other collagen-optimising strategies with better evidence to support them, including regular exercise, which has been found to increase the expression of collagen genes. Every dermatologist I have ever interviewed has also stressed the importance of sun protection, because it is well established that ultraviolet radiation from the sun stimulates the release of enzymes in the skin that chew up collagen.

Several dermatologists have told me that the best thing to rub on the skin to reduce wrinkles is tretinoin, a vitamin A derivative that has been known to increase collagen levels since the 1990s. It requires a prescription because it can cause dryness, redness and peeling if not used carefully.

Therapies that injure the skin in a safe, controlled way also increase collagen production by activating natural healing mechanisms. These include laser therapies, microneedling, dermabrasion and deep chemical peels. Unfortunately, they are expensive and often make the skin red, raw and blistered, requiring a period of hiding from public view.

When it comes to supplements to stave off the effects of ageing, columnist Graham Lawton admits he is a hardened sceptic. But he finds some evidence for a few that can improve biological age as we grow older

One of the most promising treatments I have come across in my research is a gene therapy that was originally developed for people with low collagen levels due to a rare genetic condition called recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. Sometimes referred to as the “worst disease you’ve never heard of”, it is characterised by extremely fragile skin and large, painful wounds.

The gene therapy, which introduces new collagen genes into the skin to enhance collagen production, was approved in the US in 2023 and in the UK this year for people with this condition. Now, a modified version is being evaluated in clinical trials involving people with aged skin to see if it has rejuvenating effects.

Our desire for younger-looking skin is largely driven by vanity, but as I also explore in my book, there is growing evidence that the health of our skin directly affects the health of our inner organs, which is another reason to look after it. I’ve decided not to waste my money on collagen supplements, but I have invested in a very dorky wide-brim hat, to at least try to protect the collagen I still have.

Alice Klein is the author of Skin Deep: How skin works, and why it matters (out in January 2027)

Waikato dairy farmer fined $97,500 as tougher RMA penalties take effect

New Zealand Herald November 02, 2026

Environmental offences involving dairy effluent can now attract higher penalties under the Resource Management Act. Photo / RNZ, Rebekah Parsons-King

By Penny Miles of RNZ

Some dairy farmers are starting to feel the impact of stiffer penalties of up to a million dollars introduced last year under the Resource Management Act (RMA).

A Waikato farmer, Wayne Maurice Clarke, has been convicted and fined $97,500 for unlawfully discharging dairy effluent into the environment on his farm at Te Kōwhai, near Hamilton.

In September 2025, council officers inspected the defendant’s 170-cow dairy farm and found significant ponding of dairy effluent irrigated on saturated soils.

Officers found the effluent infrastructure on the farm was inadequate, lacking proper storage and management oversight of irrigation practices.

“These unlawful discharges were entirely avoidable. Despite decades of ownership and management by Mr Clarke, insufficient investment had been made in effluent infrastructure and systems to ensure effluent was managed sustainably,” Waikato Regional Council Investigations Team Leader Evan Billington said.

“It was concerning that no one had oversight of effluent irrigation over a three-day period leading up to this incident, despite wet weather and soil conditions.”

According to Billington, this was the first case in the region using the new regime introduced last August under the RMA.

“It’s now gone up to a million dollar fine or 18 months imprisonment. This fine in part reflected the increase in the penalties,” he said.

The regional council said the effluent storage wasn’t up to the job required.

“So they had a bladder storage, but it was pretty limited. It just means they’re having to irrigate regardless of weather,” Billington said.

“The council found the irrigator had parked for three days in the same paddock, it had come to the end of its run, the manager was off on his regular days off and the owner hadn’t monitored it over those three days.”

There was a drain at the end of the paddock on the 70ha farm, and there were concerns that with more irrigation the effluent would enter groundwater.

“There was concern with any more irrigation it would get there [to water]”

The fine was imposed by Judge Melinda Dickey in a decision released by Huntly District Court on October 15, 2026, following a prosecution brought by Waikato Regional Council under the Resource Management Act.

In sentencing, Judge Dickey said Clarke’s conduct was highly careless, and prosecution could have been avoided if he’d complied with environmental obligations.

Election 2026 live updates: Electoral Commission refers complaint about Harry Mowbray’s vote-splitting campaign to police

A prominent National volunteer says he regrets a social media post saying an assault victim was a Labour voter.

Police are now investigating Harry Mowbray's vote-splitting campaign after it was referred by the Electoral Commission.

In a statement to the Herald, Detective Senior Sergeant Andrew Compton confirmed the commission had referred Mowbray's campaign to police.

"Inquiries are being undertaken and there is no further comment we can provide at this stage."

Mowbray's campaign encourages National supporters to give their party vote to Act or New Zealand First in an attempt to create an overhang and potentially make it more likely the coalition parties can form the next government.

Mowbray, a wealthy businessman whose children Mat, Nick and Anna Mowbray founded the toy company Zuru, recently had to take down his Split Your Vote website after the Electoral Commission contacted him raising several issues related to the laws that govern electoral advertising.

The website had been put back up, with Mowbray telling the Herald yesterday it had been tweaked with the hope it aligned with the law.

Mowbray admitted it was his fault the matter had been referred to police as he hadn't responded to the commission's inquiries in time. He said he hadn't heard from police as at yesterday.

Speaking to media in Marlborough in front of dozens of oak wine barrels, National leader Christopher Luxon would not be pushed for a view on the news Police were now involved in Harry Mowbray's vote-splitting campaign.

Police have this morning confirmed it is now investigating Mowbray's campaign after it was referred by the Electoral Commission.

The National Party complained to the Electoral Commission over the campaign, which a spokesman said was a "deliberate attempt to confuse voters".

"I've nothing further to say and frankly now that it's a matter before the police I'll leave it there," Luxon said.

Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March has cast his vote at the Wesley Community Centre in Auckland after holding a stand-up with co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick at the nearby markets.

Photo / Tom Rose

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick says she would want to see an investigation launched if a government was elected through an engineered Parliamentary overhang.

An overhang is created if a party wins more electorate seats than its party vote entitles it to, which distorts the proportionality of the House.

Strategies to engineer an overhang are being employed on both sides of politics. Te Pāti Māori is campaigning only for the candidate vote, aiming to drive its party vote as low as possible.

Some individuals on the right, including former National and Act leader Don Brash, are encouraging National supporters to give their party vote to Act or New Zealand First, given National could win more electorates than its estimated party vote would entitle it to. Both Act and NZ First have spoken in support of this approach as it proposes to increase their respective party vote shares.

Speaking in Auckland, Swarbrick was asked whether a re-elected National-led Government would be legitimate if that was achieved through an overhang.

Swarbrick said it was a serious matter and would require an investigation to assess how the government was elected.

She said she didn't think anyone could have anticipated how much a drive there would be from members on the right of politics to advance such a strategy, referencing wealthy businessman Harry Mowbray's Split Your Vote campaign which is currently being assessed by police.

Swarbrick was also asked about the ongoing attack ads National is running which target Swarbrick as a possible finance minister after the Green co-leader expressed interest in holding the portfolio.

Willis yesterday defended National's attacks, claiming it was important for voters to understand Green Party tax policies, despite Labour leader Chris Hipkins ruling out anyone other than Labour holding the portfolio and controlling tax reform in a potential coalition.

Willis, the current Finance Minister, is at risk of not returning to Parliament as she relies on National securing a list seat position, which will not happen if National wins more electorates than its party vote entitles it to.

Swarbrick acknowledged it would be "pretty sad" if Willis' final act in her political career was to spearhead National's attack campaign against her.

Photo / Michael Craig

Green co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick are holding a stand-up at the Wesley Market in Auckland's Mt Roskill.

You can watch the livestream at the top of this story.

West Auckland politician Independent Waitākere candidate Bianca O'Keefe has had two of her election hoardings vandalised in Sunnyvale early this morning.

Police confirmed it is making inquiries after getting a call at 2.15am of a billboard on fire near the corner of Seymour Rd and Rangeview Rd.

The 19-year-old candidate shared her disappointment in an online post this morning.

"Firstly to the families nearby these signs, seeing the flames late at night must have been nothing short of shocking, my thoughts with you and my sincere apologies you had to witness and deal with that.

"I don't think I can describe the thoughts and emotions when you wake up to being told that the police have been in touch and not one, but two signs have been burnt out.

"This is the same M. O. someone on the edge of our community moving inwards.

"This time however the police are taking this seriously and treating as arson, one of the locations has CCTV in the area so they are hopeful."

Just weeks ago, O'Keefe had swastikas and male genitalia drawn on her signs.

She told the Herald at the time each signpost cost her five hours of working her minimum wage part-time and casual jobs.

"It's really frustrating because I don't have the support of a party, so it is all my hard-earned money."

O'Keefe said although the repeated destruction was "upsetting", it did not put her off politics.

Waitematā Acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie has encouraged anyone who witnessed this morning's event to contact police.

Photo / Hayden Woodward

Police are now investigating Harry Mowbray's vote-splitting campaign after it was referred by the Electoral Commission.

In a statement to the Herald, Detective Senior Sergeant Andrew Compton confirmed the commission had referred Mowbray's campaign to police.

"Inquiries are being undertaken and there is no further comment we can provide at this stage."

Mowbray's campaign encourages National supporters to give their party vote to Act or New Zealand First in an attempt to create an overhang and potentially make it more likely the coalition parties can form the next government.

Mowbray, a wealthy businessman whose children Mat, Nick and Anna Mowbray founded the toy company Zuru, recently had to take down his Split Your Vote website after the Electoral Commission contacted him raising several issues related to the laws that govern electoral advertising.

The website had been put back up, with Mowbray telling the Herald yesterday it had been tweaked with the hope it aligned with the law.

Mowbray admitted it was his fault the matter had been referred to police as he hadn't responded to the commission's inquiries in time. He said he hadn't heard from police as at yesterday.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins says a Government under his leadership will prioritise road maintenance and public transport.

He told Ryan Bridge TODAY that to cover the costs of Labour's proposed freeze on fuel excise tax, some transport projects which have not yet been funded may "be pushed further into the future".

What will be prioritised in the National Land Transport Fund is the party's public transport fare caps and maintaining roads, Hipkins said.

"The Infrastructure Commission gave all parties some pretty stark findings on that, that we actually underinvest in road maintenance."

Hipkins said New Zealand has to "look after what you've got before you start building shiny new things".

"So we will certainly take on board that advice from the Infrastructure Commission."

Projects that have been contracted and funded will not be stopped, Hipkins said.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins appears on Ryan Bridge Today with Ryan Bridge. Photo / Michael Craig

The Green Party says while it anticipates some people might leave the country should their wealth tax be introduced, the country would still be better off financially and socially.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick told Ryan Bridge TODAY the party anticipated seeing "behavioural change" in 28.5% of people with the introduction of a wealth tax, which included the likeliness of some leaving New Zealand.

She said people that would threaten to leave New Zealand were holding the rest of the country "hostage".

Despite wealthier people paying the highest taxes, Swarbrick said it wouldn't affect the country's revenue.

She said to look at Norway for example, which she says has "a far lower threshold" of the equivalent of around $300,000.

"And yes, what we have seen is yes, while they had some high-profile people who threatened to leave, and a handful did, however they are now generating the revenue necessary to invest in rebuilding their public services which means their society is more cohesive, their people are better educated and that they are more productive and prosperous as a result."

Green co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick has responded to National's stance on why it's been aiming a good chunk of its Instagram advertisements against her.

Nicola Willis took to X to say the move was because the Greens could "play a powerful role in the next government" and therefore their plans deserve "serious scrutiny".

Swarbrick told Ryan Bridge TODAY the National Party was more interested in "cosplaying Mean Girls" than talking policy.

"I find those comments from the National Party finance spokesperson pretty galling, especially when she's talking about being a woman in politics and being subject to flak online.

"It is her literal party that is responsible for producing all of that flak and so little substance."

Swarbrick said National had used "all their might to paint to a bogeyman" of her.

She welcomed a one-on-one financial debate with Willis.

Christchurch child killer Peter Holdem caught with photo resembling murder victim in prison

New Zealand Herald November 02, 2026

The man who abducted and murdered a Christchurch schoolgirl 40 years ago was caught with a picture in his cell of a child resembling her.

He claims the photo was there to “remind him of the seriousness” of his offending, but the Parole Board is “less than satisfied” with his story.

Peter Joseph Holdem was jailed for life for murdering 6-year-old Louisa Damodran near Christchurch in 1986.

On October 15 that year, Louisa – who was days shy of her 7th birthday – was walking home from school and just 100m from her house when Holdem kidnapped her.

He drove her to the Waimakariri River north of the city, throttled her and drowned her.

Her body was found downstream three weeks later.

At the time, Holdem was on parole after serving time for the 1982 attempted rape of a 10-year-old in a Christchurch park.

He has a history of sex attacks on children dating back to the 1970s.

Before he was sentenced to life in prison in 1987, he had “five pages” of sexual offending, dishonesty and violent offending.

Holdem was first eligible for parole in October 1996 and has been refused every time he has appeared before the board.

His most recent hearing was on October 12.

The board heard that Holdem had made progress, but remained too much of a risk to be released.

The board confirmed Holdem completed a high-intensity child sex offending programme in May and, over the next few months, 10 sessions of individual treatment with a psychologist to “focus on the homicide dimension of his offending”.

“Mr Holdem explained, in some detail, the changes that he said that he had made as a result of completing the programme and the individual treatment,” said Parole Board panel convenor Neville Trendle.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

“He acknowledged previously holding a lot of anger, particularly with respect to women. He told us that he had now completely changed. The Board explored some of those changes with Mr Holdem, but we found it difficult to get a clear response as to what and how he had changed.

“He had considerable difficulty in responding directly to questions asked. We noted a return to a former pattern of engaging with his own reference to past incidents where he was a victim.

“We had some difficulty in understanding his explanation for his recent change with respect to his view of women.”

Trendle said the board also questioned Holdem about items found among his prison property.

“We were… less than satisfied with his response… when he was found in 2024 with a photograph of a young girl that appeared to resemble his victim,” he said.

“He maintained that he had a picture of a young girl that resembled his victim, so that he could be reminded of the seriousness of what he had done.”

Trendle revealed that Holdem had been approved for work outside prison and asked for the board to support him having guided releases into the community.

The board refused.

“He told us that he had recently been on his first guided release which he found somewhat overwhelming,” he explained.

“The pace of life and being in the community after 40 years was difficult for him to grasp.”

Trendle said an updated risk assessment had been sought before the hearing, but had not been completed.

“We do not support Mr Holdem progressing on a reintegration pathway until we have had the opportunity to consider that risk assessment,” he ruled.

“Parole is declined. He will be seen again in six months, by 30 April 2027.”

The board requested a “detailed” risk assessment ahead of that hearing and an updated psychological report “assessing the gains made in the treatment that he has completed”.

It also asked for recommendations “as to any outstanding treatment needs and future steps” and an assessment of Holdem’s safety plan.

Trendle noted that Holdem had an “apparent lack of understanding of the essence” of the current plan.

Anna Leask is a senior journalist who covers Christchurch issues and national crime and justice. She joined the Herald in 2008 and has worked as a journalist for more than 20 years with a particular focus on family and gender-based violence, child abuse, sexual violence and homicides. She writes, hosts and produces the award-winning podcast A Moment In Crime, released monthly on nzherald. co. nz.

Twenty-nine people have been issued move-on orders since the new law came into effect nine days ago, police say.

The new law gives police powers to order people to leave an area due to disruptive or disorderly behaviour for a specified period up to 24 hours.

Fears have been raised that the measures are overly punitive and would capture people who were begging, effectively penalising people for being poor.

But police Assistant Commissioner Tusha Penny told Ryan Bridge Today that so far begging or rough sleeping had not been the “primary reason” for any of the orders.

“All 29 have been because of disruptive behaviour, intimidating behaviour, disorderly and threatening.”

Most of the orders were issued in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch, with the district commissioners telling her they were finding the orders to be “a very good prevention tool for de-escalation”, particularly in alcohol harm areas.

It appeared the orders were allowing police to make fewer arrests and instead just send people home, she said, though it was still “early days”.

The vast majority of people had returned home or left the area when ordered to do so, with timeframes ranging from three to 24 hours.

One person in Wellington had later been arrested after police were called to deal with disorderly behaviour and found they were also breaching a move-on order.

Four of the 29 had been homeless people, Penny said, before praising police for how they dealt with vulnerable people every day.

Penny was aware of one of those four being provided with food and taken to a “location of her choice”.

“This is not just a police issue if we’re going to talk about homelessness and vulnerable. We have really open, really strong partnerships with the missions across our main centres.”

She said Reverend Murray Edridge from the Wellington City Mission had given police “an early tick”.

“He’s regularly meeting with police to make sure that if there are missteps, we’re across them really fast.”

Teaching Council under scrutiny as teacher charged with possessing objectionable material

New Zealand Herald November 02, 2026

Erica Stanford said she could not comment specifically, as the matter was before the courts. Photo / RNZ, Samuel Rillstone

By Sam Sherwood of RNZ

A teacher at an elite New Zealand school is before the courts charged with possessing child sexual exploitation material, RNZ can reveal.

The teacher was arrested on October 15 and made his first appearance in court a week later.

He faces a representative charge alleging that, on August 30, he possessed an objectionable publication, namely a video file depicting child sexual exploitation, on an external hard drive, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe that the publication was objectionable.

The man was granted interim name suppression and did not enter a plea. He is due in court again this month.

The teacher’s school has not responded to requests for comment from RNZ, which also approached the Teaching Council for comment last Tuesday.

At that stage, the teacher’s status on the teacher’s register had not been changed since his arrest.

RNZ asked whether the council had been informed of his arrest and, if it had, why his status had not changed.

After RNZ’s query, the council updated the teacher’s status to say he “voluntarily agreed not to teach”.

That evening, the council released a statement to RNZ from Teaching Council chair Patrick Walsh.

“The Teaching Council takes matters relating to learner safety seriously. When information is received that may raise concerns about a teacher’s fitness to hold a practising certificate, the Teaching Council considers that information in accordance with its statutory responsibilities and regulatory processes.”

Walsh said the council maintained the online register of New Zealand Registered Teachers.

“The register is constantly updated as we receive information and we suggest that it is regularly reviewed.

“In general, we are unable to provide information on complaints or mandatory reports that have been made to the council (including whether one has recently or previously been received or not, in relation to a specific teacher, ECE centre, school or kura). This is to ensure we act in accordance with the Privacy Act 2020 and the principles of natural justice.”

RNZ asked the council whether it was aware of the man’s arrest before RNZ asked them for comment.

Walsh said the council could confirm they were “aware of the matter in advance of your request for details”.

“However, we’re unable to confirm when or how the Teaching Council became aware of information relating to a specific teacher. Providing that information could disclose details about an individual matter that we cannot comment on, particularly where privacy and natural justice considerations apply.

“We can assure you that learner safety remains at the heart of the Teaching Council’s regulatory role.”

RNZ also asked the Ministry of Education for comment.

A ministry spokesperson said, as far as they were aware, “this matter has not been raised with the local ministry office”.

Acting deputy secretary Antony Harvey said the Teaching Council was not required to notify the ministry about every matter it manages.

“The ministry’s role is to monitor the council’s overall performance and whether it is meeting its statutory responsibilities.

“In this instance, no ministry support for the school was required. Schools can contact us at any time, if they need advice or assistance.”

A police spokesperson confirmed police had arrested a man in connection with an ongoing investigation into child exploitation material.

“The investigation resulted in a search warrant at two properties earlier this month.”

Police also said that, from their perspective, “all appropriate notifications were made in this case”.

In response to questions from RNZ, Education Minister Erica Stanford said she could not comment on it specifically, as the matter was before the courts.

“However, I have made my expectations clear that the Teaching Council must have child safety at the heart of every decision they make. This should include working closely with partner agencies, including the justice sector.

“Noting, as part of the recent changes, the ministry has a role in closely monitoring the performance of the council and will report to the Minister of Education.”

Stanford said she would raise the matter with the Ministry of Education and be “seeking assurances that the right steps are being taken, when it comes to teachers facing criminal actions”.

Weeks ago, Stanford said there was a “rotten culture” inside the Teaching Council, following the case of a sex offender who was able to teach, despite warning signs.

Barrister Katherine Anderson KC earlier released a scathing report into the Teaching Council’s handling of teacher Timothy Fisher. She found the council should have struck him off a decade before he was convicted of a litany of indecency and sex offences against children, most of them under 12 years old.

It outlined how Fisher managed to go from school to school without a practising certificate – a criminal offence – and kept teaching, despite a police “red stamp” warning that he should not have unsupervised access to children.

Stanford earlier said she long had grave concerns about the Teaching Council.

“It was very clear in this report that the Teaching Council had completely lost their way and saw themselves as a friend of the profession, to uphold the mana of the profession and to be liked, rather than to uphold teacher standards and to protect children, which is what everybody expects of them.”

She said the Teaching Council’s failures meant she couldn’t be sure this hadn’t happened before.

“They don’t have proper processes around making sure that people are teaching with a current practising certificate. This is not an isolated incident.

“There is a rotten culture inside the Teaching Council that needs changing, otherwise this will keep happening.”

Prominent Rotorua National Party volunteer and supporter Raj Kumar says he regrets posting a Facebook video of a street fight and joking that the man was beaten up for voting Labour.

The Springfield Superette owner, who represents Rotorua as a Bay of Plenty Regional councillor, said the post on his widely followed Facebook page was an “attempt at satire”, but he realised it was not constructive and removed it.

Kumar posted the video on Friday showing two men punching and kicking another man on Brookland Rd in Rotorua, across the road from the Western Heights shopping centre.

One of the men was stomping on the man as he lay on the ground. The context of the fight and when it happened are not known.

Kumar said in his post: “A normal day in the heights of Rotorua 3010. They beating up a person who’s voted for the Labour Party. Do the Right thing and stay clear of the left.”

His post ended with a winky-face emoji.

The post immediately copped criticism from some of his 2200 followers, with one calling it “poor”.

“I get the political quip, but footage of locals being assaulted & victims. Cmon.”

Another urged: “These types of videos do nobody any favours … you should take it down bro”.

Another called it “bad taste”, also posting: “People in Heights voted for you and you insult the neighbourhood negatively by generalising it as a normal day there in reference to this fight, which it is not”. The poster said he respected Kumar but expected better of him as a community leader.

Kumar initially defended his post in the comments section, saying he was not the one fighting or “making alliances with the gangs”. He said he was not advocating violence but showing what’s actually happening.

“I will continue to use satire and share the real happenings of what’s actually going around us. You have a choice to not engage.”

However, Kumar removed his post later on Friday.

When approached by the Rotorua Daily Post on Monday, Kumar said the video was sent to him by a member of the public.

“I put lots of local things on my page and the post was an attempt at satire but I quickly realised it wasn’t constructive and took it down. It was a personal post and I do regret it.”

When asked if he was a member of National Party Rotorua candidate Todd McClay’s campaign committee, Kumar said: “I’m supportive of National locally and as a volunteer like many others, have helped.”

McClay, the incumbent MP, said Kumar was a volunteer but not an official campaign team member.

“It’s been a respectful campaign on all sides and it sounds like this [Kumar’s actions] was an enthusiastic volunteer. I ask everyone to remain respectful and focus on the issues.”

Labour candidate for Rotorua Fisher Wang said Kumar’s post was “deeply disappointing”.

“It is saddening to see violence like this in our community, particularly when someone is attributing it to political views and sharing it on social media.”

He said candidates should be careful not to use incidents like this to score political points or unfairly tarnish an entire neighbourhood.

He said Rotorua people deserved to be treated with dignity and respect, and deserved leadership that brought people together.

“We can have different political views without losing our compassion, respect or our sense of community.”

Kumar served two terms as a Rotorua Lakes councillor, with his second alongside Wang from 2019.

Kumar unsuccessfully ran for the Rotorua mayoralty in 2022 before being elected to the Bay of Plenty Regional Council last year.

He was also elected to the Rotorua Trust last year and was the top-polling candidate behind Wang.

Kumar told the Rotorua Daily Post in July that he considered putting his hand up to be a New Zealand First candidate in this year’s general election, but changed his mind after race-related comments from within the party about Indian culture put him off.

Kelly Makiha is a senior journalist who has reported for the Rotorua Daily Post for more than 30 years, covering mainly police, court, human interest and social issues.

A concerned mother has complained that “radical left-wing anti-Government propaganda” was shared by a political candidate at a college’s awards ceremony last week.

But the college says it invited the candidate as an “inspirational leader” and the school held no political views.

Green Party Waiariki candidate Tania Waikato, who is a lawyer and social justice advocate, attended Tauranga Girls’ College’s Te Moana Nui a Kiwa Māori and Pasifika awards ceremony and took part in a question-and-answer session.

One Year 9 student’s mother, who the Bay of Plenty Times agreed not to name to protect her daughter’s identity, said she felt “blindsided” by the school and was “force-fed Tania Waikato’s radical left ideology”.

The mother, who has Te Arawa and Ngāti Kahu heritage, said her family lived the “real-life Treaty of Waitangi” with generational interracial blends.

Her family had voted for National before, she had scrutineered for the Mana Party and she said if she had enrolled on the Māori roll this election, she would have voted for Waikato as the “least worst option”.

Despite that, she complained to the school, saying the ceremony was hijacked by “radical left-wing anti-Government propaganda”.

The mother said Waikato discussed during the question-and-answer session how the “racist Government” prompted her to stand as an electoral candidate.

“This is not what I wanted to have to explain to my kids on the way home from a celebration for my daughter and her fellow students,” the mother said.

“The emphasis on the drive home was not on my daughter, who had just been awarded for her work this year, but on the confusion around the political candidate ... allowed to rant her left-wing anti-Government perspectives on the current coalition.”

She said her children asked her if the Government was racist and “doesn’t like us because we’re Māori”.

The mother questioned why the school chose a political candidate instead of an alumna, noting Waikato had not attended the school.

“If you are going to give preference to one Waiariki candidate to tout their carry-on, then all candidates should’ve been invited.

“We should’ve at least been notified a political candidate was on the agenda ... It would allow us to make informed decisions instead of being blindsided.”

The mother said the school’s newly minted first-time voters should be allowed to decide who they voted for “without their school presenting them a preferred candidate”.

Tauranga Girls’ College principal Tara Kanji said the school held no political views.

“It is unfortunate that in answering one of several questions on the night, Ms Waikato’s response was seen as a floor for campaigning – which I can assure you it was not.”

Kanji said one question asked how Waikato managed the challenges of being a mother, a litigation lawyer and an electoral candidate.

She said Waikato had attended a previous school event with alumni and student leaders, and was invited to the awards ceremony as an “inspirational leader”.

Kanji said last year’s Māori and Pasifika prizegiving was attended by a New Zealand representative athlete who was also not an alumna. However, a graduate did attend the school’s sports prizegiving.

She said this year’s Te Moana Nui a Kiwa ceremony was the largest celebration of the school’s Māori and Pasifika cohort in recent years.

“As the tumuaki [principal], I take on board any concerns that parents raise, and have done so with this one complaint that came in.”

The school had held mock elections through an Electoral Commission programme – which Kanji said was part of the school’s civics unit to “educate young people about the power of democracy”.

Waikato said she rejected the mother’s characterisation of her “hijacking” the evening.

She said two senior students prepared questions for Waikato, rather than her delivering a prepared speech.

“I acknowledge that not everyone would agree with my opinion of the current Government, which was a very small part of the overall conversation.

“However, the questions were asking for my personal experience and that is what I provided.”

Waikato said she received positive feedback from parents and students who said the session was “inspiring”.

“I also received a thank you message directly from a parent following the event. I believe that reflects the spirit of the night far more accurately than a single anonymous account.”

Bijou Johnson is a multimedia journalist based in Bay of Plenty. A passionate writer and reader, she grew up in Tauranga and developed a love for journalism while exploring various disciplines at university. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in Classical Studies from Massey University.

The opening of the Powerhouse Parramatta marks a significant moment in western Sydney’s history, becoming the region’s first state-significant cultural institution.

The $1 billion project, which has not been without controversy, aims to redraw Sydney’s cultural geography and provide world-class exhibitions.

Situated on the banks of the Parramatta River, the new Powerhouse Parramatta – dubbed the milk crate by locals due to its distinctive steel-lattice exoskeleton – is the largest cultural infrastructure project in Australia since the Sydney Opera House.

Spanning 30,000 square metres and reaching up to six storeys, the cultural institution features multiple exhibition spaces across the two wings.

For the opening, the museum will have about 3000 objects on display including 1600 from the Powerhouse’s collection.

Since mid-August, a clock on the Powerhouse Parramatta website has been counting down the days, hours, minutes and seconds to the opening of the museum on November 7.

To mark the occasion, the museum will hold a $4.5 million, 23-day festival program featuring 179 events. During this time, the museum will stay open until 9pm from Thursday to Sunday, and 10am to 5pm from Monday to Wednesday. The program will feature talks, workshops, food, music and performances.

General admission tickets for the opening weekend have sold out, but patrons can still experience the museum by booking a ticket to opening festival events. Each festival ticket includes entry to the museum and access to four out of five exhibitions; one, Task Eternal, will be ticketed.

The first five exhibitions will run for between 18 months and three years. They include The Dark, an immersive exhibition created for children aged four to 12 years old, and Es Devlin: The Turning, where visitors can explore five immersive installations.

Overflow, a First Nations-led exhibition grounded in the living principles of Water Country, shares practices that extend care to water systems. Aerospace exhibition Task Eternal will serve as the museum’s flagship exhibition, while The Mall will examine the cultural significance of the shopping mall.

When visitors arrive, they’ll enter the taller west wing, where there is a movable concierge stand, information displays and a gift shop. The ground floor also features food options and the entrance to the largest exhibition space. Large escalators and lifts take visitors through the space, and both buildings are linked through bridges.

The rooftop of the shorter east wing holds a productive garden, while level four in the other building is a 200-seat demonstration kitchen and event space. Level five features a library and co-working space, while the sixth floor houses 30 apartments, which will be used for creative residencies.

While all five of the exhibitions will be free to visitors aged 16 and under, those over 16 will have to pay an entry fee to Task Eternal. Costs will range from $20 for a concession ticket to $30 for a standard ticket.

For an extra $10, visitors can experience James Turrell’s colour and sensory-distorting installation Shangri La (Over the Hump).

General admission to the museum is free for patrons of all ages.

The Powerhouse Parramatta includes three food and drink venues: Folded, Green Bar and Simara. Folded, an all-day cafe located on the ground floor, acts as a first stop for visitors seeking a coffee or lunch, and Green Bar is tucked away near the museum’s rooftop garden.

Simara, also on the ground floor, is a contemporary Australian restaurant with seating for more than 290 patrons, spanning almost 600 square metres across indoor and outdoor dining areas.

The menu intends to “celebrate the diverse food cultures of Australia and western Sydney”, with bookings recommended.

There will, of course, also be gift shops.

Located at 34 Phillip Street, Parramatta, the museum can be reached through a range of public transport options. For those planning to commute via train, Powerhouse Parramatta is a 10-minute walk from Parramatta station, while the closest bus stop is located 250 metres from the site on Smith Street.

It can also be reached by light rail, with both the Church Street and Parramatta Square stops positioned a short walk from the Powerhouse Parramatta. The ferry will take visitors close to the museum as well, with the Parramatta Wharf located 400 metres from the site.

Visitors opting to drive won’t be able to park at the museum – there’s no on-site parking. However, there is a pick-up and drop-off zone on Phillip Street and paid car parks nearby.

Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 20:00:27 GMT

Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body

It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.

Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.

Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.

“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”

The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.

The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.

If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.

Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”

Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”

“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.
