Russell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court told

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:57:56 GMT

Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues

Russell Brand is not a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” and is respectful when women say no, a court has heard.

In his closing speech at Southwark crown court, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why Brand’s accusers had not fought back when they were allegedly raped, saying “not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Winter said allegations about the comedian’s sexual conduct in 2023 had “poisoned the wells” of justice. He also said there had been “monstrous delays” in the women in the criminal trial coming forward to police.

He also questioned why Brand had been accused of “only three rapes in 10 years” out of all the women he had slept with.

He said: “It is an extremely curious feature of this case that out of the many, many women that Mr Brand had sex with during this period only three of them say they did not consent to anal, oral or vaginal sex.”

Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Winter began his closing speech by reciting an 1864 quote from the theologian and philosopher John Henry Newman, saying: “What I insist upon here, now that I am bringing this portion of my discussion to a close, is this unmanly attempt of his, in his concluding pages, to cut the ground from under my feet … this I call poisoning the wells.”

He said the 2023 reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times and Sunday Times stories had “poisoned the well of justice” in Brand’s case by prompting the women to come forward with accusations afterwards.

Winter told jurors: “They poisoned the wells in the hope and intention that other people come forward and make allegations against him.”

In her closing speech on Friday, the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, denied that the 2023 reporting had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.

Winter told jurors on Monday that Brand had an “immense amount of sex” and none of it was unlawful.

“The question for you is, can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand between 1999 and 2009, he raped just three of them?” he asked.

“Living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful however morally distasteful you may find it,” he continued. “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral – who cares? It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”

Winter said another “curious feature” of the case was that the three rape complainants had alleged Brand was “normal” after the alleged incidents.

“That, we suggest, is something that simply cannot have occurred if he is guilty,” the barrister said. “He obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that’s the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal.”

The barrister said there was “no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”.

He also questioned why the women had not screamed, kicked out or slapped Brand during the alleged attacks. He asked why a woman who accuses Brand of anal rape “didn’t just roll over and kick out in any way” and said she “didn’t scream or resist or call out”. He also questioned why a woman who says she was orally raped did not “slap [Brand] in the face” and suggested she had not “sufficiently” resisted.

He also questioned how none of the women came forward during the #MeToo movement.

Winter said: “How is it that it’s only three out of the many, many women, how is it that not even these ones, not even these allegations on this indictment came to light during #MeToo?

“Many women were questioning whether they had a bad experience sexually at the hands of a famous person. It could not have been more publicised.

“How is it that not one of them thought what happened to them involved a crime during the #MeToo movement?”

The court has heard the earliest allegation dated back to 1999, when a woman accused Brand of raping her after he had performed in a fringe cabaret event during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth.

The woman told the court Brand had left his email address after raping her, while asking her if she was enjoying herself.

Winter said the woman was not a “naive and wilting flower” as he questioned her account of events. “You would have to be a psychopath to be raping someone and asking them if they were enjoying it,” Winter said. “He [Brand] said he was trying to please her but he wasn’t successful.”

Winter said rapists did not try to please their victims. He also said Brand respected when a woman said no, and sought “approbation and adoration” from women.

“He respects it when a woman says no so that makes him someone who is not a rapist,” Winter said. “He was seeking the approval in the sex, it’s the approval, it’s the ‘Yes I will have sex with you’, and that’s what he said in his evidence.”

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

The trial continues.

Half-witted at best, a people-pleaser at worst: step forward, Chris Philp

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:27:09 GMT

Responding to Shabana Mahmood’s changes to indefinite leave to remain, the shadow home secretary was detached from reality

Better late than never. It had seemed as if some apologies from the prime minister were more sincere than others. The one that he has planned to deliver for Britain’s role in the slave trade at the Commonwealth heads of government meeting in Antigua fell on the right side of genuine. There had been no need to make one at that time. Indeed Kemi Badenoch saw it as a sign of weakness. There again, she would refuse to apologise for running someone over on a pedestrian crossing. Somehow it would have turned out to be the victim’s fault.

Andy Burnham’s apology for not being able to turn up in the Commons to lend support to his home secretary might rather fall into the “sorry, not sorry” category. Making life more difficult for migrants was more one for Keir Starmer’s legacy than part of the new government’s agenda. Andy couldn’t have been more thrilled to be on a plane as Shabana Mahmood stood up to make her statement on “earned settlement”. It was almost as if the statement had been timed for when Burnham was away. At the very least, it was the perfect coincidence. If not divine intervention.

Even on Monday lunchtime, the prime minister’s spokesperson was refusing to give Burnham’s wholehearted support for Shabana’s proposed changes to indefinite leave to remain (ILR). Even after he and other cabinet colleagues had managed to water them down a little. The best that Andy would say was that “It was a good thing that immigration had fallen”.

Nothing about the home secretary’s role in this. Nothing that hinted at an endorsement. It felt as if Mahmood had been rather hung out to dry. Even more so when Angela Rayner, another of the home secretary’s critics, pointedly left the chamber by the far door so she wouldn’t have to look the home secretary in the eye after housing and communities departmental questions. No need for an awkward “That cup of tea isn’t going to drink itself”.

But at the very last minute – as if by magic – a short, unequivocal message of support from Burnham was released. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” he said. Shabana was not being abandoned, after all. Not that she wouldn’t have coped if she had. Even if she had not come to the house with Lou Haigh and Lucy Powell as her outriders, Mahmood is more than capable of looking after herself. She is a woman who knows her mind.

The statement was all much as we had expected. A reaffirmation of previous proposals with a few important concessions to Burnham, Rayner and backbenchers from the left of the Labour party. There would be a five-year route to settlement for care workers who had arrived prior to March 2025: a 10-year process for those who had arrived afterwards. Otherwise all was as it had been, plus or minus a couple of tweaks. New safe routes for refugees and a 30-year wait for those who had arrived in the country illegally. All with the usual caveats of speaking English, national insurance contributions and no criminal record.

We haven’t seen much of the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, in recent months. A relief to us all. Partly because even he had begun to have a sense of his own ridiculousness, partly because immigration had ceased to be such a hot topic for the country. There was more than a sense that the government was legislating for a problem that no longer really existed. Legal immigration has fallen to the tens of thousands a year from its high point of one million during Boris Johnson’s time in office. And the small boat crossings have more than halved. But Shabana doesn’t believe in taking chances. Happy to double-lock the doors to the country.

But this was The Philpster’s time to shine. To remind us all that he is at best half witted; at his worst, a people-pleaser par excellence. The ultimate nose in search of a bum. And so we got Philp at his most absurd. A joy to behold. A performance to make the whole statement worthwhile. A chance to give the entire Commons its Proustian madeleine moment. The Unbearable Lightness of Chris. Just when you think you’ve seen it all, The Philpster searches for the futility inside himself.

It had taken a whole year for Mahmood to establish her credibility, Philp declared. And she had destroyed it all in the space of her 12-minute statement. There will come a time when Chris compiles a show reel of all his political lowlights. A chance for him and his therapist to try to make sense of his career. How can someone of so little ability have come so far? Would Kemi really be daft enough to make him her home secretary if she won an election? Luckily she will never have to answer that one.

But know one thing. The Philpster’s reply will feature heavily in any lowlights reel. Above all else for his lack of self-awareness. The government should be ashamed of itself. This was virtually an open-doors policy. There would be foreigners everywhere if we weren’t careful. You could not be more detached from reality if you tried. It had been the Tory government that had presided over the mass wave of immigration. A Tory government that had failed to secure the country’s borders. And who had been a Home Office minister while this was going on? Step forward, Chris.

Mahmood scarcely bothered to grace The Philpster’s delusions with a reply. She would have been doing him a favour to offer him a prescription of some anti-psychotic drugs. Nor was it just Labour who put the boot in. The Tory father of the house, Edward Leigh, is becoming increasingly disinhibited in opposition. Determined to make up for a decade or more of supporting a failing government by telling inconvenient truths.

The former Tory government should be holding its head in shame, Leigh said. And anyone who had been in the Home Office should wear sackcloth and ashes. It was a complete evisceration of The Philpster and his empty words. Enough to almost make you feel sorry for Chris. Almost. Philp gestured half-heartedly towards Robert Jenrick, another former Home Office minister. Anything to try and mitigate the shame.

For the rest of the statement, various Labour backbenchers protested about the lack of fairness to immigrants; the retrospective nature of some proposals. Shabana really wasn’t bothered. She had given away as much as she was going to. The Labour party would just have to live with it. Elsewhere, Nigel Farage and Zia Yusuf were holding a press conference on ILR. The government had been weak, they claimed. The only answer was to deport every immigrant. It would have been nice if, to show he meant what he was saying, if Zia had promised to deport himself. Not for being brown or Muslim. But for being thoroughly unpleasant.

Andy Madley and VAR should take credit – they got major Anfield calls right

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:15:12 GMT

Timber’s shirt pull on Isak was not a penalty on review, and Madueke’s clash with Mac Allister was clearly not violent conduct

There was one incident that got everyone talking at the weekend, and that was the decision not to award Liverpool a penalty in their match against Arsenal after Alexander Isak had his shirt pulled by Jurriën Timber as he tried to get his head to a Bradley Barcola cross.

The on-field decision from the referee, Andy Madley, was no penalty and it was a call backed by the video assistant referee, Stuart Attwell. After the match the Liverpool head coach, Andoni Iraola, said there had been a “clear, clear pull” and when the footage is slowed down or freeze‑framed, that looks to be true. But at full speed, the contact appears minimal and not sustained: Timber is using one hand and tugs briefly on the shirt, and the impact on Isak’s movement is arguable.

There is a high bar for penalising contact in the Premier League and that has to be taken into account by Attwell. Iraola said that he would encourage his players to go down in similar situations in future, but the incident was assessed by the VAR and didn’t clear the bar in his opinion on the day. For the VAR to overturn an on-field decision there needs to have been a “clear and obvious error” and that is not the case here in my view.

Later there was a great piece of refereeing from Madley that got approval from a lot of pundits, and I agree with them. The moment came in the 79th minute after a foul by Alexis Mac Allister on Martin Ødegaard. There is a coming together of a number of players and Noni Madueke squares up to Mac Allister. The pair’s heads touch with Mac Allister then falling to the ground as if seriously hurt. It’s always been the case that players look to ask a question of the referee. This was how it was when I was refereeing in the Premier League and it has not changed, with or without VAR. Here the question Madley had to answer was whether the contact by Madueke on Mac Allister added up to violent conduct. Clearly the answer to that was no. Madley gave a yellow card to Mac Allister but not to Madueke, who had been carded earlier, and the VAR did not intervene to recommend a review given there was no evidence of a missed red card. Madley deserves all the compliments he received for the way he handled it.

This was the busiest weekend of the season so far for VAR, with seven overturns across the first nine games. One intervention helps to draw a contrast with what happened, or did not happen, at Anfield, and that’s the decision to send off Jean-Philippe Mateta after VAR upgraded a yellow card to a red.

The situation followed a foul by the Crystal Palace striker early in their game against Tottenham. Mateta was trying to recover possession and tackled Micky van de Ven from behind. The Frenchman was awarded a yellow card by the referee, Michael Oliver, but when the VAR, Jarred Gillett, reviewed the footage he could see that not only was Mateta coming in from behind, he was well away from the ball and made full contact with his studs on Van de Ven’s achilles. Gillett recommended that Oliver go to the monitor to review his decision, which he did, sending Mateta off.

The VAR can initiate a review if he believes a “serious incident” has been missed by the referee. Here, Gillett was able to see what Oliver couldn’t: that Mateta’s challenge was a case of serious foul play which occurs when a player endangers the safety of an opponent or uses excessive force. The contact with Van de Ven’s achilles was clearly dangerous. It clears the high bar for intervention in a way that the pull on Isak did not. It was a good piece of work by Gillett and Oliver.

Elsewhere, VAR helped to achieve the correct outcome in a number of crucial events. An overturn in the Aston Villa v Fulham match rightly ended in Villa being awarded a penalty after the ball struck the arm of Sander Berge in an unnatural position. Chelsea were given a penalty against Manchester United after an aggressive challenge by Lisandro Martínez, who led with an arm, was initially missed on-field. Martínez was correctly handed a second yellow card, and a dismissal. At Stamford Bridge there were also two goals – one for each side – correctly overturned after they were assessed by the VAR using semi‑automated offside technology.

Sign up to Football Daily

Coventry conceded a penalty in their 3-1 win against Sunderland after the VAR spotted a handball by Ethan Pinnock. Leeds had a goal overturned at Bournemouth after Dominic Calvert-Lewin was found to have handled the ball on its way into the net, which has to be disallowed even if accidental under the laws of the game.

That is a lot of activity at the Premier League’s VAR hub and the most notable thing was overall how quickly and smoothly it was dealt with by various sets of officials. Debate over the Isak decision may provide the main refereeing talking point before the next round of fixtures, but we should also take note when the system is working as it should.

Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:07:40 GMT

After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives

Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack

Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F).

The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SupaValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia.

It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software.

Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.

This is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control.

No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay – which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat.

“The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos.

The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea is believed to have been behind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame.

Western intelligence chiefs say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months.

Discerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”.

The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates.

Nick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline – an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”.

In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France.

The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France.

In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NSCC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.

Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout.

Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”.

A spokesperson for the NCSC said it was “working with its international partners and industry to fully understand details of an incident”.

Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 19:06:40 GMT

Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years

Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade.

Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.

But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement.

The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”.

But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement.

She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”

In particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.

The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.

Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.

Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”

The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.

The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”.

She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”

Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.

Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element.

“People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”

But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.

The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.

Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.

In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.

Home Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood’s softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.

Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years.

The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds.

Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.

Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn’t unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”

Business groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.

Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.

The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood’s decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.

Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.

The Guardian view on a migration U-turn: it still leaves unfair changes intact

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:53:07 GMT

Britain needs migrant workers, yet ministers would make many wait longer for secure settlement because their essential work commands low wages

Shabana Mahmood has made a partial retreat on her policy to lengthen the wait for some foreign workers who were soon to be eligible for settlement in the UK. But while the home secretary lost the argument in cabinet on a particularly damaging aspect of her proposals, she has won the larger battle that settlement ought to be based not just on residency but also on how much tax has been paid, English language proficiency and the “character” of applicants. Significantly, she has also won the “full support” of the prime minister for this approach.

The home secretary plans to double the standard qualifying period for settlement from five to 10 years for most workers. Importantly, she dropped the proposed 15-year qualifying period for some workers in occupations below graduate level. That is a good thing. Differences in pay, however, should not determine how soon people can put down secure roots. The Home Office’s own figures suggest that a person earning £41,700 makes a similarly positive lifetime fiscal contribution as someone earning £50,271. But the former has to wait five years longer to qualify for settlement than the latter. It is only three years for foreign workers who make enough to be in the top 2% of earners – about £125,000.

It was right that Britain recruited people to perform essential care work after the pandemic to fill gaps in the workforce. But it was wrong for Ms Mahmood to propose using the poor remuneration of that work to delay their permanent place in society. Ms Mahmood’s concession corrects that for some people. But it will cause insecurity for others. Those who came to this country between 2022 and 2025, meet their care worker visa conditions and are paid £25,000 or more will still be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) – effectively permanent residency – after five years. The Home Office says that that could cover as many as 146,000 care workers and 136,000 dependants.

However, those who do not meet the requirements will have to get another five-year “health and social care” visa before applying for ILR. The care sector has been beset by allegations that unscrupulous employers have exploited migrant staff by taking advantage of their vulnerable visa status. The government is less clear about how it will be able to tell whether earnings had been deliberately kept low by unprincipled firms.

On asylum, Ms Mahmood makes settlement depend on how people reached Britain. Those admitted through “safe and legal” routes can settle after five years; others face much longer waits – up to 30 years for “illegal entry” by small boat, even after their need for protection has been recognised. But the UN says that refugees cannot apply directly for UK resettlement. Ministers must explain how penalising people for failing to use a route largely unavailable to them amounts to fair play.

Ms Mahmood’s plans are a step towards a Gastarbeiter Britain. The guest-worker logic of the home secretary’s proposals – like that of postwar West Germany – is to admit foreigners to fill labour shortages in lower-earning work while keeping their membership of society conditional. Calling this integration seems a stretch. Settling down, changing jobs at will and planning a family life are how people put down roots. Ms Mahmood’s plans are likely to frustrate the integration that she says she wants.

The Guardian view on Poland’s political turmoil: an ominous portent of bigger battles to come

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:52:32 GMT

Donald Tusk is attempting to restore legitimacy to the country’s constitutional court. In a polarised country and continent, that carries political risks

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, must occasionally look towards Budapest and sigh. A landslide victory in elections last spring enabled Hungary’s new prime minister, Péter Magyar, to act with ruthless determination to clean up the country’s politics after 16 years of corrupt Orbánisation. Mr Tusk, whose centrist coalition ousted the far-right Law and Justice party (PiS) in 2023, is similarly taking on the legacy of a government which undermined the rule of law and democratic norms. But his efforts have been relentlessly boxed in by the blocking tactics of Poland’s (PiS)‑backed president, Karol Nawrocki.

At the weekend, this standoff escalated into a crisis with wider implications for the European Union as well as Poland itself. Exasperated by Mr Nawrocki’s attempts to veto the appointment of new judges to the country’s constitutional court – which has been illegitimately dominated since 2015 by PiS‑friendly appointees – Mr Tusk backed the enforced appointment of a new head, and the suspension of the court’s president and vice‑president. Extraordinary scenes followed, as rightwing demonstrators massed outside the court building in the early hours of Saturday morning and Mr Nawrocki pushed past security forces to protest.

As a high-octane constitutional confrontation now plays out, the legal and moral facts of the case are on Mr Tusk’s side. Last month, the Venice Commission, an advisory body of the Council of Europe, ruled that the new judges had the constitutional right to take up their positions with or without Mr Nawrocki’s endorsement. The European Commission, which spent years confronting PiS governments over rule-of-law issues, reaffirmed that position on Sunday. Over the course of two terms in office, PiS ministers made concerted attempts to intimidate judges and manipulate the judicial system to create an unlevel playing field for their political battles. The weekend’s drama is the result of Mr Tusk’s legitimate attempt to deal with illegalities perpetrated in that period.

Nevertheless, this feels like a risky move ahead of an election due by next autumn in a deeply polarised country. Mr Tusk’s decision to force the issue in such a way has potentially handed a political opportunity to PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, who is in need of a cause to unite a far right that has split three ways. More broadly, Marine Le Pen has used the crisis to decry a rise in “strong‑arm tactics” in the EU. The tone of her intervention echoed comments by Mr Kaczyński, who last week accused Brussels of wishing to turn the EU into a centralised state and suggested that like-minded nationalist governments may choose to rebel.

With elections imminent in Spain and France, as well as Poland, Europe’s far right is manoeuvring ahead of a period that it hopes will change the balance of power in the continent’s politics and precipitate open confrontation with Brussels. Given her intention to challenge the primacy of EU law on migration, Ms Le Pen will soon be involved in her own legal controversies should she win the French presidency in the spring. Playing fast and loose with the rule of law and attacking those who resist as “enemies of the people” was the go-to tactic for Poland’s far right throughout its eight years in office. Its revival in Warsaw at the weekend feels like an ominous portent of confrontations to come.

Melbourne Cup betting rules show UK the way to prevent illegal gambling boom

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:28:56 GMT

From January, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulation

The 2026 Melbourne Cup is not due off until 4am GMT on Tuesday – which is 3pm local time on what is still a public holiday in the state of Victoria – but there has already been some spectacular action in the betting market for the “race that stops a nation” over the last few hours, with the Irish punting legend JP McManus, no less, leading the charge.

McManus and his fellow owner, Paul Byrne, were among the attendees at the “Call Of The Card” luncheon, a A$340-a-head (£178) event in Melbourne on Monday, which has been a popular feature of the big-race buildup since 1958.

The centrepiece of the event sees four leading bookmakers “take on the room”, and give everyone in the 1,000-strong sell-out audience a chance to back each of the 24 runners, starting with the outsiders and concluding with the market leaders.

When George Boughey’s Hopewell Rock, the runner-up in the Ebor Handicap at York in August, was offered to the room at $10 – ie 9-1 – Byrne immediately grabbed the microphone (at 2h31m in the video of the event here). “We’ve travelled a long way now,” Byrne said, “and this is the horse, we’ve been studying the form on the way down we’re thinking we might try and beat last year’s record [bet of A$500,000] and get us a million dollars win.”

A million to win A$10m is a chunky bet even by Australian standards, and after one of the four bookies agreed to lay A$500,000 at 9-1 and another accepted A$30,000, the remaining A$470,000 was laid at 17-2 and 8-1.

McManus and Byrne also placed bets on several more runners, including Joseph O’Brien’s James J Braddock (A$150,000 at 20-1), and McManus’s own runners in the race, Trustyourinstinct and Goodie Two Shoes, last year’s runner-up.

It is perhaps no great surprise that a lifelong punter (and former bookie) like McManus was in his element as he experienced Monday’s event for the first time. “I certainly enjoyed it. It’s exciting, I must say,” he told the Racing Post afterwards. “It’s something different and I think we can learn from it. I don’t know if anything like this will ever happen in Britain and Ireland, but it certainly adds to the occasion and it creates a lot of excitement. I only wish they would do it elsewhere.”

For a punter and racing fan following the event on the other side of the world, meanwhile, it was a fascinating glimpse into a very different betting culture, not least on the bookies’ side of the equation.

There are many thousands of racing fans in the UK and Ireland who will greet the sight of a bookie laying a sizeable bet with a hollow laugh. For years, backers – or rather, would-be backers – have seen their accounts closed or restricted to betting in pennies if there is any hint that they might turn a long-term profit from their betting.

Australia, though, has an official Minimum Bet Limit (MBL) for racing, which requires an operator to lay an advertised price to lose a standard minimum amount, currently A$2,000 on a major race like the Melbourne Cup.

That is, clearly, well below the level at which McManus and Byrne – and many of the other punters at “Call of the Card” – are playing, but establishes the principle that when a bookie advertises a price, the backers deserve a fair crack before it is cut. There were occasional boos, in fact, at Monday’s event in Melbourne when Robbie Waterhouse, perhaps the most familiar name in Australian bookmaking, offered a price that was a half-point or point below his rivals, or accepted only part of a requested stake.

The MBL is not the only aspect of Australian gambling and betting culture and legislation that differs markedly from that in Britain. Operators have been banned from offering online slot-machine gaming to Australian customers, for instance, since 2001, and subsequent legislation passed by the Australian parliament in August will make it much more difficult for Australians to access illegal offshore casinos.

We have, of course, heard a great deal about the illegal market in this country in recent years, as the Betting and Gaming Council, the main industry body, has often claimed that tax hikes on gambling will inevitably push gamblers towards unregulated, offshore alternatives.

Yet nothing has done more to push racing punters towards the illegal market over the last 20 years than the operators’ own use of restrictions and account closures against punters who are – or simply threaten to be – long-term winners.

Warwick 12.18 Un Sens A La Vie 12.53 Kelly Burn 1.28 Trigg 2.03 Lucy The Wire 2.38 Court In A Storm 3.13 I Love You Sivola 3.48 Ballymoreen

Sedgefield 12.44 Jeteye 1.19 Moment Of Light 1.54 Roxy Russet 2.29 Treaty Boy 3.04 Cadillac Ranch 3.39 Curious Mrs Fox

Lingfield 1.02 Burk Flight 1.37 Analogical 2.12 Chosen Hero 2.47 Away For The Night 3.22 Calshot Spit 3.57 A Great Excuse

Wolverhampton 4.30 Mini Mac (nb) 5.00 Sonbelievable 5.30 Crown Of Ivy 6.00 Red Blue Point 6.30 Fancy Dancer 7.00 Politely 7.30 Lipsink (nap) 8.00 Tiger Beetle 8.30 Man Of Desert

From 1 January 2027, when the latest legislation comes into force, Australia will arguably be a world leader in gambling regulation, and an essential part of that is the fact that the country’s lawmakers see and understand the distinction between the most harmful forms of gambling – casino-gaming and slots – and betting on sport. They are also taking meaningful steps to protect their citizens from the dangers of the unregulated market, while ensuring that bookies will lay an advertised price to a reasonable sum.

There will, surely, be many lessons there for our own government to absorb, if or when a successor to the outdated Gambling Act 2005 finally appears on the horizon.

French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 18:17:33 GMT

Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday

Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living.

The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.

As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end the lycée blockades, which have been running since September and have prompted one of the biggest protest movements and social crises of his presidency.

From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demanding more replacement teachers and repairs to buildings barricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.

University students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities across France to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.

Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.

He said measures offered by the government last week to cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.

He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”

Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.

How the EU can resist the divisive influence of the far right

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 17:58:01 GMT

Thomas Laffitte on the threats facing the European Union and Giorgio Re on why the strongest defence must come from the democratic right and centre-right

Your editorial rightly highlights the European far right’s maturing plans for Brussels’ political machinery (The Guardian view on the far right’s plans for Brussels: doing the work of Xi, Putin and Trump, 27 October). Alongside these developments, the evolution of Euroscepticism itself deserves closer attention.

As I argued in a recent report from the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics, anti-EU politics may have entered a phase of “post-Euroscepticism”. The discourse remains, but the ambition to dismantle the union has increasingly given way to blocking the march towards an ever closer union while retaining the existing structure and exploiting it.

Ten years after Brexit, this shift reflects a deeper change in the global geopolitical order. With the return of great-power politics and the rise of geoeconomic rivalries, even radical nationalists may be reluctant to part with the great instrument of power that the EU has become. Giorgia Meloni’s unexpectedly pragmatic approach to EU cooperation is a prime example.

The EU’s institutional architecture offers some resilience. Its weak centre and dispersion of authority make it comparatively difficult for any one government to capture the entire polity. Yet this strength is also a weakness. Institutional divisions can translate into misalignment, dysfunction and, ultimately, decay. The EU will endure, but escalating nationalist rivalries risk compounding this tendency for inertia and the irrelevance that results.

This makes the negotiations over the next multi-annual financial framework (2028–34) particularly important. The EU must strengthen its competitiveness and strategic autonomy, while preserving the cohesion funds that remain one of its greatest success stories. Peripheral regions, where Euroscepticism has gained considerable ground, must not be forgotten.

The danger facing Europe is no longer confined the prospect of its dismantlement. It also lies in the erosion of its capacity to act at a time when the return of geopolitics makes collective European power increasingly necessary. Thomas Laffitte Research fellow, Brussels Institute for Geopolitics

I felt compelled to write this letter after reading your editorial. I believe my feelings are shared by millions of Europeans whose voices are too often overlooked in today’s political debate – Europeans who value the freedom to live, study, work, do business and access healthcare across borders. And who believe that our common future deserves greater ambition.

As an Italian, coming from one of the six founding countries of European integration, and as a committed liberal conservative, I see no contradiction between defending individual freedoms, free enterprise, national identities and a stronger EU. Quite the opposite: in a world increasingly shaped by competing superpowers, European sovereignty can only be meaningfully exercised together.

However, defending Europe also requires acknowledging its shortcomings. Excessive bureaucracy, fragmented decision-making, sluggish economic growth and inadequate coordination on immigration and defence have contributed to public frustration. These deserve serious political answers rather than being dismissed as expressions of Euroscepticism.

That’s why I also believe that the strongest defence against nationalism must come from Europe’s democratic right and centre-right. We need European institutions that concentrate on what we can achieve better together: defence, external borders, strategic infrastructure, research and foreign policy. Mainstream conservative parties must resist the temptation to imitate nationalist rhetoric. They should instead articulate a confident, patriotic and genuinely pro-European alternative.

Some of Europe’s founding fathers, including Alcide De Gasperi, Konrad Adenauer and Robert Schuman, came from the Christian democratic tradition of the political centre-right. Their successors have a responsibility to carry that ambition forward.

I remain optimistic. Millions of centre-right Europeans believe in democracy, freedom and European unity. Their political voice could prove decisive in Europe’s future. Giorgio Re Agrigento, Sicily, Italy

Levelling up projects require long-term commitment

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 17:57:35 GMT

Dr Rob Richardson and Dr Olivier Sykes argue that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary term

The fact that the vast majority of levelling up projects are unfinished is disappointing, but not surprising (Most levelling up projects still unfinished years after funding allocate, 24 October). Trying to push through such top-down projects in unrealistic timescales, hoping for electoral rewards, was a characteristically misguided approach from Boris Johnson’s government. Decades of UK and EU policy experience show that urban regeneration takes time to plan and deliver, over periods that extend beyond one parliamentary term.

Recent research from the universities of Manchester, Liverpool and Salford engages with several local authorities in north-west England that are still committed to these projects. Our findings show that addressing regional inequalities requires stable, long-term funding, and targeted support for local capacity to deliver. One positive from levelling up was that many authorities began to rebuild some of the regeneration skills and capacity lost over a decade of austerity – although such gains were mitigated by the resources needed for competitive bidding, and uncertainty around the rules governing funding eligibility.

It is to be hoped that Andy Burnham’s government learns from this, and that local leaders and communities are given the stability and tools to deliver long-term regeneration where it is most needed. Dr Rob Richardson Lecturer in urban planning and placemaking, University of Manchester Dr Olivier Sykes Senior lecturer in European spatial planning, University of Liverpool

Brickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloom

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 17:23:41 GMT

Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter

With John Healey’s Your First Home scheme on the way, is the mood improving in the housebuilding sector? A couple of the builders have results later this week, so can speak for themselves. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it.

Industry data, said Ibstock, show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. For the whole of the third quarter, it said, sales were 22% below expectations, forcing a one-fifth cut in its production volumes versus plans set out as recently as August.

Cue an 11% fall in the share price to virtually its lowest level since the firm relisted on the stock market in 2015. Top-line earnings for the whole of 2026 will be “in the mid-£40m range” versus a figure close to £60m expected by the City.

The short moral from Ibstock’s woes is that the sector’s slowdown is pretty entrenched. Across the board, we’ve heard shareholder-friendly vows from housebuilders of “financial discipline”, corporate-speak for saying expansion is off the table and the job is about hammering away at costs. Berkeley Homes, focused on the south-east of England, even said six months ago it will stop buying new land and hiring new staff.

Everybody knows one deep cause: the turnaround in interest rate expectations with the Iran war. The Bank of England will probably raise rates this week (finally); then we’ll be on to wondering how many more increases will follow. In addition, housebuilders complain about costs of regulation that are harder to lose when the prices of new houses are going sideways.

So is Healey’s Your First Home a reheat of Help to Buy, a gamechanger? From the point of view of housebuilders, the scheme is clearly welcome – they had been lobbying for action for ages. But there are a couple of caveats. First, the caps on the size of the transactions means it is not a copycat scheme for the very good reason that Healey can’t be seen to be adding too much inflationary pressure at a time like now.

Second, it will only be launched next April, the chancellor said in his budget last week. The delay “may weigh on demand in the intervening period”, Ibstock chief executive Joe Hudson said, echoing others. He is surely right: for many qualifying buyers, it will make sense to wait five months for the discounted loans.

Healey also said there will be no more changes to building regulations in this parliament (except where critical for safety), a nod towards the sector’s other grumble. On the other hand, he’s not proposing to remove existing regulations.

So one suspects 2027 – a year of 1% growth in the economy, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts – is probably not going to move housebuilding volumes meaningfully. Your First Home should be “modestly helpful”, reckons Peel Hunt, but “lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity”. Yes, it all comes back to borrowing costs. And the upturn, when it comes, will surely be too late to save the government’s ambition of 1.5m new homes this parliament. The target isn’t officially rubble, but it may as well be.

A decade of magical thinking since Brexit has taught me that it’s always OK to hope for better

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 17:01:41 GMT

The world has changed enormously since 2016, yet the pro-Brexiters believe remainers like me have no chance of achieving a closer relationship with the EU. I’m choosing to ignore them

However sunny your disposition, it wears you down, 10 straight years of being asked to accept facts about Brexit that aren’t true: 52% as an “overwhelming majority”; a flaky, half-baked referendum as the endpoint of purest democracy; the severance of a complicated trading and geopolitical relationship that took decades to build as the dawn of a new prosperity. All such nonsense, all delivered with such conviction, by such a wide variety of sources, many of them self-describing as impartial, that in the end you just surrender to it. None of it magically becomes true, don’t be silly. It’s more that you come to accept that everyone else talks nonsense now.

Nobody get too excited – just because Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that upside-down world said couldn’t be reopened, it doesn’t mean the UK is on the brink of coming to its senses. I have no idea what’s going to happen; all I can say for certain is that times have changed more than I realised. The pro-Brexit crew have updated their arguments. They no longer say leaving the EU will bring untold riches, and they never even namecheck all the control we were meant to have taken back. They rarely mention any immigration benefits because that unwieldy issue now has a life of its own – or, to put that more simply, it turns out that in or out of the European Union, we can still fight about our borders like rats in a sack.

Instead, they have a new narrative, and these are its contours. Remain sympathisers are apparently very divided. Some of us want freedom of movement, especially for young people, while others of us just want our trading relationships rebuilt with our nearest gigantic market. Different remainers again wish for greater collaboration on security and defence with nations who share our values. Those who can be trusted, for example, to oppose Vladimir Putin and his war of aggression, rather than opposing him on a Tuesday and calling him a great guy by Thursday. Some of us just miss the days when we made coherent, continent-wide decisions about the climate emergency. Given that degrees of global heating observe no nationality and pick no favourites, given that people who believe in scientific evidence tend to get on quite well together, however stark that evidence is, it would be quite relaxing to club together, no?

All these different interest groups, I’ve heard it said by those who defend the status quo, can cooperate from a distance, but sooner or later, the remain coalition will fall apart. Here, I rediscover the certainty I thought I’d lost for ever in the post-2016 melee: there is absolutely no way will we fall apart. We are a match made in heaven. I have a fair idea which of those issues I care about the most, between climate, young people, defence and trade, but seriously, this is like choosing my favourite song on Surfer Rosa (the Pixies album), or adjudicating my favourite guest at the wedding of, say, my sister. In the joy of the moment, my preferences could take a backseat. I’d really just want everyone to have a good time.

There’s one other new rhetorical strain: Brexit supporters point to Europe and say, that place is on fire. It’s not a blip caused by arson-happy French protesters, nor the housing-impoverished Spanish, it’s not a peculiarity of new German political movements, nor rage at the policing tactics of the Portuguese. Everyone, everywhere, is absolutely furious. Would this not be a good time to keep our distance? This might be the weakest argument of all, since all it underscores is that the cost of living crisis affects us all; the wars in Ukraine and Iran have hit everyone; the long tail of the financial crash and subsequent austerity has left no one unscathed; the disfigurement of the housing market was only temporarily a London thing, a Madrid thing – sooner or later, it would be an everywhere thing, and later’s where we are. There is no isolationist course that protects you from civic unrest, unless you can miraculously protect yourself from the conditions driving it. And those conditions were not made in Strasbourg.

Again, if a decade of magical thinking has taught me anything, it’s that predictions are futile, and however absurd an argument looks, you can’t bank on toppling it. But these fresh lines are so weak it’s almost endearing.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

‘It’s really, really unusual’: tender bond between male donkey and bull baffles scientists

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:53:15 GMT

Patroclo and Achille’s interspecies affair sheds new light on social and sexual relations between animals, scientists say

In ancient myth, Achilles and Patroclus were two Greek heroes of the Trojan war whose intense bond was believed by some to have turned into a sexual relationship.

In modern science, they are a bull, Achille, and a donkey, Patroclo, whose tender interspecies affair has helped to shed new light on social and sexual interactions between animals.

Researchers say the two males have been spotted licking and rubbing each other, with the bull sometimes mounting the donkey.

The team said while other donkeys attempted to avoid Achille’s attentions and showed threatening facial expressions towards him, Patroclo often presented his hindquarters to Achille and nibbled him.

“It is really, really unusual,” said Dr Elisabetta Palagi of the University of Pisa in Italy, who co-authored the study. “And it is the first time it is reported in literature.”

André da Cruz, a PhD student at the University of Pisa and another author, said the relationship had been discovered by accident while the researchers studied geladas, or bleeding-heart monkeys, in Ethiopia.

“We were having a little break for lunch, and in the distance I see something – it seemed a bit odd,” said da Cruz. “I told colleagues: ‘I think I saw a bull mounting a donkey.’ And they didn’t believe me.”

Writing in the journal Current Biology, the researchers said the bull and the donkey belonged to different owners and only came into contact with each other when, as part of their daily routine, their herds used the same pasture.

The researchers studied Achille and Patroclo over four days when they were both grazing in the same area, and four days when only one was present.

The team not only recorded 51 mountings of Patroclo by Achille, but noted licking and rubbing often occurred before and, more surprisingly, after such events.

“Rather than being solely attributable to sexual arousal, these interactions appear to play a role in prolonging the social interaction beyond the sexual act,” they wrote.

Despite ample opportunity, neither Achille nor Patroclo tried to mount a member of their own species of either sex, although Achille did show courtship behaviours towards some female cattle.

Sign up to Down to Earth

The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential

after newsletter promotion

While rare, there have been other examples of interspecies hanky-panky, including a case of a male snow monkey attempting to have sex with female sika deer, and an Antarctic fur seal that not only sexually harassed king penguins but engaged in necrophilia.

However, Palagi said there was no indication that the relationship between the donkey and the bull involved force.

“We interpret our data as a special relationship,” Palagi said, adding that the two males searched for each other. “When Achille approached someone else in the plateau, Patroclo went to him and tried to distract him,” she said.

Da Cruz said the mounting behaviour of Achille was unlikely to simply be a case of the bull exerting dominance.

“We saw on several occasions what might have been semen from the bull, or he might have been orgasming, although we cannot verify [that] completely,” da Cruz said, adding that Patroclo was highly aggressive to bulls other than Achille.

Palagi added that the relationship was an example of a sexual interaction that was disentangled from reproductive function.

“When two individuals belonging to the same species or different species need to develop a special relationship, they fish simply from their entire [behavioural] repertoire,” she said.

Palagi said it was unclear whether the sexual and social relationship between Patroclo and Achille had always co-existed or if one had led to the other. But, she added, the bond appeared to bring benefits, both in terms of attention but potentially also support.

Josh Luke Davis, the author of A Little Gay Natural History, said interspecies relationships were not necessarily unusual and that the widespread and common nature of queer behaviours in the natural world meant it was “probably not that surprising” that they overlapped.

“There is obviously value in reporting these kinds of behaviours,” Davis added. “But I would caution against reading too much into the significance of it and would be concerned about how it could be misconstrued or twisted by those who already deem homosexuality ‘unnatural’.”

Rachel Reeves and the Starmerites are back – and they’re pointing out how little has changed

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:42:18 GMT

Labour’s recently departed grandees are keen to defend their legacies. Is Andy Burnham really offering Britain something new?

Rachel Reeves wants you to know she thinks Britain’s future belongs in Europe. She would also like to mention that she “absolutely” got all the big calls right as chancellor, even if there were a few things she would have done differently, and that John Healey’s budget last week would have been far harder for him if she hadn’t put in so much of the groundwork.

The gist of her argument in last weekend’s Sunday papers – previewing a lecture at Harvard University today, reflecting on her time in power – was essentially that if anyone imagines Andy Burnham somehow invented pro-Europeanism and putting more money in people’s pockets, they can think again.

Reeves was clearly devastated by losing a job she loved, and her return to the fray after a summer of quietly licking her wounds has inevitably sparked speculation over whether she now seeks a comeback. But her timing is acute enough to suggest that this goes a little deeper, coming as it does days after a deliberately low-key budget that left some Labour MPs wondering what happened to the much-hyped end of neoliberalism.

How much of the Burnham agenda is really new, and how much is essentially the old Starmer one, repackaged with rather more warmth, charm and political skill?

Inside what’s left of the old inner circle, loyalists point out that Reeves and Starmer were both fervent remainers at heart and of course they would have loved to be back inside the EU one day; it’s just that the time wasn’t yet right to talk about it when they ran for office.

Similarly, the package of sanctions on Israeli settlers that the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced in September, alongside an apology for what he considered Starmer had got wrong on Gaza, wasn’t a dramatic break with the past but essentially the measures his predecessor, Yvette Cooper (now health secretary), had spent her last weeks at the Foreign Office working up, which couldn’t be published until a new prime minister was formally in place.

Starmer’s former close lieutenant Darren Jones, meanwhile, is openly arguing that this administration’s answer to a looming crisis in defence spending – basically shunting the hard questions about funding it into next year’s spending review – is “what Keir and Rachel were going to do”, if only they hadn’t been forced out by the very same John Healey resigning as defence secretary in protest at something remarkably like the strategy he’s now pursuing. Starmer himself, who has kept his counsel over the summer, made a rare public intervention in Dublin last week to warn pointedly that the US withdrawal from European defence will outlast the Trump era, and Europe cannot afford to be left exposed.

If the Starmerites are understandably smarting at what some see as history being rewritten by the winners, some are also failing to recognise their part in their own downfall. Starmer was ultimately ousted by his own MPs because they wereexasperated by his failure to lead and sensed the country had turned inexorably against him.

Burnham has shown not only that he can take decisions – across Whitehall there seems to be more clarity now about what Downing Street wants – but that he can build the emotional bond with the public his predecessor couldn’t, without which even the boldest moves wouldn’t have worked. He might only have moved the needle fractionally on issues such as Palestine or Europe, where the manifesto red lines effectively mean nothing significant can change that wouldn’t have under Starmer, at least this side of a general election. But each time he has done just enough to achieve the political impact that Starmer was seemingly chasing but couldn’t pull off. Where his predecessor could never quite get the dosage right, Burnham seems to instinctively know how far to go: it’s the difference between a novice cook clinging fixedly to a recipe that isn’t quite right, and an experienced one who tastes and adjusts the seasoning as they go. And judging by the polling, it’s working.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Yet still some MPs are anxious to hear a bigger vision of where Burnham wants the country to go than fixing social care and banning people listening to loud music on the bus. Since there wasn’t one in the budget, all eyes are on the 10-year plan, now expected some time in December.

Burnham has made much of promising to give Britain some breathing space after years of rolling crises and financial struggle. But the small, popular changes he has offered so far – £100 off your energy bills, a No 10 North office in Manchester – have also been in part about buying some breathing space for himself while he gets to grips with bigger and potentially more controversial challenges, from welfare reforms to defusing a Labour revolt over Shabana Mahmood’s plan to make migrants wait longer for the right to settlement.

A confident and relaxed debut has masked the fact that transitioning from mayor to prime minister was always going to be a steep learning curve, and that he didn’t get the long summer of planning that his team had wanted to prepare for power. But now that period of grace is coming to an end, along with a period of silence from those he ousted, some of whom are keen to defend their legacies. By Christmas we should know whether Burnham is offering genuine new thinking in British politics, or something more like the old kind, regifted.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:39:20 GMT

Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops

Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?

Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France.

Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked.

The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros.

A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”.

The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit.

It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.”

A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.”

He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.

The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops.

after newsletter promotion

“It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly.

Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result.

In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected.

At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster.

“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

Ireland’s third-largest supermarket ⁠chain, ⁠SuperValu, said ​refrigeration systems limited ⁠to ​a ‌specific ‌model ‌in 13 of its 223 shops ‌had been affected by ​a cyber-incident, ⁠and that chilled and ​frozen products ​had been removed from ​sale.

Many cyber-attacks involve extortion or are politically motivated and are potentially carried out by state-level actors, said Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne. But the supermarket attacks, with no financial demands, point to sabotage, he said.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Hegel told Reuters.

Patrick Lamplmair of the cybersecurity firm Tributech said cyber-attackers would keep going “until it stops working” because the method was “cheap and the damage is immediate”. Many refrigeration systems had known and as yet unfixed flaws, he said.

“Thousands of these controllers were still reachable from the internet after the French attack,” he added. “A few commands to a temperature controller can destroy stock overnight and close stores.”

In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss, which said subsequently that it had identified some security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The hackers remotely overrode the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets at chains including Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C.

The shops had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products. Individual supermarkets reportedly suffered losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000).

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigation into the French attack and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, Ansii, to investigate.

The agency subsequently reported that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies had also been targeted in the attack, but authorities have not indicated who could have been behind the incidents. There have been no claims of responsibility.
