Newcastle hospital told woman whose unborn baby had died to go home and ‘book a slot to give birth’

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 16:36:27 GMT

Trust admits Danielle Brown’s baby would have survived had she not been sent home from RVI days earlier

A woman whose unborn baby had died was sent home from hospital with a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth.

Danielle Brown, 31, was seven months pregnant when she was first discharged from hospital with pre-eclampsia, a potentially life-threatening pregnancy complication. She returned to hospital days later, when scans revealed that her daughter, Maisie, had died.

Brown said she was devastated to have to return home knowing the baby she was carrying was no longer alive. “When it was confirmed Maisie had died, we burst into tears. Nobody explained what had happened to Maisie,” she said.

Brown, from North Shields in north-east England, said she was then “given a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth”. She said: “Hearing that with no compassion angered me so much.”

Brown and her partner, Anthony Miller, were delighted to be expecting a baby but seven months into the pregnancy, in February 2023, she fell ill and was diagnosed with pre-eclampsia. Monitoring by doctors at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI), Newcastle, had also raised concerns about Maisie’s heart rate.

A consultant obstetrician said Brown should remain in hospital until she gave birth, given her potentially life-threatening condition. However, she was discharged 24 hours later on 14 February after a review by a different consultant.

A day later, Brown phoned the RVI’s maternity assessment unit with more concerns but was told she probably had a stomach bug.

She insisted on being seen and returned to the hospital, waited 90 minutes to be assessed, and was told medics could not find Maisie’s heartbeat. The couple were then told that their baby had died.

Instead of delivering Maisie straight away, Brown said she was handed a booklet for bereaved parents and told to book a slot to give birth on another day,

Brown spoke of her ordeal after being awarded an undisclosed settlement from Newcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS foundation trust. The trust admitted a breach of duty and that Maisie would have survived had her mother not been sent home during her first admission.

Faisal Ali, of the solicitors Irwin Mitchell, said pre-eclampsia was serious and required close monitoring.

“What happened to Danielle and Maisie vividly highlights the human cost of care failings and how families left needing answers and access to specialist support are left trying to pick up the pieces,” he said. “Sadly, this isn’t an isolated case and we represent hundreds of families nationally affected by maternity failings.

“Put simply, maternity services aren’t good enough, resulting in mums and babies being put at risk because of deep-rooted problems nationally.”

The couple have since had a son, Harrison, who is two.

“While we feel so blessed to have Harrison, it remains difficult knowing Maisie should be here with us too. She will always be part of our family,” Brown said. “More needs to be done not only to improve maternity care but also, when something goes wrong, families need proper and compassionate support.

“After saying goodbye to Maisie, we had to walk through a labour ward seeing parents going home with their babies. That will stay with me for ever.”

Ian Joy, an executive director at Newcastle upon Tyne hospitals NHS foundation trust, said: “Maisie’s family have experienced a devastating loss which has undoubtedly had a profound effect on everyone who loved her.

“We fully accept that aspects of the care we provided fell short of the standards the family had every right to expect and offer a heartfelt apology for this. Following a detailed review in 2023, we improved urgent assessment for women who come to our maternity services with unexpected symptoms or suspected complications.”

The trust had recently been assessed as performing well against national standards, Joy said.

Name: Greenland (or Kalaallit Nunaat, the land of the people in the Greenlandic language).

Age: The landmass is believed to have been settled about 2500BC.

Appearance: Huge (2,166,086 sq km), almost 80% ice and 100% excited to welcome more tourists.

So, 80% ice, eh? That doesn’t make Greenland the easiest sell for tourists. There are also no roads outside towns. But there is a new international airport in Ilulissat, known as the “city of icebergs” and Greenland’s third-largest city, offering direct flights from Denmark and Iceland. Joining the airports opened in Nuuk (the capital) in 2024 and in Qaqortoq in April, it means Greenland is now extremely open for tourist business.

Really? It still seems awfully remote. Yes – it welcomed more visitors than ever before in 2025 – nearly 180,000 (the population is only 56,000) – and this year is set to beat that.

Aren’t Greenlanders unhappy about being outnumbered? Lots of destinations now want less tourism, not more. Yes, local people in tourist hotspots – especially in Spain, Portugal, Italy and France – have protested at how tourism negatively affects their lives. It’s an issue in Greenland, too – when Nuuk airport opened, there was concern about how the influx of tourists might affect a historically isolated population and pristine environment. A cruise ship was also blocked from entering Ilulissat, where locals feel they see little benefit from foreign tourist operations.

So Greenland isn’t, actually, ‘100% excited’ to welcome tourists? OK, no. There’s still ambivalence, but Donald Trump and the climate crisis may be shifting perspectives. The president’s threat to acquire Greenland filled inhabitants with anger and apprehension, while disruption from melting polar ice means the traditional fishing industry is existentially threatened. The country is also striving for independence from Denmark: “If Greenland wants to be independent, we need to have a strong foundation, economically and in terms of industry and business,” prime minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen commented on Ilulissat’s maiden flight.

I suppose it’s never going to be rammed like Ibiza either. There is actually a vibrant music culture, with lively hip-hop and heavy metal scenes, and an Indigenous Electronic music festival in Nuuk, but no. Tourism only accounted for 4.9% of GDP in 2024.

Is a new airport enough to attract more visitors? Maybe Visit Greenland could take inspiration from other chilly destinations that are getting creative about attracting tourists: Finland’s Turku archipelago is hiring a smell ambassador to promote what it calls “the best-smelling destination in the world”.

I wonder how Greenland smells? Delicious, like roasted reindeer; fascinating like fermented seal blubber. You can also enjoy whale watching, dog sledding or ice fishing and bathe in hot springs. Plus, it looks extraordinary – the stunning spectacle of the polar ice sheet, astonishing icebergs, exquisite light (including the northern lights and the midnight sun) and unparalleled darkness. Way to up your Instagram game.

Sold! Get me on the first flight to Ilulissat! Angalalluarina (that’s bon voyage, apparently).

Do say: “Tikilluarit!” (Welcome!)

Don’t say: “Unless your name is Trump.”

Arsenal have everything they need to repeat as Premier League champions

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:47:19 GMT

Sunday’s win at Liverpool showed the Gunners are deeper, more experienced, and are playing against a weaker class of contenders than last season

Sign up for our free newsletter here

Arsenal are three points clear at the top of the Premier League table. But given the team in second are Manchester City, who are likely to be facing at the very least a major points deduction, perhaps more significant is that they are five clear of Brighton in third. The season of domination that many anticipated from the champions appears to be coming to pass.

Liverpool challenged them on Sunday. There was a 20-minute spell before half-time when they swarmed all over Arsenal, and Anfield felt at least like it did in the golden years of Jürgen Klopp, when it buzzed with an energy that could overwhelm visitors. But Arsenal got through that, reset at half-time, and navigated the second half with relative comfort. For the second league game running, they denied Liverpool a shot on target.

If there is a lesson, it is that Liverpool, like Brighton, demonstrated that a very aggressive press can unsettle Arsenal. But then, a very aggressive press can unsettle anybody. In Arsenal’s loss at Brighton, Pascal Gross and Charalampos Kostoulas took difficult opportunities; at Anfield Liverpool were denied what should surely have been a penalty when Jurriën Timber tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt – another bad moment for VAR, in that the no-call essentially mandated players to go down and highlight contact. Later, Alexis Mac Allister put a free header over. That was the difference, and this Arsenal team will not give opponents many chances. They are good at closing games out. Ezri Konsa in particular was outstanding on Sunday.

They also have a strong bench. The policy has been to make the squad deeper rather than adding the very highest quality – which is why the links with Vinícius Júnior over the summer were so unexpected. That has frustrated some, but it has been successful. Arsenal on Sunday could bring on Myles Lewis-Skelly, Piero Hincapié, Viktor Gyökeres and Mikel Merino to protect their lead with very little diminution of quality. But it’s not just on a man-to-man level that Liverpool’s options suffer by comparison; their changes upset the balance. They never really had control of the game once Dominik Szoboszlai had come on for Trey Nyoni.

It’s been a recurring feature of this season that Arsenal turn half-time draws into full-time wins – it’s already happened seven times. Winning individual games, though, is only part of it; a deeper squad means there can be more rotation, which should help prevent fatigue as the season goes on, as well as providing additional cover when injuries do occur. That said, their depth was not sufficient to get them past Fleetwood in the Carabao Cup last week, although they will face few games in conditions as challenging as those on the Lancashire coast.

There are still three-quarters of the season to go, and Arsenal were in a similarly commanding position at this stage last season, four points clear of second-placed Bournemouth after nine games. The expectation then was for a procession that didn’t materialise and looked, amid a spring wobble, to have gone awry. Then as now the feeling was not merely that Arsenal were very good, but that none of their rivals looked especially threatening.

But this season they have the memory of winning the title; the insecurity of three successive second-place finishes should be lessened. There is a resilience to them that has already brought a first win at Anfield since 2012 and a victory at Nottingham Forest after successive goalless draws at the City Ground. They’re picking up points at grounds where they’ve stumbled.

Last season, City were more resilient than had been anticipated. It may be a different story this time, and not just because of the potential for a savage points deduction. After seven straight wins they have lost successive league games to Aston Villa and Brighton, but the vulnerabilities that have been exposed had been apparent earlier in the season: a high defensive line that can be exploited. Liverpool are starting to coalesce under Andoni Iraola but they haven’t clicked quite yet and are, anyway, nine points adrift. Chelsea are a point better off but still a work in progress. Brighton have probably been the best other side, but they don’t have the depth to be considered a title challenger.

Sign up to Soccer Desk

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

after newsletter promotion

Sunday made clear what was already widely suspected: Arsenal are the best team in the league by some margin. It’s not just their depth, their cohesion and the wide variety of situations from which they can score goals, it’s that they now have belief and are picking up points at places where they have often failed in the past. And if they do build up a substantial lead by Easter, that could be hugely beneficial to their European challenge, which remains the one unconquered frontier.

“I can’t look into the future, I don’t know what’s going to happen,” Carrick insisted. “That doesn’t change the way I feel, that’s how we’re preparing for the game tomorrow and I’m really looking forward to the game.

“You might think I’m crazy with the results we’ve had and what’s going on, but I genuinely can’t wait for the game tomorrow and that’s all I’m focused on. Whatever happens is going to happen after that, in whatever direction it goes in.”

“I feel like our way to repay that [the manager’s support] is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it and fight for us and fight for us as a team.”

A global youthquake is happening. Promises we made young people have been broken – and they know it

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:17:36 GMT

Anger and protest have put liberal democracy on trial. It’s vital to understand the rage that now unites a generation

We have not yet reached a 1968 moment, when students at the Sorbonne lit a fuse that detonated a crisis that eventually brought down the De Gaulle government. But in late 2026, starting with the symbolic act of young French people climbing the July Column at Paris’s Place de la Bastille, the world is experiencing the biggest outbreak of student demonstrations for 60 years.

When Italian students subsequently occupied a high school in Rome, they opened their demand for change with the words “like in France”. Youth demonstrations are now raging from India – where the government has responded with repressive force to the Cockroach movement – to Albania, where, after being out on the streets for nearly five months, students are demanding not only an end to corruption, but the replacement of the government.

But the most momentous set of protests has been in Serbia, where the Student List of candidates for national parliamentary elections has succeeded not just in dislodging a long-established, corruption-tainted government alleged to have links with organised crime, but in securing an electoral mandate. It is now poised to form a new administration. Nothing of this kind has ever happened before.

Student List is not only changing the political leadership of Serbia but popularising new methods of organising; it is building a system for selecting candidates from outside its own ranks, using methods such as open public assemblies with rotating delegates and specialised working groups. Eighty-five student assemblies selected the candidates, as an analysis of their internal rules explains. And the results are often surprising: the rector of Belgrade university, Vladan Djokić, was not selected as a candidate, despite being a longterm supporter of the movement and expected by many to play a major role in government.

Student List has been compared by the Croatian philosopher Srećko Horvat, who situates the movement within a longer tradition of direct democracy and collective self-organisation, to the Paris Commune of 1871. Its fundraising activites, however, are very much up to date: it reportedly crowdsourced almost €2m (£1.7m) from more than 26,000 individual donors during the election campaign.

The wave of youth protests comes after mobilisations in Kenya in 2024 and across Nepal, Indonesia, the Philippines, Madagascar, Morocco and Peru in 2025. How far the Serbian grassroots model of organising will shape youth movements elsewhere remains to be seen. But according to Olivier Ertzscheid, a senior lecturer at the University of Nantes, “young people’s sense of belonging and social interaction is at play”, with social media now actively fostering a sense of connection and shared identity among protesters – and driving momentum.

September and October have seen youth protests in Belgium, Austria, Greece and Italy over education funding; in Germany over the threat of compulsory military service; and in Spain and Portugal over the lack of affordable housing. But the protests have also spread well beyond Europe, to Indonesia, where youth demonstrations are focused on pollution; to Argentina over austerity; and to Chile and Colombia over funding cuts. Last weekend in Germany, a group called Gen Z regelt led demonstrations in 21 cities.

The protests will only intensify this month. In Australia, a big student demonstration is planned for 11 November, and student unions in Britain and Italy are planning a joint day of action protesting against the rising cost of education on 20 November.

Some years ago I wrote about a new generation of youth activists – of Bangladeshi schoolgirls campaigning against forced child marriage who had declared “child marriage-free zones”, and of Nigerian and other young people in Africa demanding their right to education. But the current youth rebellions are of a different order, breaking out in a new and more dangerous global environment and challenging authorities on issues well beyond education. Young people face an AI-led unemployment crisis; they lose out from the skewing of public spending towards older people, from restricted provision of education; they face a housing crisis and governments underplaying the importance of the climate emergency and intergenerational justice.

The youth jobs crisis will grow. The number of UK graduate jobs postings advertised on one big employment agency has declined from about 180,000 four years ago to 50,000 today. AI is thought to be a factor. Hi-tech employment of 18- to 24-year-olds declined by 30% between December 2019 and December 2025, whereas the sector itself expanded by 33% in that period. So as the government prepares to announce its review into youth employment, it is urgent we get nearly 1 million unemployed under-25s into work, giving priority to pre-apprenticeship training and restoring educational maintenance allowances, as well as radically reshaping a benefits system that is failing the younger generation.

But this is a worldwide problem. Because of ever-rising debt burdens and spiralling expenditures on defence and energy subsidies, governments are trapped in such a fiscal straitjacket that they will struggle to find the resources to meet young people’s aspirations. A large portion of public spending is captured by older generations, with schools and universities losing out as a result. Across the OECD, about half of health and social security spending goes to elderly people – those over 65 – despite them making up only 18.5% of the total population. In this tally, pensions are the biggest item, accounting for 38% of all social spending – but an understandably high portion of all health spending goes to older people, too. And with young people now taking home a far smaller share of income than earlier generations, income and wealth gaps between young and old have widened.

It’s time to join the dots. Valérie Becquet, a sociologist at CY Cergy Paris University and co-author of Geopolitics of Youth: Engagement and (e)Mobilisation, warns that the protests are morphing into a wider social movement. “There are inequalities at all levels,” she says, “with gaps widening between different social groups.” The triggers for the demonstrations vary from country to country, but the basic complaint is strikingly similar. Young people believe that any promises that they would do better than their parents’ generation have already been broken – and that case is a strong one. Liberal democracy itself is now on trial.

Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010, and is United Nations special envoy for global education

Republicans were hoping to flip this New Hampshire Senate seat – will Trump get in the way?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 15:00:45 GMT

Republican John Sununu tries to distance himself from unpopular president in race against Chris Pappas that has gone from ‘toss-up to ‘lean Democrat’

Chris Pappas is stopping himself from getting too excited ahead of Tuesday’s midterm election.

“I take nothing for granted,” said the four-term US representative and Democratic nominee for New Hampshire’s open Senate seat. “This is a very purple, competitive state. Elections are never in the bag here.”

The race to replace the retiring Democratic senator Jeanne Shaheen has emerged as a source of 11th hour anxiety for the party.

In their attempt to gain four seats and reclaim control of the Senate, Democrats can’t afford to lose one they already hold. But September polling showing Pappas virtually tied with his Republican opponent, former senator John Sununu, rattled party strategists and raised the prospect that New Hampshire could become an unexpected battleground.

The warning signs were striking in a state Donald Trump has lost in each of his three presidential bids.

While Pappas has regained a narrow advantage in most polls, and the Cook Political Report moved the race in early October from “toss-up” to “lean Democrat”, his closing message has focused heavily on tying Sununu to an unpopular president.

Trump’s approval rating sits at just 32% in the state, according to a recent University of New Hampshire poll, giving Democrats hope that voter frustration with the administration will ultimately benefit Pappas’s run.

“Sununu has spent most of the last year on team Trump, and now that we’re getting within range of the election, he’s recognizing how unpopular the president is,” Pappas said as he traveled the state in the final days on the trail, often joined by party heavyweights, like Arizona senator Mark Kelly and former vice-president Kamala Harris.

Democrats believe political headwinds facing Republicans have been strengthened by rising high gas prices and heating-oil costs linked to the war with Iran. More than a third of New Hampshire households rely on heating oil, and colder temperatures have pushed the issue to the forefront of voters’ minds ahead of election day.

“People are now starting to get really angry,” said Jim Demers, a veteran New Hampshire Democratic strategist. “I think a lot of people see Sununu as just one more Republican who will try to talk a good game, but when push comes to shove, he will not stand up to Trump because Republicans in Washington have a record of not doing it.”

For voters like Randy Marchand, who is supporting Pappas, but considers himself an independent, the Republican party is ultimately a rubber stamp for the president’s agenda. “I’m afraid for our democracy … right now the Republican party is no more,” said the 54-year-old flight attendant, who lives in Manchester. “They will say one thing to get in, and will ultimately come down to what Trump wants.”

Sununu, however, has spent much of the campaign arguing that independence, not loyalty, defines his political record.

The former senator has emphasized his criticism of Trump’s trade war with Canada, which has affected several industries in the state, and in a recent campaign advertisement, he even claimed to have “never met” the president.

The former senator’s anti-Trump bona fides do have some roots. In 2024, he voiced his support or Nikki Haley in an op-ed during Republican primary campaign, and also branded Trump a “loser”.

This week, during the final televised Senate debate, Pappas argued that Sununu initially backed the administration’s decision to launch strikes on Iran. Sununu countered that the congressman “exaggerates” his position and noted that he has consistently opposed putting American troops on the ground.

Democrats dismiss those distinctions as largely tactical. “Sununu has spent most of the last year on Team Trump, and you know now that we’re getting within range of the election, he’s recognizing how unpopular the president is,” Pappas said in an interview. (The Sununu campaign did not respond to the Guardian’s request for an interview.)

Sununu’s Trump problem is also causing consternation for some Republican operatives in the state.

While New Hampshire voters like “local Republican control”, it might “be a little too much to send Trump an additional senator when the president’s numbers are just so low. It’s very difficult to articulate why a Republican should win that seat,” said one New Hampshire strategist who spoke on the condition of anonymity to comment candidly on the race.

“The war in Iraq is what broke the back of the Republican party in New Hampshire 20 years ago,” the operative added, noting that Sununu’s support for the initial authorization contributed to his failed re-election bid in 2008. “Now we have a war in Iran, and while it’s asymmetric, it is economic. That psychological toll certainly doesn’t help.”

New Hampshire’s habit of ticket-splitting complicates any effort to view the Senate race solely through a national lens.

The state’s congressional delegation is all-Democratic, while Republicans control the state legislature and the governor’s office. In 2024, voters backed Kamala Harris for president while electing Republican Kelly Ayotte as governor.

This year, that same kind of mixed vote is prevalent throughout the state. John McAllister, a firefighter in Nashua, said that he and his association were supporting Pappas this election, while also backing Ayotte – who is leading the polls in her re-election race against Cinde Warmington.

Pappas has been a “true supporter” of firefighters’ issues “as long as he’s been in the House”, McAllister said. Meanwhile, Ayotte’s work on pension restoration for public safety employees in New Hampshire has put “thousands of dollars” back into first responders’ pockets, he said. As a result, a consistently blue or red vote is never guaranteed. “We have proven time and time again to go either Republican or Democrat,” McAllister said.

Unlike many of this year’s Senate contests, New Hampshire’s race pits two deeply familiar political brands against one another.

Pappas has represented the state’s first congressional district since 2019 and previously served on the executive council. His family also owns the Puritan Backroom restaurant, a fixture of New Hampshire political campaigning, and the alleged birthplace of the chicken tender. If Pappas wins this year’s election, he will be the first out gay man to serve in the US Senate.

Sununu, who served as a congressman before winning his upper-chamber seat in 2002, comes from one one of the Granite state’s best-known political dynasties. Both his father and younger brother, Chris, served as governor.

The latter even joked that he would be “up by 30 points” if voters thought he was running for Senate this year. Sununu responded by saying: “I love my brother but he’s totally wrong.” If he triumphs, Sununu would also be the first Republican senator that New Hampshire has sent to Washington since 2010.

In a national midterms cycle that is characterized by energy for insurgents and anti-establishment energy, the New Hampshire race appears to be an outlier. Two familiar names with robust records to scrutinize.

At their final televised debate this week, Sununu chided Pappas for his eight years in office where he “hasn’t gotten the job done” and accused him of siding with his party leadership too frequently.

But Pappas made sure to list the ways in which he has broken ranks when necessary and crossed the aisle, pointing to “yes” vote for the Laken Riley Act, the Republican-led legislation that requires the detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft-related crimes, and his support for a congressional stock trading ban.

Meanwhile, Pappas targeted Sununu’s previous support to privatize social security when he was last in the Senate. “I’ve never voted to cut social security benefits, I never will,” Sununu said. “But Chris attacks me for introducing legislation 20 years ago that would have made the system solvent.”

The campaign has also occasionally veered into personal attacks. In September, Pappas referenced a 2010 email released as part of justice department files related to Jeffrey Epstein, in which the late sex offender wrote that “John Sununu has great stories” in a message to his associate Boris Nikolić.

The exchange followed attacks from national Republicans mocking a photograph of Pappas on a Zoom call with his cat. Pappas responded on social media: “I have a cat, and John Sununu’s name is in the Epstein files.”

It remains unclear whether Epstein was referring to the Republican nominee or his father, former governor John H Sununu. Earlier this year, Sununu’s campaign said neither man had “ever met or communicated in any way” with Epstein or Nikolić.

Some Republicans argue that Democrats are betting too heavily on antipathy toward Trump to defeat a candidate they view as genuinely independent.

“As someone who is a fiscal conservative … and wants to make every penny count, Sununu is a brilliant guy, and he really cares about the bottom line,” said Kate Day, a 69-year-old retiree from Chesterfield. “He’ll let you know if he doesn’t agree with the rest of the Republicans. I think his number one job is going to be standing up for New Hampshire, which is how it should be.”

Republicans also contend that voters are evaluating the race through a longer lens than the remainder of Trump’s presidency. “[Voters] know that this is an election for the next six years,” said Joe Sweeney, a state representative and deputy majority leader in New Hampshire’s Republican-controlled house of representatives.

“I think that the Democrats have been in this pattern for the last 10 years, where every other word they talk about is about President Trump,” Sweeney added. “They have this sort of obsession with him, and I think New Hampshire voters are wiser than that.”

Some Republicans argue that Sununu would really be the state’s only opportunity to elect a stronger voice to check Trump in his final years in office.

“If you really want to modify what the president’s doing, you need someone in his own party fighting back, not someone who’s going to be a rubber stamp,” said David Carney, a longtime New Hampshire Republican strategist, pointing to senators such as Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

Yet even Carney acknowledged the challenge facing Sununu in a state where Trump remains deeply unpopular.

“We’re not immune in New Hampshire from the national environment,” he said. “We get influenced by what we see and what we feel is happening across the country.”

‘It’s been a while’: hero’s welcome for UK man after 28-year walk across the world

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 14:49:03 GMT

Former paratrooper Karl Bushby arrives back in Hull and becomes first person to walk continuously across planet

After a 28-year odyssey spanning 29 countries, 36,000 miles, facing down polar bears, kidnappers and a spell in Russian custody, Karl Bushby was finally back in the arms of his longsuffering mother, Angela.

“Where have I been?” he joked as Angela sobbed into his chest with a mix of relief, pride and no doubt the odd sleepless night.

Surrounded by television cameras and with a Sky News helicopter overhead, the 57-year-old was given a hero’s welcome as he completed his record-breaking voyage on foot from Punta Arenas in Chile, the southernmost city on the South American continent, to his home town of Hull on Monday.

“There has never been a welcome home quite like this, I’m sure,” said Bushby, shaking his head in disbelief as he greeted a crowd of well-wishers in the city’s Queen Victoria Square. “This is absolutely madness.”

It has been 28 years since Bushby, then aged 29, left the army to walk the world on what he intended to be a 12-year journey. He finally crossed a misty Humber Bridge back to the city on Sunday – on the same date he set off in 1998.

In that time he has stuck by two simple rules: not to return home until he had fully completed his feat, and not to use transport to advance.

In all, he walked 36,000 miles across four continents, a frozen sea, deserts, jungles and mountains. Quite a trek for a man not keen on walking. “It’s boring as hell,” he told the Guardian last month.

His return on Monday will make Bushby the first person to have walked continuously across the world, visiting 29 countries, having already exceeded the record for the longest unbroken foot journey (far outstripping the 25,000-mile circumference of the world).

The voyage took him across the frozen sea of the Bering strait between Alaska and Russia and across the notorious Darién Gap in Central America. He described last month how he had been threatened at gunpoint, faced down a polar bear, was convicted of being a spy, and been held in custody in Russia and sentenced to deportation.

Bushby strode into Queen Victoria Square like a modern folk hero, his passage only slowed by the dozens of people rushing to shake his hand and take photographs.

Yet for a man who had navigated much of the planet, he did appear to get a little lost on his way through the crowds of his home city. “I’ve no idea which direction I’m going. Everybody point the way,” he said. “Sorry to keep you all waiting – it’s been a while.”

Through the crowd he pushed his heavily loaded trolley, dubbed the Beast 2 (his first one broke down) laden with essentials such as medicine, sleeping bags, headtorches – and two very worn tyres. “Sorry everybody, sorry,” he said as he manoeuvred through the well-wishers.

About three miles away, Angela, 75, was waiting at the gate of Bushby’s childhood home as she had promised. After a tearful embrace, they took a long look at each other.

“You’ve changed a bit,” Bushby told her. “I’m older,” his mother replied through tears. “We both are,” he said. “Well done for hanging in there.”

He was then whisked inside the small terrace house, festooned with union flag bunting, where he was reunited with his son, now 36, and a 12-year-old granddaughter whom he was meeting for the first time.

Earlier on a makeshift stage, Bushby thanked the city for his hero’s welcome. “It took a world to get me here,” he said. “The kindness of strangers – so many, from individuals to nation states, to get me back here. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth.

“We faced down governments, we faced down some of the hardest challenges, we had to create two world records just to get back here. It was a global effort.”

At one point, the great German film-maker Werner Herzog appeared on stage alongside Bushby, overseeing what will surely be one of the closing scenes in Herzog’s documentary on the 28-year odyssey.

Karl Turner, the Labour MP for Kingston upon Hull East, brought with him a message from the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who congratulated Bushby on his “truly remarkable” feat and thanked him for his service as a paratrooper.

In a statement read on stage by Turner, Burnham said: “Your journey has taken nearly three decades, crossed continents and tested you in ways most of us can barely imagine.

“But today, as you return to the city from which you left 28 years ago, you bring with you something far greater than any world record or a remarkable personal achievement. You bring a story of what can be accomplished through extraordinary determination and self-belief.”

As he was ushered away for a big lunch before the walk to his mother’s house, Bushby had one last message for the city he left in 1998: “I guess I’ll be seeing you around.”

Tomb Raider’s creators on how the game changed their lives: ‘Skint staff were suddenly pulling up in sports cars’

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 14:40:35 GMT

‘Giving Lara Croft pistols meant we could show off her acrobatics. And when she goes to Peru, we threw in a T rex!’

I joined Core Design in the summer of 1994 and met Toby Gard, who showed me his concept sketches for Tomb Raider. He’d already come up with the title and drawn a mock-up box cover with a woman holding two pistols.

I was working on a golf game called The Scottish Open when Toby persuaded me that we should pitch his idea to Jeremy Heath-Smith, Core’s co-founder, who gave us the go-ahead to make a prototype. If I had stuck to the golf game, I would have had a much easier life.

We had a couple of brainstorming sessions, and settled on the game’s four main pillars: platforming, puzzles, combat and story. Combat was always the weakest element but we didn’t have time to improve it. We also came up with the plot and level themes, and whittled a long list of interesting archaeological locations, including Petra and Angkor Wat, down to four: Peru, Greece, Egypt and Atlantis.

Lara was originally Latina and her appearance was more realistic, almost androgynous. We felt that more stylised movement would play better, so her physique changed to reflect that. She became a British mercenary and then, thanks to scriptwriter Vicky Arnold, an aristocrat who tracks down historical artefacts just for fun.

Toby and I came up with the movement metrics by measuring out a hopscotch grid in the car park. Lara was three paces tall and each block in the game’s environment was four paces. All of the gameplay systems grew from those measurements and constraints.

It was brutal getting it delivered on time. I took just three days of holiday in two years. Toby and I were in the office until 2 or 3am every day, including weekends, for the best part of a year. Toby made himself sick with the stress.

We were on the cusp of 3D games going mainstream and the action-adventure focus made us somewhat unique. Then the marketability of Lara thrust Tomb Raider into the stratosphere. The game’s publisher, Eidos Interactive, took the character and ran with it. I like to think the quality of the game spoke for itself, regardless of the way Lara was sexualised.

We never imagined Tomb Raider would blow up in the way it did. It was the right time, right place, and it was different from the competition. We showed that ideas that go against conventional wisdom – a female character will never sell! – can uncover new territory and find success. It was gratifying and humbling to see our hard work rewarded by so many people playing the game. We managed to bottle lightning, although I’m still carrying the scars of its creation.

We developed most of Tomb Raider in a big Victorian building on Ashbourne Road in Derby. We sat there sweating our guts out in the summer and freezing cold in the winter. I was the only female developer, but that didn’t faze me. I felt respected and was almost seen as a sister by some – the team was like a family. It was a defining time in my life.

Toby was lovely. Very eccentric and a bit of a genius. He’d put together a demo that was like a simple top-down version of Prince of Persia, with an Indiana Jones-like character jumping and tumbling from platforms. Although management thought no one would want to play a female character, they went with it. There’s a certain empathy you get from playing Lara. It’s probably the number of times she dies and that awful scream. She was taciturn and mysterious: a loner who played her own game and didn’t answer to anybody. Women hadn’t really been portrayed like that before.

Giving Lara pistols enabled us to show off her acrobatic movement. She was mostly pursued by animals rather than people. Hearing a bat, or the growl of a bear, was much scarier than a gunshot. You felt at the mercy of the wild. And we pushed the 3D environment to its limits. We only had so much memory and processor speed, but we were clever with it, giving players the sense that they were in this vast, cavernous space that was actually lots of rooms bolted together.

Before designing a level, we always had a team meeting where we’d come up with a rough schematic. We all enjoyed history. We chucked in whatever myths and legends we thought would be fun and interesting. Our imaginations ran wild – to the point where we threw a T rex into Peru!

Eidos saw the potential of Lara, rather than the game, so they focused on her. That was the right thing to do, but I think it went a bit too far with what she was wearing or the poses she was put in for some marketing campaigns. They showed a lack of imagination by oversexualising her.

I knew we’d made a great game, but it didn’t really sink in until I saw the sales figures. It was life-changing for all of us. People who were skint before were suddenly pulling up in sports cars. I was able to buy a house from the royalties.

Lara is right up there with iconic characters such as Mario and Sonic the Hedgehog. Feeling as if you’ve left a mark, and connected with millions of people through something you’ve created, is amazing.

As cancer treatments become more effective, we must ask: what is life like for the people who receive them?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 14:00:42 GMT

Many treatments are now extending lives, but the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve

Two decades ago, a dear friend called me in a trembling voice. Was there hope for his young nephew, whose cancer had spread to the brain? Sadly, “no”, I said. But today, for such patients, there are options that were unimaginable back then.

Recently, researchers at the European Society For Medical Oncology presented the latest chapter results from a randomised controlled trial of a bespoke cancer vaccine for patients with high-risk melanoma. The trial involved 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed but remained at high recurrence risk. They received either pembrolizumab, an established immunotherapy, or pembrolizumab combined with an experimental mRNA vaccine, designed to help the immune system recognise and attack targets unique to the patient’s tumour.

At two years, 82.2% of those who received the combination were alive without their cancer returning, compared with 70% of those given pembrolizumab alone – a difference of about 12 percentage points. The combination also reduced the relative risk of distant metastasis or death by 38%.

These results raise the prospect that personalised vaccines could become an important addition to cancer treatment. Whether they will deliver similar benefits in other cancers remains to be established.

Overall survival data are not yet mature, so we don’t know whether the combination helps people live longer. Fever, injection-site pain and fatigue were common with the vaccine combination. Rates of severe treatment-related adverse events were similar between the groups; quality-of-life data is not yet available.

The standing ovation for the researchers was deserved, as was praise for the pharmaceutical companies that backed an idea that was once a pipe dream. Yet as cancer treatments become more effective, another question gains importance: what is life like for the people who receive them?

Treatment can delay a cancer’s return, but can impose a considerable burden. Side-effects, fatigue, impaired mobility, psychological trauma, financial strain and the disruption of family and career all shape the experience.

In my work, I am often sobered by the juxtaposition of scans showing no cancer with a patient who cannot sleep, work or enjoy what others take for granted.

Recently, a retired academic approaching 90 told me: “My dear, the best thing you could do for me is get me safely home.” For this patient, their priority was clear; pursuing intervention would have caused a serious decline in their quality of life.

That does not mean some people should automatically be offered less treatment, or that the value of treatment depends on age alone. But it does mean oncologists must understand what each person hopes treatment will achieve, and explain what they may have to endure to get there.

My experience with elderly patients has made me more conscious of my other patients who are mid-career, raising children or caring for relatives.

The parent whose persistent nausea makes school drop-offs impossible.

The hairdresser who can’t work due to neuropathy.

The executive dismayed by cognitive fog.

A treatment that offers a cure or extra months of survival may be worthwhile to one person, even with significant toxicity. Others may place greater value on earning an income, caring for a child or living independently. These are not competing definitions of success: they are individual priorities that good medicine should respect.

Yet quality of life is often reported less rigorously than response, recurrence and survival. Less than a third of trials report quality-of-life measures in the primary publication, which most professionals read, and just half publish them at all.

Patient-centred care demands that information about quality of life should appear alongside the main findings, not years later in a separate publication, or not at all. When patients ask, “Doctor, how will this treatment affect my life?”, the information gap can become an indirect permission for oncologists to skim over the granular details.

A recent paper in The Lancet Oncology urges better reporting of health-related quality of life in trials of adjuvant treatments (treatments given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence). The researchers argue that average scores conceal important differences between patients: trials should instead report how many people experience a clinically meaningful deterioration, how long it lasts, and whether and when they recover.

Collecting quality-of-life data is not simple, but when data is missing, we should know why. Questionnaires are burdensome for sick patients and doctors have a different notion of quality of life from their patients. Of course, for a patient facing a life-threatening diagnosis, a chance at cure may reasonably outweigh significant toxicity concerns, but imperfect measurement is a reason to improve the status quo, not to look away.

From where I sit, I see immense gratitude for modern therapies, but not inconsiderable decisional regret: “If only I had known.” We should empower patients to ask and be ready to tell them not only how likely a treatment is to work, but also what it may cost them in daily life. Far too often, they find out later that treatment can bring months, years or even a lifetime of adverse effects.

None of this downplays scientific progress. Many treatments are now extending lives, and personalised medicine may bring further gains. But the measure of progress should not end with a scan or a survival curve. Researchers must collect quality of life outcomes diligently, clinicians should discuss them openly, and health systems should treat them as central, not optional, to care.

While writing this column, my thoughts returned to the young man and his family, whose happiness for today’s melanoma patients is tinged with regret for their own loss. Today’s advance stands on the shoulders of the patients who generously volunteered to a take part in a study not knowing if they would themselves benefit. They deserve our gratitude.

Our ambition should be not only to keep people alive, but to protect the lives they want to live, and to recognise that the true cost of treatment is measured in more than money.

Ranjana Srivastava is an Australian oncologist, award-winning author and Fulbright scholar. Her latest book is Every Word Matters: Writing to Engage the Public

Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 13:10:08 GMT

Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations

Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area.

Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA.

The Southern North Sea is an area of importance for harbour porpoises, supporting nearly 20% of the UK North Sea population. But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily.

Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said.

“Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.”

The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks.

The Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective.

“We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said.

The action coincided with the nationwide premiere of Blue Planet III, the latest BBC wildlife documentary narrated by David Attenborough to focus on the oceans and the human-made threats they face. In 2025 bottom trawlers and dredgers tore through a cumulative 55,600 sq km of MPA seabeds, an area 58 times the size of Dartmoor national park, according to a Greenpeace analysis.

A number of notable figures added their names to boulders tipped from the Arctic Sunrise into the North Sea. Among them was the Labour MP Kerry McCarthy, a former climate minister and a member of the all-party parliamentary group for the ocean, who said: “Industrialised fishing is having a hugely destructive impact on our marine environment, yet less than 1% of our seas are protected from it.

“[Fishing boats] can legally tear through supposedly protected areas of the ocean, wreaking havoc upon the seabed, precious habitats and the sea life that lives there. Progress is too slow and nature can’t wait, which is why I’ve added my name to one of Greenpeace UK’s boulders. We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries, both here in UK waters and right across the Atlantic Ocean.”

The government has been contacted for comment.

Five dimensional chess: inside James Talarico’s extraordinary bid to break Texas Democrats’ losing streak

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 13:00:42 GMT

The Texan could pull off a historic victory in the Lone Star state, which hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1988

When a young, untested former school teacher stood up to address a modest gathering of local donors in Austin, the state capital of Texas, Wendy Davis felt sorry for him. “Poor kid,” she remembers thinking.

Then James Talarico began speaking. “He was like five or six sentences in and I knew that something was different about him,” recalls Davis, a former Democratic state senator. “He was as articulate and unique then as he is now. From that day, I started calling him ‘Baby Obama’.”

Eight years after that first fundraising event, “Baby Obama” is no longer a precocious candidate for the state house with paper slogans that read “A future as bright as Texas”. Now 37, Talarico will aim to redraw the political map next week by becoming the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in the Lone Star state since 1988.

The threat that he poses to Republicans’ grip on power has become clear in the final stretch of a fraught campaign. Over the past month Donald Trump rallied in Texas and branded him “James Talafreako”; JD Vance implied that Talarico is gay (he has a girlfriend); and rightwing influencers spread a baseless lie that he checked into a mental health clinic in Ohio (in fact, he was ill with flu).

Despite the desperate attacks, most opinion polls give Talarico a narrow edge. On Tuesday the voters will have their say on whether the four-term state representative, a Presbyterian seminarian preaching a gospel of hope, can overcome Republican Ken Paxton, a scandal-haunted state attorney general and Trump ally who has financial backing from tech billionaire Elon Musk.

Facing a barrage of culture war attack ads funded by the world’s wealthiest man, Talarico has responded with an unorthodox blend of economic populism, progressive politics and an unapologetically Christian message that challenges the religious right on its own turf. His campaign raised a record $64m in the third quarter, including donations from a vast number of small-dollar contributors.

Last week Talarico told a crowd of young voters and local activists gathered at his alma mater, the University of Texas at Austin, that Republicans’ billionaire donors were starting to fret.“They are terrified because they see what we see: we are about to win this election,” he said.

An eighth-generation Texan, he was born James Dell Causey in Round Rock, a small town north of Austin, in 1989. His mother, Tamara Causey, was a preacher’s daughter who left home at 19 and met his biological father, whom she has described as an alcoholic prone to violence.

One night the abuse became too much. Tamara drove James and all her belongings in a small Ford Escort to the hotel where she worked as a sales assistant. They lived in an empty room at the hotel until they found an apartment in Austin. Tamara subsequently married a sales manager named Mark Talarico, who adopted James and gave him his surname.

At school, Talarico was a keen debater and actor, with roles including Danny Zuko in the musical Grease. Allegra Hobbs, author of a profile in Texas Monthly magazine, reported: “His high school theater director, Aaron Johnson, joked to me that the young Talarico did not so much inhabit the character as play a version of himself. When the theater department handed out superlatives, ‘Jimmy’ was voted most likely to be president – a running joke among his friends that he would laugh off.”

Talarico studied at the University of Texas at Austin, where Mike Garcia, a 38-year-old lawyer and former legislative staffer, first encountered his political ambitions. In 2009, Garcia presided over the College Republicans while Talarico led the University Democrats. Despite their ideological differences, the pair initially found common ground in nonpartisan voter drives and a campaign for tuition relief.

Speaking from Fort Worth, Garcia recalls: “It was a little strange but I was glad that we were putting our differences aside and doing something that would help everybody.”

The goodwill did not last. During student government elections, Talarico’s organisation endorsed establishment candidates who opposed tuition re-regulation, according to Garcia. The move provoked outrage among Democrats who had supported the campaign, some of whom turned up at a College Republicans meeting to protest.

Garcia suspected Talarico had calculated that the endorsement would win him favour with university administrators ahead of a possible run for student body president. “That sounds like exactly something Jimmy would do,” he says.

Years later, when the two crossed paths again at the Texas capitol – Garcia working for Republican legislators and Talarico now an elected representative – Garcia felt he saw a similar gap between political rhetoric and personal charm. Talarico would “routinely just rail against all these people I work for, calling us the worst names ever”, he recalls, before greeting him warmly in the corridor minutes later.

Garcia remains unconvinced by Talarico’s current presentation as a moderate. “He is probably one of the types that is willing to tell you exactly what you want to hear, especially if it helps him politically. Right now he’s running as a moderate and he’s doing a very good job of it,” Garcia says.

But others dispute Garcia’s account. In a statement provided by Talarico’s campaign, Muneezeh Kabir, who was at the University of Texas with him and involved in student government, said: “James has always raised his hand to serve others. Throughout his time in student government at UT, James worked with everyone, even those he disagreed with, to make life on campus better for all of us. He delivered for his classmates at UT, then his community in Austin, and now, he’s ready to step up and serve Texans from every corner of the state.”

After college, and before the state house, Talarico went into education. His first job was teaching sixth-grade language arts at the Rhodes middle school on the west side of San Antonio, a predominantly Latino neighbourhood.

Edward Garcia, 56, who was principal of Rhodes at the time, remembers hiring Talarico during the summer of 2011. In a high-poverty school district where teacher turnover was relentless, Garcia was struck by the young applicant’s poise and purpose. “He knew what his mission statement was in terms of working with students that are in high poverty and high need. He was ready to start the next day,” he says.

Even before the academic year began, Talarico turned up at the school accompanied by his sister, hauling enlarged prints of Rosa Parks, Martin Luther King Jr and Gandhi to create a classroom display devoted to human freedom.

“Teachers are supposed to be universal,” Garcia explains. “There wasn’t an approach in terms of partisan politics. It was just the concept of freedom and what it means for students to truly acquire freedom and leadership in their lives.”

Talarico’s connection with his middle schoolers was immediate. In a profession where novice teachers frequently struggle with classroom management and rely on administrative referrals, Talarico never wrote up a single student or sent one to the principal’s office. “He was an exemplary teacher. Kids were enthralled with his presentation and took a shine to him,” Garcia says. “What you see is what you get: smart, articulate and guided by his heart.”

When Garcia walked into Talarico’s room during his second-year formal observation, he discovered that the young teacher had physically removed his official administrative desk from the room.

“I went in to do his evaluation,” Garcia recalls with a laugh. “I looked around and said, ‘Where’s your desk?’ He goes, ‘Oh, I took it out and turned it into a reading space.’ He put a carpet down right where his desk should be.”

After two years in San Antonio, Talarico returned to the Austin area to lead an education non-profit before making his leap into elective politics in 2018. Winning a state house of representatives seat in a suburban swing district, he quickly established a reputation in the Texas capitol as an authority on public school finance and an exceptionally persuasive orator.

His Republican colleagues in the house began calling him “Baby Gov”, recognising that his ambitions might extend well beyond the state legislature. Talarico focused heavily on public education, prescription drug pricing and property tax relief.

During bitter legislative battles over voting rights and school vouchers – proposals to restrict access to the ballot and use public funds to help families pay for private education – Talarico emerged as a prominent opponent of Republican priorities.

In 2021, he joined fellow Democrats in leaving Texas to block a vote on Republican-backed voting restrictions by denying the state house the minimum number of members needed to conduct business. He later returned to the chamber before the standoff had ended, drawing criticism from some of his own party.

He also repeatedly clashed with conservative committee chairs over LGBTQ+ rights. Talarico used the phrase “God is non-binary” while opposing a bill concerning transgender children in school sports. Republicans have sought to weaponise it against him. Talarico has defended the underlying theological argument while acknowledging that he was being provocative.

While serving in the state legislature, Talarico enrolled at the Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary, which has a picturesque downtown campus of neat lawns, light-filled buildings and functional classrooms with blackboards and rows of desks. He pursued a master of arts in theological studies, diving into church history, ethics, systematic theology and ancient biblical languages.

The seminary’s president, José Irizarry, says: “We are not an assembly line for dogma. We are a place of faith formation which requires people to think deeply and thoughtfully about their faith practices. What does it mean to take your belief system and actually do the work of justice in the world?”

Irizarry recalls working in his office across from the classroom building during Talarico’s first year. “I had no door when I arrived here – an actual open-door policy. He was studying Hebrew across the hall. I could hear the whole Hebrew class because it was with a rabbi and he started the class singing in Hebrew. I would go out during the breaks and see him interacting with all the students. He was a student like everybody else around here, engaged in ministry.”

When Talarico called Wendy Davis in late 2023 to disclose his intention to surrender his safe house seat and launch a long-shot bid for the US Senate, she tried to stop him. Davis, now executive director of the the Blueprint Texas political action committee, admits: “I tried hard to talk him out of it. I told him that my fear was he’d been so impactful in the legislature and I thought it would be a big loss for him. I told him he was probably going to lose and he was going to regret leaving his office. And now look at him.”

Talarico went on to defeat Jasmine Crockett, another rising star of the party, in a bruising Senate primary election. He has since been working hard to unify the Democratic coalition, including Black voters who supported Crockett.

His theological training has proven not merely a personal spiritual exercise but the construction of a political armour. In a state where conservative evangelicals have long dominated public discourse on religion, Talarico’s fluid command of scripture has allowed him to carry out a counteroffensive.

He attacks Christian nationalism, opposes state-mandated displays of the Ten Commandments in public schools and argues that Jesus’s core commandment – to love one’s neighbour – demands support for healthcare, public education and marginalised communities.

Cal Jillson, a professor of political science at Southern Methodist University in Dallas, says by phone: “Usually the vote that takes religion seriously in Texas is an evangelical conservative Republican vote. There’s a possibility that he has a little more purchase beyond the Democratic base into moderates and independent voters in the middle. With Talarico, there’s more of a Sermon on the Mount vibe as opposed to this ‘I’m an angry God’.”

Talarico demonstrated that approach during a legislative committee hearing on a bill requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in Texas classrooms. Rather than offering a standard secular objection, Talarico quizzed the author on the text of the Commandments themselves – showing on camera that the politician could not recite them.

For Democrats, there have been plenty of false dawns in Texas. In 2018 Beto O’Rourke’s charismatic campaign for Senate against Republican Ted Cruz attracted national attention and record-breaking fundraising, but he ultimately lost by 2.6 percentage points.

Bill Minutaglio, a prominent Texas author and political historian whose books include A Single Star and Bloody Knuckles, argues that Talarico’s campaign represents a far more calculated and controlled evolution of Texas Democratic strategy.

“Beto was deemed to be the chosen one who would break the spell and obviously it didn’t happen,” Minutaglio observes. “He was a victim of inflated expectations. He seemed too ambitious and too coated with endorsements that didn’t resonate well outside the borders of Texas. People here don’t take kindly to the sense that a candidate is being shaped and endorsed by places like California or New York.”

Talarico, Minutaglio contends, studied O’Rourke’s missteps to avoid repeating them. “O’Rourke appeared on the cover of Vanity Fair magazine. Talarico has learned his lessons. I don’t mistake his quietude and his seminarian step for him not being a truly shrewd politician. He is that and then some. The ability to walk that fine line is rather amazing to me. I find it almost Obama-like. There’s a calmness about him and a thoughtfulness in public. He’s playing right now five-dimensional chess in Texas,” he says.

Part of that strategy involved building a political identity of his personal narrative and Christian faith. “It’s become that sense of armour – holding up the Bible – and people can’t get around it,” Minutaglio says. “Paxton, of course, is the greatest foil that anybody could pray to have. Talarico has found the cheat code in Texas.”

The contrast between the two candidates could hardly be starker. In 2023, the Republican-controlled Texas House voted overwhelmingly to impeach Paxton on 20 articles alleging misconduct, including bribery, abuse of office and obstruction of justice. The state senate later acquitted him.

A long-running state securities fraud case ended in 2024 with an agreement requiring Paxton to perform community service, pay restitution and complete legal ethics courses in exchange for prosecutors dropping the charges. Paxton has remained bogged down by public revelations regarding his personal life, including an alleged extramarital affair and a high-profile divorce.

Paxton, 63, has also been lethargic on the campaign trail with even Trump poking fun at his dress sense and speaking style. Jon Taylor, a professor of political science at the University of Texas at San Antonio, says: “Paxton is afraid to meet people. He tries to stay in this shell and avoid voters.

“Everywhere Talarico goes, he attracts a substantial crowd. He’s got rock star status. Talarico is charismatic, personable and tells stories that resonate. Meanwhile, his opponent is basically screaming that Talarico believes God is non-binary and that he’s ‘far left’. The message is viewed by voters as shrill and ineffective.”

As the race entered its final lap, national Republicans realised that Paxton’s vulnerability risked forfeiting a seat crucial to maintaining their narrow Senate majority. In response, conservative Super Pacs launched an unprecedented financial bombardment.

Musk, who moved Tesla, SpaceX and his personal residence to Texas, gave $158m to the Senate Leadership Fund in September. The Republican Super Pac subsequently transferred the money to the Texas Pac, which has blanketed the state’s 22 media markets with anti-Talarico advertising. The blitz focused almost entirely on trans culture-war themes, falsely claiming Talarico supported taxpayer-funded gender reassignment surgeries for minors.

At the same time, cracks have emerged in the conservative coalition along the Texas-Mexico border. While Trump made significant inroads among Latino voters in 2024, recent aggressive immigration raids and agricultural disruptions appear to have produced widespread buyer’s remorse.

Cristina Tzintzún Ramirez, a political consultant and former Democratic US Senate candidate, says: “I always say that the portion of Latino voters up for grabs are neither Republicans nor Democrats – they’re poor, and they need candidates who speak to their poverty, their pain and their power.

“Talarico leans more on a moral calling than a political persuasion, and that vision connects to people across a much larger swath of political persuasions than Democrats historically have reached. People are sick of the brazen political corruption and the system not working for ordinary working people.”

Democrats are taking nothing for granted in a state that Trump won by 14 percentage points against Kamala Harris in 2024. Talarico is still careful to characterise himself and his movement as the people-powered underdog against the oligarchy, the David taking on a Goliath that includes the world’s most powerful man and the world’s richest man. For supporters who have spent decades enduring Democratic defeats in Texas, the prospect of a Talarico victory feels less like an ordinary midterm result than a profound turning point.

Minutaglio comments: “If Talarico wins, it will be huge – a sea change in modern Texas history. The reverberation will rocket from the Fortune 500 companies in Dallas to the oil barons in Houston and the high-tech moguls around Austin. For decades, Texas has been addicted to deregulation and unfettered capitalism. Here’s a quiet seminarian who says, ‘Pump the brakes. Let’s think about oversight.’ It will challenge every perception of what Texas is.”

Beaches, Beatles and a broken marriage: how Wilhelmina Barns-Graham became a radical art icon

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 12:30:20 GMT

The artist who was inspired by Swiss glaciers, the Vietnam war and her own divorce was sidelined from St Ives’ art history – but finally has a major retrospective at Tate

At the centre of Tate St Ives’ newly opened retrospective of the British modernist Wilhelmina Barns-Graham, her monumental altar-piece Glacier (Blue Cave) pulls viewers into its frozen tendons of turquoise and white. Its mouth is agape and the blue slit of its eye casts downwards to the rest of its body. The glacier feels human: a vivisection of rock, ice and snow that brings to mind the fragmented facial features of Picasso’s Weeping Woman.

Standing in front of this glassy colossus, the exhibition’s curator, Katy Norris, talks about these “mangled” and “twisted” forms – so alive on the canvas. “Barns-Graham was so distinct in her approach,” Norris says. “There are always questions of: what am I seeing? What is in front of me really? And how does that relate to what I feel inside?”

Glacier (Blue Cave) was painted not far from this gallery space in 1950 – only 10 years after the Scottish-born painter moved 500 miles south to the tiny fishing town of St Ives – but it goes some way to showing just how radical she was over the course of her eight-decade career. From her early 20s, Barns-Graham’s quest for connection saw the self-described “lone wolf” become a key player in the St Ives school which congregated in and around the Cornish harbour during the second world war. She continued to experiment relentlessly with colour, geometry, kineticism and repetition until her death in 2004, aged 91.

Anne Barlow, director of Tate St Ives, points out this major retrospective – the first to span Barns-Graham’s full career – is a “long-overdue celebration” of an expressive master. The art historian Virginia Button wrote that “Barns-Graham clearly felt that as a woman she had been unfairly sidelined from the history of St Ives” with its focus on Ben Nicholson, Peter Lanyon and Patrick Heron. She had a brief period of fame in the 1950s, but it waned in the 1960s as her landscape modernist work became increasingly “hard-edged” (as Rob Airey, director of the Wilhelmina Barns-Graham Trust, puts it) and more daring; less commercial and harder to categorise.

With her “blue eyes that flashed like knives” (so her husband, the writer David Lewis, remarked) and her delight in toying with gender stereotypes (she took great pleasure in the sexual ambiguity of her preferred nickname “Willie”), Barns-Graham ploughed her own furrow from the beginning. Born into an upper-class family in the seaside town of St Andrews in 1912, Barns-Graham’s resistance was tested early when her stern father became hostile towards her plan to pursue artmaking as a profession.

Nonetheless, ignited by her love of Cézanne, at the age of 18 Barns-Graham started studying at Edinburgh College of Art. “She had a single-mindedness,” Norris says. “She didn’t see any limitations, she just saw the path ahead.” It’s a focus you can sense in her 1945 oil painting Froth and Seaweed. Painted in her beloved St Ives, the artist homes in on the spidery tendrils of algae and slithery copper rock. “It’s almost as if she has no peripheral vision, she’s just seeing beauty at her feet.”

Film-maker Mark Cousins first encountered Barns-Graham’s paintings in late-80s Edinburgh. Whether depicting the silvery shorelines of St Ives and St Andrews or the crystalline glaciers of Switzerland, he says, “she just leapt off the walls”. He made a pilgrimage to her St Andrews house during lockdown, and in 2024 released A Sudden Glimpse to Deeper Things, which delves into the artist’s distinctive gaze and synesthesia. Barns-Graham associated colours with people, places, emotions and even letters of the alphabet – something she called a “total experience”. “If we think of Turner’s relationship to landscape, he saw a vortex. And Leonardo da Vinci saw a machine. She was like that as well; she saw a living thing,” Cousins says.

Her encounter with the Grindelwald glacier in Switzerland came in 1949. “That day was almost like a rebirth, a kind of rapture,” Cousins says of her life-defining hike and the 60-odd paintings and drawings that followed over a three-year period documenting the glacier’s “many moods”. In a letter to the Tate in 1965, she wrote: “It seemed to breathe!” This wasn’t an artist above the landscape, Norris says, but of the landscape. The glacier’s interiority was her interiority – a close symbiosis that intensified for the rest of her life as she pushed further into abstraction, moving away from figurative landscape painting in favour of “systems, rhythm, repetition and spatial tension”.

Yet the underlying presence of nature was still there: “bird flights, dancing diamonds on water, dots inside foxgloves, cell formations,” Norris writes. For the curator, Barns-Graham’s work in the 1960s-70s (titled Things of a Kind in Order and Disorder) is where she truly pioneered a new way of experiencing the world – “like chaos theory, really” – by laying out small cardboard squares in neat rows on her studio floor before randomly nudging them with her foot. On a stormy morning on the golden stretch of Porthmeor beach, I got to see this paint-splattered studio for myself; its floor-to-ceiling window looking out on to fast-moving clouds and ferocious waves.

Like Merce Cunningham’s “choreography by chance”, Barns-Graham was thinking about “how things hold together” – not least her marriage, which ended in divorce in 1963. Referring to her 1968 oil painting on board Olive Green Squares on Vermillion, she compared the erratic block of squares against a rage of red to “a broken marriage” – her own. Yet with Protest – another volatile blockwork which was made in 1967 as the Vietnam war raged and a year after the Beatles had released Revolver – “she was [also] thinking about participation and action and what you can do as an artist or viewer. She’s making the moves, she’s a part of it, she’s no longer in awe of a natural phenomenon that’s doing its own thing.”

When the Beatles came along, “working-class men were cool and posh women weren’t,” says Cousins. “But she just kept going.” In the 1980s, Barns-Graham’s tumult of squares made way for the thumbprint pen-and-ink lines of her Small Energy Drawings. “Are they soundwaves? Is it the wind?” Norris ponders. “Sometimes she’d look out from the cathedral-esque window of her studio in St Ives and turn her back to it, playing music and drawing lines that replicated the sea.” Another “choreography by chance”: first you observe, then you listen, then you feel. That precision and intuition can exist in such harmony in these artworks speaks profoundly to Barns-Graham’s own particular genius.

“At my age there’s no time to be lost,” Barns-Graham said in the 1990s. “I say to myself: ‘Do it now, say it now, don’t be afraid.’” Drawn to the late works of Picasso and Joan Miró, and incensed by the environmentally ruinous decade in which she was living (“the most appalling time of abuse of living things,” she remarked), the octogenarian slapped colour on to the canvas with an energy that was both urgent and physical. “The St Ives narrative flattened her,” Cousins says of this late flourish. “It saw her as one of many. It is important to extract her from St Ives and see her as a singular imaginative person.”

Wilhemina Barns-Graham is at Tate St Ives until 3 May

From puregatory to lifehoarding – how best to describe our strange, anxious times?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:00:39 GMT

The new words that end up a part of everyday speech can tell us a lot about the zeitgeist. In a world changing faster than ever, we need to coin some more

‘Maxxing” may be one of our words of the year – sufficient unto the joyless, self-optimising day, dreary as hell – but I’ve been introduced to some fun future contenders. How about “flawnting”? I’ve certainly rolled my eyes at influencers playing “the new parental status game of publicly performing imperfection to signal authenticity” online. I like “lifehoarding”, too – “optimising so hard for longevity that life itself goes unlived”. And which Guardian reader hasn’t experienced “puregatory” (“The plight of trying to live ethically, where even responsible choices feel compromised”)?

These coinages come from Future Words, a book by trend forecasters Rohit Bhargava and Henry Coutinho-Mason that seeks to fill some lexicographical lacunae for describing life in the fretful late 2020s. Out next week, it’s fun, but its list of suggested words conjures a world where life is whatever your devices, data, algorithms and AI decide it is, interspersed with attempts to fight for authentic human connection and experiences. That sounds about right, if depressing (I was also dispirited to discover the part AI played in creating the book – the authors say they “couldn’t have written Future Words without it” – but it makes sense AI would know what it’s doing to us.)

To cheer me up, I’ve been considering what other contemporary concepts we need words for. For a start, I’d like one for the seductive product you’re algorithmically hounded into buying that turns out to be rubbish (“perfect” trousers that feel like wire wool and fall apart within days, say), and one for the 10-minute (two-hour) break you guiltily grant yourself to watch online nonsense you know will rot your brain.

And do we need a word for “gambling on AI going rogue and killing us all by giving up saving and spend, spend, spending” now? Because Business Insider just reported an “AI safety leader” (Nate Soares, the president of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute) has stopped saving for retirement for that reason, which is … sobering. Will we even be around to find out if any of these inventions actually enter everyday speech in the next few years? The crap socks I bought online last month certainly won’t last that long.

Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist
