The pet I’ll never forget: the tiny horse with a big personality – who helps psychiatric patients

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:00:39 GMT

Black Pearl is a therapy animal, who works with military veterans. This sweet show-off has completely changed my life

I trained and competed in dressage for many years and after I retired, I decided to buy a miniature horse for company at home in southern California. I bought Black Pearl from Quicksilver Ranch in Solvang, California, in 2008, when she was six months old. She was a fluffy little thing and would run around at warp speed, then run back to snuggle. She stole my heart from the beginning. I had no idea that Black Pearl would inspire me to change my whole focus in life.

I started training her for fun and began to teach her tricks. She learned quickly. I thought of a great way to give back to the community – Black Pearl and I could find ways to help people. I started to wonder where I could visit with my little horse.

Black Pearl inspired me to start my charity, Mini Therapy Horses. If it wasn’t for her outgoing personality, I wouldn’t have attempted it. Now I run a programme with her and eight other miniature therapy horses, visiting patients in the lockdown psychiatric unit at a veterans’ hospital in Los Angeles. The vets have been through so much: they have PTSD, traumatic brain injuries and/or drug addiction and many are homeless. They can pet and hug the horses – they love them. It helps them to feel less lonely and isolated.

We also visit several other hospitals – many of the kids and adults are away from home for a long time and the time they spend with our minis is very comforting. If a child is visually impaired we can take their hands and help them to feel our little horses. They can brush their coats and this tactile experience makes them very happy.

Black Pearl will also walk beside a patient in a wheelchair while they hold the reins. Some patients are missing their own animals at home, so cuddling her might be just what the doctor ordered.

Of all our miniature horses, Black Pearl is the biggest show-off. She feeds off everyone’s positive energy and loves to do her tricks. She is by far our best keyboard player – tapping and rubbing her little muzzle back and forth on the keys. She can stand and walk on her hind legs, give a high five with her hoof, smile, nod and shake her head “yes” and “no”, strut with her front legs, and much more.

Working with Black Pearl has given me the opportunity to meet people from every walk of life. She inspired me to follow my passion, with her as a partner, in helping others. I love this little horse – she has been a blessing.

What can Democrats actually do if they win Congress?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 11:00:38 GMT

Democrats are fighting to win control of the House and Senate in the midterms. Here’s what winning would mean for them – and Donald Trump

If Democrats win back the US House of Representatives or the Senate in the midterm elections on Tuesday, the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency will look markedly different from the first half. But what would the Democrats’ actually be able to do with either – or both – chambers of Congress in their control?

If Democrats take the House, Republicans would lose their ability to pass legislation through that chamber without Democratic support. A Democratic majority could launch investigations into the administration, demand documents and testimony, and subject senior officials to sustained congressional scrutiny. They might come under pressure from their support base to impeach Trump for a third time.

The Senate confirms cabinet officials, ambassadors and federal judges, including supreme court nominees. A Democratic majority could block or delay many of Trump’s appointments, and force the White House to negotiate over legislation.

Even if Republicans retain one or both chambers, a reduced majority could make governing more difficult, particularly when legislation requires near-unanimous support from the party’s own members.

Political reporter Joseph Gedeon laid out the most consequential investigations Democrats could launch if they take back Congress. Here are a few of the investigations:

The family business: Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, has ranked Trump family corruption first on his list of priorities, while Representative Jamie Raskin has requested information on the business dealings of Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.

Epstein and the emails: Thanks to a tag-team effort by Representatives Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie, the Department of Justice was forced to release millions of files related to Jeffrey Epstein last year. But off the bat, the justice department blew the legally mandated deadline to disclose the files. Then it released only about 3.5m pages of the 6m in its possession; it said it had deemed the rest duplicates. And there has been bipartisan consternation about heavy redactions in some places, and the apparently accidental disclosure of the names of victims in other places. The justice department is now facing a lawsuit from journalist Katie Phang over many of these issues. Even under a Republican-controlled Congress, the oversight committee under its GOP chair, James Comer, has been a rare spot of bipartisan comity, with members of both sides routinely (but not always) acting in concert to subpoena witnesses and hold them in contempt when they don’t cooperate. Expect that to continue in any new Democratic Congress.

The Pentagon and the war: Jason Crow, a Colorado congressman who sits on the armed services and intelligence committees and co-chairs the House end corruption caucus, says he will start with the Pentagon, citing reports of defense money steered toward companies linked to the Trump family.

Impeachment: House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries says Democrats have ruled nothing out regarding impeachment this time around, while the Republican House majority leader, Steve Scalise, predicts an attempt on “Day 1”.

In 2018, halfway through Trump’s first term, the Democrats flipped the House of Representatives in a sweeping blue wave. House committees quickly launched dozens of inquiries into his businesses, his handling of the Russia probes and possible conflicts of interest.

Just over a year after the 2018 midterms, after months of leftwing calls for impeachment, the House voted mostly on party lines to impeach Trump.

Democrats had accused Trump of pursuing a scheme to cheat in the upcoming presidential election by pressuring Ukraine to manufacture bad news about Joe Biden and then blocking congressional oversight. Trump was later acquitted in the Republican-controlled Senate on both articles of impeachment.

In 2021, Trump was impeached – and acquitted – a second time for inciting the January 6 attack on the US Capitol.

How Kimi Antonelli saw off the grid to become F1’s youngest world champion

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 10:00:38 GMT

Mercedes driver makes history at 20 years old by exceeding all expectations in only his second season

Before the 2026 season had begun there was something of a consensus within Formula One. Mercedes appeared to have the fastest car and George Russell was favourite for the title. Beside him in what was indeed a dominant Mercedes, his teenage teammate, Kimi Antonelli, was the prodigious talent who was expected to require honing after a tricky rookie season. Said consensus lasted one race, by the sixth it had been turned on its head and Antonelli was squarely on his way to being champion.

Few had doubted that the then 19-year-old Italian would prove to be strong in a car that for the first two-thirds of the season was the class of the field but for Antonelli to come out of the blocks with such verve, aggressive skill and also the judgment and at times maturity of a veteran was revelatory. As the youngest F1 world champion and Italy’s first since Alberto Ascari in 1953, Antonelli made history this year but it was the way he did it which truly caught the eye.

As the sport’s youngest world champion at 20 years old crossed the line in tears, wracked with emotion at the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez, what it meant to him was clear, as it was for his mother, father and sister, the family with whom he is so close and who have played a key part in his success. They embraced and shed their own tears too.

It might have been an inevitability for some time but when he climbed from his car to the roaring approval of the fans in the hugely atmospheric stadium section it was understandable that the Italian, only just out of his teens, could barely take it in.

“We did it,” he said. “I wouldn’t be here without Mercedes, without my family. This moment is one that will live for ever. I am speechless. I am just trying to process this moment.”

In his rookie season Antonelli had struggled with the ground-effect cars as he came to terms with F1 and endured a run of poor performances mid-season. Questions were asked about whether he had been promoted too soon. They were answered emphatically this year but not quite from the off.

At the season opener in Australia he crashed out in final practice with an air of the over-eager charger that was costly and familiar from 2025. The repairs to his car meant he almost missed qualifying and Russell went on to win. The bookies it seemed had called it right.

What followed, for all that it was so early in the season, was nonetheless gamechanging. Fifth place in the sprint in China including a penalty for hitting Isack Hadjar was not entirely auspicious but it was the last foot put wrong in Shanghai. Having become F1’s youngest driver to claim pole he converted with an inch-perfect run to take his debut grand prix win by five seconds from Russell.

With a handle on how to maximise the driving style required by the energy management of the new cars and a feel for it that was tantalisingly out of reach for his teammate, Antonelli was on another level. Victory in Japan after dropping to sixth at the start followed, albeit with good fortune from a safety car call, and with it a championship lead he would not relinquish again.

Miami fell to the Italian, then Canada. The narrative had changed, Russell and the rest of the grid were being schooled by the kid with only one season under his belt.

If emphasis were needed as to the who was calling the shots Antonelli performed emphatically in Monaco. He saw off a fierce charge from Max Verstappen to claim pole and then made an indelible mark with victory on the streets of the principality. He held his lead from the off and was flawless beneath the looming walls before having to hold his nerve to see off two restarts that had eradicated the 30-second lead he had built.

The second, a standing start alongside the seven-time champion Lewis Hamilton was as nervy a test as one might ask of any driver, let alone one in only his second season. Antonelli passed with flying colours, held his line, the place, and the lead to the flag.

Questions were asked of him repeatedly and every time he had the answers. If there were weaknesses in his game, that he might be impetuous or overexcitable, by Monaco they had been banished by the calm, cold commitment of a champion in waiting.

It was his fifth consecutive win, a record run after a debut victory and with it he had amassed a lead of 66 points over Hamilton and 68 over Russell.

Russell to be fair had endured more than his fair share of bad luck and it was undeniably a factor but not decisive. The safety car at Suzuka which benefited Antonelli cost the British driver, he was unfairly penalised for pit lane speeding at Monaco and then had an engine failure while leading in Canada, a body blow. Yet he admitted at the time that he was not as at home with the car as Antonelli and it was visible on track, the Italian often quicker even when behind his teammate.

This was demonstrated in Barcelona when he had passed Russell to take second place with five laps to go. However, the Italian too had to weather his own share of misfortune. Having taken second place he ground to a halt with an electrical shutdown to his immense disappointment and that of some observers missing the good old days when engines used to at least give out with a bang.

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

That ill luck was followed by a wheel shield failure at Silverstone dropping him out of contention just as he had been challenging for the lead. The resulting points swing put Russell within 25 points but that was as close as the British driver was to come.

McLaren and Ferrari both came at Mercedes taking two wins apiece but while Mercedes no longer had it all their own way Antonelli consistently performed. His brief mid-season frustration behind him, a dominant win in Belgium was followed by two podiums. Russell did cop some more bad luck but there were two further races which defined why the season belonged to the 20-year-old.

The first at his home race in Monza where he started from 19th after an engine change-prompted grid penalty but went on to take the win was a masterclass, proving he had the race craft, control and judgment to scythe through the field from a seemingly impossible position. It was another blow to Russell who had started from second and was expectant of clawing back points yet dropped a further seven.

Only one driver has come back to win from further down the grid, John Watson from 22nd at the Long Beach GP in 1983. Watson’s drive is long remembered, as will be Antonelli’s.

The second was of a similar vein; it indicated the depth of his talent and what greater heights the Italian may go on to reach. In a season marked by only marginal errors, misreading yellow flags in qualifying in Austria, and a penalty for failing to slow under yellow in qualifying in Hungary among them, the most egregious by far was his crash in qualifying at Baku, where Russell went on to take pole by a huge margin.

Antonelli admitted the mistake was unnecessary and started from 16th. Yet how he dealt with it illustrated a champion’s mindset. Instead of charging at the race trying to make up places and taking chances on a circuit he knew could bite, he played the percentages, moved through the field with care and decisiveness, even as chaos and crashes at a restart caused him to pick up floor damage making the car a brute to handle. He kept his head and his nerve to grind out fifth, despite still castigating himself for the accident in qualifying.

He had accepted the blame and learned from it, then assessed his position, how to handle it and what course was best in the bigger picture of the title fight. Not all titles are won with derring-do, but they can be lost. Antonelli had dropped points but with as much damage limitation as might reasonably be expected, the title inched inexorably closer.

A similarly cool head saw off a late resurgence from Verstappen in an impressively improved Red Bull as Antonelli ground out podiums behind him. Indeed, grabbing third in Singapore with a dash past Lando Norris and Hamilton as they fought each another typified why the title was all but in his hands.

An emphatic victory in Austin followed, his ninth, which Wolff hailed as one of his best, which was not quite enough to seal the deal but it left him so far ahead that ninth or better would suffice this weekend here in Mexico, where he duly closed it out with a nerveless run to take third place.

Better than anyone had anticipated, perhaps even than his Mercedes team might have hoped, Antonelli delivered on his promise in emphatic style and prompted a new consensus: that there is surely only more to come.

Kamala Harris returns to campaign trail – as focus turns to 2028 presidential race

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 10:00:38 GMT

Former vice-president has not yet ruled out another run for the Democratic nomination as she campaigns for others in the midterm elections

Two years on from her devastating presidential election defeat, Kamala Harris was greeted like a rockstar as she took the stage before a rapt audience at Georgia’s Clark Atlanta University.

When a politician is greeted by a friendly crowd, they often hear chants of their name. But at Clark, a historically Black college (HBCU), students instead delivered a school spirit chant for the Atlanta University Center, celebrating an HBCU alumna – and the country’s first female and first Black vice-president – as one of their own.

Harris is “big sister general”, said Sanaiya Archer, a sophomore at Spelman College in Atlanta. “I’m able to see myself in her. Not that I personally relate to her, but she went to an HBCU, she’s an HBCU alum, I’m at an HBCU. And it’s just amazing to see a Black woman that I can see anywhere else in my life on a presidential scale.”

That scale has yet to reach the Oval Office. In 2024, following the reluctant withdrawal of Joe Biden, Harris launched a 107-day campaign for the White House which again brought to the US tantalizingly close to electing its first female president. She lost.

Donald Trump’s return left Democrats reeling – again. Even as it contests this week’s midterm elections, the party has yet to settle on who could lead it back into power, and how.

Harris, forced by Biden’s late exit to conduct the shortest presidential campaign in modern US history, has not yet ruled out another run for the Democratic nomination. But is a figure so closely associated with the party’s past really the person to manifest a more successful future?

At Clark on Thursday, she was treated like a returning hero. “I’ve come here to remind you, don’t ever let anybody take your power from you,” Harris said. “Don’t ever let anybody tell you who you are. You tell them who you are!”

She was aware, she stressed, of how her loss affected some of the young Black women before her. “You know, we’ve been spending the last year and a half, so many of us, going through a range of emotions,” Harris said. “You cried. I heard you. Anger, depression, sadness, frustration, a sense of – of helplessness and powerlessness, folks feeling like, ‘I’m watching all this happen, but I can’t do anything about it’.”

“Well,” she said, “that moment has passed.”

Harris has spent the last month recultivating relationships, appearing in front of the friendliest of audiences on behalf of Democratic candidates around the country.

In Mississippi earlier this month, Harris appeared at a high school rally in Columbus and took part in a rural healthcare roundtable in Clarksdale, campaigning for Scott Colom, the Democratic challenger of US Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Polls point to a surprisingly close contest in a historically Republican state.

Similarly, Nevada’s Democratic attorney general, Aaron Ford, is now in a toss-up race for the state’s governorship against the Republican incumbent, Joe Lombardo. Harris met with unionized culinary workers in Las Vegas in October.

Harris has also campaigned for the Democratic gubernatorial nominee, David Crowley, in Wisconsin, and the party’s New Hampshire Senate nominee Chris Pappas. She returned to Michigan – a state which Trump flipped in 2024 – in September to campaign for Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate candidate.

After dozens of trips to Georgia as vice-president, and having all but rented an apartment in Atlanta while campaigning for president, Harris returned to the state last week to campaign alongside the Democratic senator Jon Ossoff – who has also been mooted as a potential 2028 contender.

Ossoff is popular in his state, confident on stage, and widely expected to retain his Senate seat by a convincing margin. But even he looked a little awkward when walking out after Harris had instead been erroneously announced too early, leaving a roomful of Democrats momentarily disappointed.

“Let me be really blunt,” Ossoff said, dissecting Trump’s obsession with voting results from the 2020 election in the county that covers the core of Atlanta. “Why Fulton county? It’s the same reason he’s obsessed with Philly. It’s the same reason he’s obsessed with Detroit. It’s because for this committed, lifelong racist, the fact that Black voters were instrumental to his defeat is even more offensive than the defeat itself.”

Voter turnout has been surging in Georgia – particularly in Black communities, and Atlanta’s politically potent purple suburbs. Early voting set a record on the last day of open polls before election day, with about 2.8m votes cast: turnout of 37% so far.

Harris, who has been channelling Black anger and anxiety on the campaign trail for others, has been pushed back on questions about her own political ambitions, even while shoring up relationships in swing states on the road. Speaking to the actor Keke Palmer on a podcast earlier this month, she swatted away a question about another run for president.

“Oh, girl, come on!” Harris replied. “I haven’t decided. I haven’t decided yet. I will. I promise you. But the midterms, the midterms, the midterms. ’28 doesn’t matter if we don’t do ’26 right: what’s right in front of us.”

While Harris had to navigate a short runway in 2024, the last two years have offered the former vice-president an opportunity to redefine herself and offer a new vision for a Democratic party that faltered. She has tried to do that, at times – while opting to lie low, at others.

At a fundraising dinner in Atlanta for Fulton county Democrats on Friday evening, Harris reinforced themes she has returned to over the last year; that the country cannot simply be repaired after Trump’s departure, but must be fundamentally changed for the better.

Trump, whom she dubbed the “decorator in chief”, was leading “an administration that is stone cold corrupt”, Harris said, recounting highlights from his second presidency – from the offer of checks from tariff revenue to a teleprompter handler who profited on prediction markets with wagers on the president’s next words. “This is the most callous, corrupt presidential administration in America’s history.”

Democrats must not squander power if they recapture it, she said.

“It is the job of the Democratic party to be ready to match the resolve of the people with the resolve to govern. And to be candid, that’s going to require a certain kind of ruthlessness,” Harris said. “Not ruthlessness in the sense of cruelty, because that’s not who we are. But in our willingness to use our power to deliver on our commitments.

“And we must be uncompromising to deliver actual relief. We must be impatient with injustice. We must be intolerant of cronyism and corruption. And we must be intolerant of the status quo, because it’s ain’t working for a whole lot of people.

“Our party can no longer let process stand in the way of progress, because … the American people cannot afford to wait for that time.”

At Clark, at least, the bright-eyed students of the AUC who waited for a glimpse of Harris outside the hall like theater fans seeking autographs seem to want her to run.

Carington Hill and Naomi Blakey are two first-year students at Clark who attended Harris’s address. “We just turned 18,” Blakey said. “We were just talking about how when voting came and the election ended, how we were upset about how he won.”

Blakey wants Harris to run again, she said. “Because me and my friends weren’t ready … I didn’t get to vote. And I feel like my vote could have made a difference, and it could have not, but still, I wanted to.”

Hill also wants Harris to run again, but expressed apprehension about the public’s appetite for a Black woman in charge. “We’re not progressive enough,” she said. “I feel like all their biases would come back and we would vote for the bad person in a way again.”

“Well, not we,” she added, pointing at her friend and herself. “But other people would vote for that bad person again. You know what I mean?”

Zero passing yards, one win. Did the Bucs just reinvent the NFL in all the wrong ways?

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:00:35 GMT

In a downpour against the Atlanta Falcons, Tampa Bay decided throwing was for losers. They were proved right

I don’t think I’m being cheeky when I say that passing is the most exciting part of football. A solid hit is nice, and a big run can thrill you, but this is a quarterback-centric game. When a QB is bad, teams usually lose and fans get bored. So, Sunday’s performance by Baker Mayfield and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers had me positively gobsmacked. I wouldn’t say their 16-0 win over the Atlanta Falcons was thrill-a-minute, but it certainly was historic. By completing a grand total of zero passes out of a paltry three attempts, Baker Mayfield led the Bucs to the first game with no passing offense since the Buffalo Bills beat the New York Jets 16-12 on 29 September 1974. If you are miraculously old enough to remember the NFL before the advent of the forward pass in 1906, first off, congratulations on being over 120 years of age. Please email me your full diet and exercise regimen. You’re probably on your feet (if standing is still something physically possible), cheering a bit of hard-nosed, classic football. The rest of us young whippersnappers still grinding through our first century are holding our noses.

This article includes content hosted on embed. bsky. app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Of course, Mayfield – a former No 1 overall pick – can throw. As recently as 2024 he threw for 41 touchdowns and 4,500 passing yards in a season. But Sunday’s game was played in pouring rain that led to farcical moments like this, and Tampa Bay clearly decided that the ground game was the only way to go. That the Bucs could score at all, let alone 16 points, is a credit to Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell running as though their lives depended on it. Irving finished the day with 170 rushing yards and one touchdown, while Gainwell had 140. Combined with Mayfield, they rushed 56 times for 324 yards – the most ever in a single game for the Bucs. They more than made up for Mayfield’s borderline irrelevance in the pocket. Mayfield made himself useful blocking for his runners, but otherwise, I probably could have started at QB for the Buccaneers and the game would have been the same, other than the high likelihood of me suffering at least one gruesome injury.

“If I’m not going to throw the ball, I have to get active somehow,” Mayfield said after the game. He certainly was more valuable for his team than Falcons quarterback Michael Penix Jr, who had a game that would be front-page terrible if not for the historic passing futility on the other side. Penix went 8-for-24 with four interceptions. The field was wet and as slippery as a greased-up ferret with a sugar rush. But even a wet playing surface wasn’t enough to stop Tampa’s run game, or kicker Chase McLaughlin’s three field goals. Having said that, McLaughlin didn’t even need to make one – Atlanta were just that bad. Next week, the Falcons face the Bengals in Spain. If Atlanta play like this in Madrid, they’ll be the worst American export to Europe since David Hasselhoff’s first album.

Joe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals. We’ll start with the positives: Burrow threw for five touchdowns, ran for another, racked up 462 passing yards and led his team back from 13 points down to a 43-36 overtime win on Sunday. On the downside, he threw three interceptions and all this came against the Tennessee Titans. But Burrow gets MVP this week for a refusal to do anything dull. And the Bengals are off to their best start since the 2021 season, when they made the Super Bowl.

The Chiefs-Broncos game was absorbing until the final moments. Kansas City, down 28-24, looked set to pull of a late victory when they had a first and goal on the Denver 4-yard line with 35 seconds left. But stout Broncos defending and a sloppy penalty from the Chiefs when they thought they had scored the winning touchdown meant they needed to score on the final play of the game. When Patrick Mahomes is under center in this type of situation, a Chiefs win is automatic. Not this time, though.

This article includes content hosted on embed. bsky. app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

259. That’s the number of career touchdown passes across the regular season and playoffs by Josh Allen for the Bills after his pair during his team’s victory over the Baltimore Ravens on Sunday. In reaching that milestone, he broke the record set by Buffalo legend Jim Kelly. The victory moved the Bills to 6-1 and they now have the best record in the AFC. Sadly, the game was also marked by a thumb injury to the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson. It may end his season, a sad turn of events for one of the most thrilling players in the league.

The Vikings are undefeated no more. The Lions pulled out a thriller to end Minnesota’s hopes of a perfect season. Jared Goff found Jameson Williams for a score with 4:35 left in the game to squeak home 19-15. This was Detroit’s third straight victory, but they also lost linebacker Jack Campbell to a neck injury. Campbell had to be carted off the field on a backboard early in the fourth quarter, which put an undeniable damper on the post-victory celebrations. Instead of reveling in his late-game heroics, Goff was somber and reflective when speaking about Campbell. “That was definitely scary. He’s a husband and a father.”

There’s more heartbreak on display at AT&T Stadium this year than a Kazuo Ishiguro novel. The Dallas Cowboys looked to be in the driver’s seat against Arizona as the fourth quarter began. They led 24-10 and their defense was looking well-prepared to lock down a win. Except, folks, they weren’t. Arizona exploded for 20 points in the fourth, as Gardner Minshew took over from an underperforming Jacoby Brissett. Minshew marched the Cardinals down the field in 63 seconds late in the fourth to tie the game at 30. A simple Chad Ryland extra point would have been enough to win the game, but the PAT flew wide left. This was Ryland’s first extra-point miss in the last 58 tries. To overtime they went. Ryland was able to rescue his no-good, very-bad day by hitting a 42-yard field goal to finally clinch the comeback. The Cowboys are 3-5, and a brutal 1-3 at home as we near the halfway mark of the season. Lucky for Dallas that they play in a division where only one team is above .500.

Are the Rams back? Or are the Chargers just awful? Time will tell, but in the Battle of Los Angeles, it was the Rams who took care of business, 24-9. The game was close until a pivotal second-half period in which the Rams scored two touchdowns. The Chargers are 0-7. They’re the only team in the NFL who haven’t scored 100 points or more combined this season – 99 points for, versus 175 against. All this with alleged offensive mastermind Mike McDaniel at OC.

The Jacksonville Jaguars remain the most pleasant surprise in the NFL, destroying Indianapolis at home, 42-7. The Jags are top of the AFC South, above three teams with sub-.300 winning percentages. Trevor Lawrence was superb for Jacksonville, sporting a 153.3 rating, 210 yards on 10-of-14 passing and three touchdowns. The Jags’ defense forced three turnovers – two interceptions and a fumble – and surrendered just one pity touchdown in the third quarter. Jacksonville are at the top of a terrible division. Is there any reason to think they won’t stay there?

As someone who has dated both a woman from Cleveland and a woman from Pittsburgh (not at the same time), I can attest that Steelers v Browns is one of the most heated rivalries there is, primarily because Pittsburgh and Cleveland are cities with chips the size of dinner plates on their shoulders. Personally, I prefer the food in Pittsburgh (specifically the giant hotdog they sold at Pirates games that has pierogies on top), and so I was pulling for the Steelers on Sunday. They did not let me down. This was the 23rd straight home win for the Steelers over the Browns. Pittsburgh sacked Deshaun Watson eight times. Eerily, the last time I did this column, Deshaun was sacked … eight times by the Jets in Week 5. Maybe next time I’m writing this, I’ll give the Browns a heads-up.

The Raiders pulled off another of the day’s improbable comebacks, scoring 24 points in the second half to beat the New York Jets 38-33. Las Vegas broke a four-game losing streak and are 4-4 on the year. Kirk Cousins threw for 247 yards on 19-of-26 passing and three touchdowns, plus a TD run in the third quarter that he punctuated with a peculiar Arrested Development-style chicken dance that he called his “wellness celebration”. The 38-year-old said, “We do a lot of tissue work here. At my age, it’s especially helpful. … So I said someday if I run a touchdown in, I’m going to give a shoutout to all the staff that works so hard to help us feel good and be one of the healthier teams in the league.” Cousins almost forgot to do this peculiar celly, but Brock Bowers reminded him. Perhaps the first and last time anyone will ever say “Hit them with the wellness celebration!” on an NFL field. Or at least I hope so.

As for the Jets, they were content to make jokes about themselves. “I think we had some bad penalties, bad mistakes,” their veteran safety Minkah Fitzpatrick said. “Jets being Jets.”

‘We both know how we feel about death and dying’: Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney on their brutally honest Parkinson’s drama

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 08:00:34 GMT

Written by Vicar of Dibley co-creator Paul Mayhew-Archer, who has the disease, Onwards and Sideways sees the actors play a couple who bond over their diagnoses – a devastating subject but laced with humour too, they say

Ahead of production on their first job together, Rhys Ifans and Laura Linney didn’t undergo the standard “chemistry read” to make sure they got on. Which is remarkable, given what their characters would have to do to each other in Onwards and Sideways.

In the Norfolk-set BBC film directed by John Madden (Shakespeare in Love), Ifans would have to nearly throttle Linney while in the grip of night terrors, she’d have to collapse in his arms in a weeping mess having bankrupted herself with a gambling addiction; both situations arising from the neurological condition afflicting their characters: Parkinson’s disease.

But despite being thrown into the deep end in this hugely emotional, often hilarious film, both actors acknowledge an immediate feeling of safety around each other as they embarked on a project that would require them to strip themselves bare. “It’s odd,” says Ifans, “you learn so much about each other so quickly. I couldn’t tell you what kind of car Laura drives. What her home looks like. But we both know how we feel about death and dying.”

Linney, 62, is a triple-Oscar-nominated star with a diverse array of roles on her CV, from her breakthrough in The Truman Show (1998) onwards through Clint Eastwood’s Mystic River and Richard Curtis’s Love Actually (both 2003), then the TV series Ozark and The Big C. Ifans, 59, frankly burst through in 1997’s Twin Town, AKA the “Welsh Trainspotting”, and went on to play Hugh Grant’s scraggly flatmate Spike in Curtis’s Notting Hill (1999), Daniel Craig’s stalker in Enduring Love (2004) and drug smuggler Howard Marks in Mr Nice (2010).

Divergent backgrounds, then. But equally time-served, too. So the actors were able to dive in, no chemistry read required. They did, though, do dance classes. They waltzed together in London, and separately nearer their respective homes, the better to understand one popular form of recreational therapy for people with Parkinson’s. In Brooklyn, Linney was introduced to David Leventhal at the Mark Morris Dance Group. He runs a programme there called Dance for PD.

“That’s the mothership of this wonderful organisation that now has offshoots all over the world, including here,” the New Yorker says when she, Ifans and I meet in the central London offices of the producers behind Onwards and Sideways. Both are dressed casually and low-key, each clearly easy in the other’s company, their conversation frequently erupting into gales of laughter.

“I spoke with David for a long time – and then I learned that Juilliard has classes for this once a week,” Linney says of the acting school that’s her alma mater. “So I just started hanging out there. It’s incredibly moving what the arts will do,” she says – in this case, how dance and music could relax people grappling with a condition that, among its 40-plus symptoms, causes uncontrollable shaking, stiffness of gait and involuntary freezing in doorways and thresholds. “How brave it makes people. How it opens up the imagination, and then the body follows somehow, when it shouldn’t. And the difference between someone moving in a dance class and then, when the music stops, to see what happens to their bodies – it’s shattering in a good and a sad way. So … it gets right to the bone of things.”

Ifans, meanwhile, attended weekly sessions with a group who meet in Pontio, an “arts and innovation centre” in Bangor, north-west Wales. “There was a harpist accompanying the dance,” says the Pembrokeshire native. “Then there was a support dog running around the room who happened to be a sheepdog.”

“Herding!” adds Linney, laughing.

“It was peak Welshness!” acknowledges Ifans, to hoots all round. Then, quietly again: “They were so inspiring, these classes. And a great leveller. You’d be sitting next to a nuclear scientist and a school cleaner. Both dancing to the same tune and wrestling with the same diagnosis.”

The writer of Onwards and Sideways is Paul Mayhew-Archer. He’s an actor, writer – he co-created The Vicar of Dibley with Richard Curtis – and accidental activist. The 73-year-old is a founder member of the Movers and Shakers podcast, which raises both awareness and laughs, alongside fellow “Parky people”, including journalists Jeremy Paxman and Mark Mardell. He was diagnosed with the disease at 58, with the canary in the coalmine, symptoms-wise, being that “my handwriting was very small and unclear”.

His experiences directly inform the experiences of the fiftysomething characters played by Ifans (Tony, a teacher) and Linney (Emma, a musician). They also, full disclosure, inform my writing of this feature: my dad has Parkinson’s and I’m in the age bracket Mayhew-Archer was when he was diagnosed. My handwriting is appalling.

True to Mayhew-Archer’s mission, Onwards and Sideways is painfully, honestly funny. The scene where Rory Kinnear’s doctor rather cavalierly informs Tony that he has the condition features a joke lifted from Mayhew-Archer’s own diagnosis.

“My neurologist told me one of the symptoms is the difficulty of smiling, and that I seemed to have difficulty smiling,” Mayhew-Archer relates to me when we meet on another day in the same office. “And I said: ‘Well, that could be because you just told me I’ve got Parkinson’s.’ As soon as I said that, I knew I wanted to be funny about Parkinson’s, because I saw no point in being serious.”

Ifans – who’s been staunchly committed to this project for the duration of its lengthy gestation, stretching back pre-Covid – seconds that emotion. “I loved the way Paul’s story about a life-changing diagnosis was handled, funny and devastating all at once. My attraction to it was also that I have friends and family who’ve been impacted by Parkinson’s. That gave me a fast track into the telling of a story like this.”

“You don’t have to scratch very far to find someone somewhere who knows someone who has Parkinson’s,” echoes Linney of a condition that, in the UK, 166,000 people are living with, with one person being diagnosed every 20 minutes according to Parkinson’s UK. “I certainly have friends who do.”

To “act” Parkinson’s, Ifans and Linney were aided by the Neuro Heroes, “remarkable women who do physio for people with Parkinson’s and various related conditions”, says Linney. “They helped us with our basic understanding of Parkinson’s, and then also the physicalisation. [Because there’s] a mercurial element to this condition – it’s bespoke. No one has the same Parkinson’s.” Or even the same side-effects from the drugs prescribed to help manage the incurable condition: they can cause increased libido, appetite, and compulsive spending and gambling.

after newsletter promotion

“Parkinson’s was like a physical dialect for us,” continues Ifans. “We had to learn its physical language. They [the Neuro Heroes] could say what was happening at the muscular level, or the skeletal impact, of Parkinson’s. But we needed poetry to understand what that felt like. Whether it felt like moving through tar or sand. Just to be able to arrive at an image that you could apply to the body, that you could take with you to set each day, to help you achieve the shapes and positions that Parkinson’s puts people in.”

And those people, ultimately, were always in the actors’ minds. Mayhew-Archer knew the film had to honour those with the condition, but that that noble aim did have its bluntly practical limits. “We knew we couldn’t cast people with Parkinson’s in those two central roles,” he says. “Partly because Laura’s character has [a medical procedure] done which means she stops doing certain things. And it would be very hard for people with Parkinson’s to stop doing some things!” he adds with a laugh. “Once you start freezing, you can’t stop!”

“We had the added responsibility in getting Parkinson’s right,” says Ifans. “Not just right, but bang-on. Because there’s a whole demographic watching that deserves to be represented. That was the scary bit, wasn’t it?”

Linney, staring intently at her co-star across the table, nods. It was, she says, fundamentally about “doing it justice”. And then, “the possibility of failing at that?” says Ifans. “Huge responsibility. That brought us closer together. That’s the stuff that woke us up at night.”

When we meet, Linney is about to be unveiled as one of the cast of DC superhero TV series Lanterns. She’s a Guardian of the Universe, “or so I’ve been told”, she says with spoiler-savvy diplomacy. “But a green beam might come down and evaporate me if I utter a word!” She’s also two weeks into filming, alongside Colin Firth and Julianne Moore, Comfort and Joy (formerly The Joy of Sex), a romcom about the north London throuple who helped produce Alex Comfort’s groundbreaking 1972 illustrated sex manual. So, another unconventional midlife drama but lighter, certainly, than Onwards and Sideways.

“There was something about this world of Parkinson’s that forced me to be very present in a way that I normally am not, particularly while working,” she admits. “It forced me to be over my skis a bit. And off-balance, and vulnerable, and experiencing things in very different ways. “This movie rearranged my cellular structure!” she adds, beaming in gratitude. “Most movies don’t do that. I love my work. But very few experiences have literally rearranged my soul. This one certainly did.”

As for Ifans, this year we’ve seen him alongside Anna Maxwell Martin in Apple TV’s cold war-era sci-fi thriller Star City. When I meet him, he’s just been beheaded on House of the Dragon. Onwards and Sideways, in stark contrast, is acting in the raw, with no high-concept narrative or CGI to hide behind. Acting of a different order.

“Yes. You can have spaceships, lunar landscapes, swords and castles, but you ain’t gonna have a co-star like this,” Ifans says, beaming at Linney. “That’s where the money is. Not the coin … That’s why we go to work. As Laura says: all these [roles] are different and thrilling and enjoyable in their own way. But this film is particularly nourishing.”

Having seen Onwards and Sideways in the company of my mum, who cares 24/7 for my dad, I couldn’t agree more. We watched it bathed in both tears and smiles. It’s a beautiful achievement; empowering, educational entertainment, and Ifans and Linney deserve all the credit in the world for how they’ve portrayed the multiverse of Parkinson’s. I would send them a personal note to thank them for what they’ve done for those with, and connected with, the disease. But I’m not sure they’d be able to read my handwriting.

Onwards and Sideways is in UK cinemas from 6 November, and on BBC One and iPlayer later this year.

These midterms could effectively end the Trump era – but neither side is yet ready for what comes next

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 06:00:32 GMT

Despite the US president’s ratings being at rock bottom, undoing his legacy will be difficult, not least because the Democrats are in disarray

The stats and polling all suggest one thing: the Republicans are set for a hammering in the midterms. Donald Trump has the lowest approval rating of any US president going into a midterm election since Harry Truman. And it’s still dropping. The Democrats are projected to win by a margin of 11 percentage points, the largest swing by any party in almost 20 years. It is possible that the Democrats flip the Senate and secure a large majority in Congress. Those majorities would make a material difference, perhaps finally establishing oversight of the policies Trump has brought in during his second term: immigration enforcement, trade disputes, gutting the federal workforce, the Iran war, to say nothing of his own family’s corruption. The tide seems to be turning, and one question is on everyone’s mind: is the Trump era really ending?

“Nobody wants to jinx it,” wrote David Wallace-Wells of the New York Times, but: “All the signs we have suggest that, historic or not, these midterms are likely to mark the end of a political era.” What that gives way to is a much more complicated picture in which the US will be delivered from Trump himself, but remains a country riven and undermined by what he has unleashed. By the time he is gone, Trump will have been president for eight years, and a toxic force for more than 12. That is a long time even for a normal politician. Under one who shatters norms and forces himself into the centre of everything, Trump’s effect is as if he were president for decades.

He has already enacted policy that is nearly irreversible, things that can only be overturned with a huge amount of work and legislative wrangling and improbable bipartisan consensus. USAID is gone. Probably also gone are government departments effectively eliminated or incapacitated by Doge, the “department of government efficiency”. There are entire global tariff regimes and the executive and budgetary empowerments of ICE to deal with. And most difficult to unspool is a war with Iran that, despite its promised, imminent end, is looking to be an open-ended conflict. Even if the midterms augur a win for the Democrats in 2028, the country they will inherit will have been permanently shaped by Trump.

And that is still a big if. Trump is a singular figure who cohered an otherwise inchoate and disparate coalition, from white evangelical Christians to working-class Latinos to Silicon Valley billionaires. Maga is a movement that is bound up with Trump, and feels increasingly weakened by his incumbency. Like Brexit and other insurgent movements, the galvanising anti-establishment power is lost when you are the establishment and have been for quite a long time. Looking for new people to blame, new grievances to exploit, becomes less an exercise in rebellion, more in whining and negativity. But whoever comes after Trump as a candidate, even if it is the black hole of charisma that is JD Vance, may still find some success using the same general pitch. That combination of combativeness and fractiousness might still read as authentic and subversive to the base. It may even seem comparatively sharp and legible against the opaque generic blah-ness of the Democratic establishment.

And that Democratic establishment itself is reason to worry. It is a ways to go yet, but the Democrats themselves seem unable to go either back or forward decisively. The party’s old guard is spent, either gerontocratic or gerontocracy-adjacent. In the latter camp is Kamala Harris, whose last campaign summons not the hope of a fresh candidate in 2026, but an apparatchik who offers only continuity without gravitas. In the former, there is a cohort who now only project entitlement and the out-of-touch, glassy-eyed bloat of so many years of capital acquisition - Nancy Pelosi, Chuck Schumer, Hillary Clinton.

Only Barack Obama still enjoys some sprightly relevance, and has used it to back Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who is making that break with the past in a journey that Obama has cast as a passing of the baton. “He’ll finish the job we started,” Obama has said.

But even as El-Sayed is on the verge of making history as the first Muslim senator in a state that is pivotal to the presidential race, he is either drawing lukewarm, reluctant endorsements from other senior Democrats or he is openly attacked, primarily on his position towards Israel, which he believes has committed genocide in Gaza and should be defunded. Only a few days out from the election, Democratic congresswoman Haley Stevens, who El-Sayed narrowly beat last August to clinch the candidacy, has been taking big swipes at El-Sayed and his comments on Israel, and demanding he disavow election ads not even run by him, but by a leftwing group that backed him. The result is an unseemly scuffle that resulted first in El-Sayed saying he did not want Stevens appearing with him at a party unity event held on Sunday, and culminated later that day with an extraordinarily disgraceful development: Stevens endorsed El Sayed’s Republican opponent, Mike Rogers.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Divesting from Israel has become a flashpoint that appears to be less about political and ideological positions than the emergence of a new orientation in the party that breaks from an old guard overtaken by rapid changes of attitude. This was encapsulated by a quote from David Kramer, a Democrat who chaired Stevens’s primary campaign: “There’s a lot of talk about it being a big tent party, but sometimes we worry the tent is maybe devolving into a circus and we’re going to be pushed out.” Kramer is also voting for Rogers for the Senate. And there you have it. Some Democrats would rather lose than win on the left’s terms and be pushed out.

All of this suggests a future in which Trump is no longer on the scene, but there is still enough residual momentum among Trump’s acolytes, and disarray within the Democratic party, to render a midterm surge a temporary setback for Trumpism, not the restoration of the old order or the beginnings of a new one.

We have been here before. In fact, it’s worse than that, we have been here before in vastly better circumstances for the Democrats. Trump’s loss in 2020 happened in a context where there was a strong and familiar Democratic candidate in Joe Biden, a pandemic that research found hit Trump’s support, and no big live crisis in the Middle East roiling domestic politics. The midterms may spell the end of a certain Trump era, but what follows may probably be a case of long-Trump: a Republican party still unable to plot a path without him, and a Democratic party still unable to locate what it stands for outside of opposing him.

Nesrine Malik is a Guardian columnist

‘It’s far too late for me to go to the gym every 10 minutes’: Jo Brand on ageing, raging, fitness and grief

The Guardian Mon, 02 Nov 2026 05:00:31 GMT

The comedian turns 70 soon, and in her new book, she contemplates the years ahead. She explains why she loves a work in progress, the importance of anger in mourning, and how she gave up smoking – only to become a champion vaper

Had Jo Brand, who turns 70 next year, been spending a long time thinking about getting older? Had it become the subject that consumed her, and the reason why, now, she felt impelled to write a book about the vagaries of ageing? No, she says, laughing. She was simply asked if she’d like to do it.

Still, it encouraged introspection about what she wanted her future to look like. “Now’s the time, if you want things, to get them in place. I think a lot of people say, ‘I really want to do that, but I’ll forget it for now.’ And then they get to a stage where they can’t.” Does she mean bucket-list things? “No, I mean … what do I mean?” Brand pauses. “I mean the ability to perhaps end your own …” She doesn’t go there, but the end to that sentence is obviously: life.

“I know it’s not legal yet, but I think it will be, sooner rather than later.” Her mother had procured drugs to end her own life when she was ill, though she didn’t use them. Two minutes in, and we’re already talking about assisted dying. Off-duty comedians – such a laugh.

I’m being unfair. Of course Brand is fun, but ageing isn’t, sometimes. In her book, Decline and Falling Over, she calls the point past middle age “your shitter second half”. The book is funny, as you’d expect, but also surprisingly sober, covering such cheering topics as the decision to go into a care home and, yes, assisted dying.

Despite thinking about what she wants her future to look like, Brand has not yet come to any solid conclusions. As a teenager, she worked in a residential home (for adults with learning disabilities, rather than older people), and complained after she witnessed some “appalling behaviour” by male staff. It was not investigated; instead, she was sacked. She was left with a fear of care homes. “That was in the 70s. Are they that different now? Who knows?” But, she adds, “I can’t imagine I can persuade any of my family to get interested in looking after me.” (She has two grown-up daughters.)

Are there any benefits of getting older? “Being rude to people.” She laughs. “No, not really. But saying what you think, I suppose. I like the whole ‘grumpy old woman’ sort of thing. I do quite like being grumpy. I’ve never really been a grumpy person. I’ve been a bit friendly, and tried to be pleasant to everyone – not on stage, I accept that, because a lot of people think I’m probably horrible, but in my personal life.” It is, she says, “that whole thing that a lot of women suffer from, which is putting everybody first and themselves last”.

Brand writes several times that she’s a “people pleaser” – which, given her bolshie stage persona and unflinching attitude, surprises me (although she has always seemed thoughtful, and very kind). “It surprises me as well,” she says. We’re in a meeting room at the Guardian offices, Brand glorious in layers of black with dark pink hair, looking queenly but punk. “I have always been one because … well, why? I’ve no idea. My dad was quite hard to please, so maybe I spent quite a lot of time doing that.”

Did the on-stage version of her character not influence the way she was in real life? “I don’t think it really did,” she says. “I think that was because there weren’t many women comics around when I started – you needed a sort of shield.” If she could be more vulgar, more aggressive than the drunk men who heckled her, they’d back off – or at least, she hoped, word would get around that she wasn’t to be messed with. “If you’re heckled, you have to deal with it because audiences lose faith in you if you don’t, so I had a sliding scale of pleasant through to soul-destroying. I never wanted to use soul-destroying, but I occasionally would.”

Growing up in Hastings, where the family ended up after moving from London and Kent, the teenage Brand was rebellious rather than people-pleasing. She had unsuitable boyfriends, stayed out, discovered drugs. “But that was more to do with the circumstances we were in,” she says. “At the time my dad was in a very bad place, and so he was really difficult to live with.” He could be violent. “I mean, not as bad as some poor women have it on a regular basis, but quite a few times. Mainly when I answered back to him, or my little brother did.” Brand, I notice, tends to downplay a lot, but it must have been scary. “It makes you a bit jumpy, hypervigilant. So I was only too delighted to get out of home.”

She moved into a bedsit at 17. It was quite exciting, looking back. “We had the freedom to behave appallingly, if we wanted to.” Was she in danger of going out of control? “I always had a sense of when the brakes should be applied. So I was never in danger of, let’s say, becoming a heroin addict, even though I was around a lot of people that used drugs. I think I would have quite happily drunk a lot more if I could drink.” But she couldn’t hold it. “When I was at university, I was very cheap to get pissed.”

Becoming a comic had been Brand’s ambition since she was a teenager. “I liked making people laugh, but not in any well-formed sense of doing an act.” She became a psychiatric nurse instead, trying standup at 29. “I imposed a pointless line on my life: that you can’t get to 30 and not have tried comedy.” It helped that she was older, she thinks, and that no heckler could ever be as shocking or as aggressive as some of the patients she had dealt with, who suffered with psychosis. “I was a bit hardened.”

Still, how did she not let it get to her, listening to drunk men making personal attacks? “My self-esteem had gone as low as it probably could. It’s hard, because it’s embarrassing if someone says something really gross and awful to you in front of a big group of other people. And the way to deal with it, to me, is to come back with something better. It’s like a battle. If we’d had to fight each other, obviously I wouldn’t have done terribly well.” She smiles. “But I might have done.”

What was it like to be a young woman on the circuit? Was sexual harassment part of her experience? “Not the way I looked,” Brand laughs. Then she reconsiders: “Actually, there were a few comics occasionally trying to get in my room at two o’clock in the morning. I just shouted through the door, told them to fuck off, and they did. So it was nothing that I couldn’t deal with.”

Still, the 80s comedy circuit sounds as if it must have been thrilling. It was, she says. “There was such a variety of people doing such weird things, like melting a block of ice or whatever it was they did,” she says, referring to the performance artist Anthony Irvine, known as the Iceman. “These days, it’s much more uniform. I think there are some really brilliant comics around, but it’s become very stand-uppy.” It’s expected to be more polished now, I venture, less anarchic. “Yes, maybe anarchy needs to come back.”

The birth of alternative comedy in the 80s must also have felt exciting, politically, after decades of old-style comedians with their racist and sexist jokes. For a while it must have felt as if a generation of progressive comics could change, or at least help change, society. But it doesn’t feel like that now. “Yeah, the world is in a mess,” says Brand. “But there are an awful lot of good people, and I just hope the good people win out. I’m not an optimist, but then again, I’m not a terrible pessimist, either.”

By 1993 Brand had her own show, Jo Brand Through the Cakehole. It was a mix of standup and sketches. In one segment – Drudge Squad, her spoof cop show – two female detectives worn down by domesticity try to fight crime amid laundry baskets and useless husbands.

There were men in the tabloids who were unforgivably awful about Brand, especially about the way she looked. But as for the teenage girls (myself among them) who watched her Friday night Channel 4 show, it’s hard to overstate the thrill of seeing Brand, a woman who looked and spoke differently from everyone else: hilariously rude and unapologetic.

Is she envious of female comedians starting now? Does she think they get an easier time? “I’m not, actually. There’s a lot more really good competition these days, and because we were quite unusual – I think there were 15 of us out of, like, 200 male comics – we were a bit of a novelty act, so that was a help. And people didn’t quite know what to make of us, and that was a help, too.”

Until last year, Brand presented the Great British Bake Off after-show, An Extra Slice, and this year she is doing a book tour. She has already won a Bafta for her role as a kind but harassed nurse in Getting On, the BBC comedy she co-wrote with Vicki Pepperdine and Joanna Scanlan, set in an NHS geriatric ward. Over the years, she has – for television – learned to play the organ at the Royal Albert Hall, performed as Britney Spears and, for Comic Relief in 2016, walked 140 miles from Hull to Liverpool.

One aspect of getting older, she says, is that she is less adventurous than she used to be. “I used to do quite a lot of stupid things, like jump off things or learn how to rally drive. I couldn’t imagine being a rally driver now. I love a bit of madness like that, but I’m much less mad than I used to be, physically.”

Brand also doesn’t do as many live shows. She thinks her memory took a hit during the pandemic, which makes remembering long sets a bit harder. But she has been doing some “work-in-progress shows”, which takes the pressure off a polished performance. “I was so delighted that I could use that tag, which basically means: most of this might be rubbish.”

One of the worst things about ageing, she says, particularly as a woman, is that “you get ignored. Putting my job for a moment out of the equation, older men still get much more respect than older women, because we all think older women are just one big blob that looks the same. I think it’s going to take a while longer to cherish older women for the fantastic variety that they are.”

Brand has experienced tragedy in the last 10 years – she lost her parents, both brothers, and two of her three best friends. How has she dealt with it? “I’ve been very good at suppressing my emotions,” she says. “I was always taught not to show any weakness in public, which used to be just a bloke’s thing, didn’t it? So I probably haven’t handled it all very well – I just pretended it wasn’t happening for a long time because I couldn’t believe how awful it was.”

In her book, she writes about being stuck at the “angry stage” of grief for a while. “I like the angry stage,” she says. “I think anger is just as valid as crying – you can be angry about people leaving you. I think being angry is very good for me.” As for denial, another part of the so-called five stages of grief, Brand says she could probably do it for the rest of her life. “So yes, I’m not terribly good at grief, because I’m not terribly good at acceptance, either – I don’t think I’ve done that yet at all.” Sometimes she’ll think she hasn’t heard from one of those best friends for a while. “And then I remember. That weird stuff happens with grief all the time, doesn’t it?”

Has it made her agonise about her own mortality more? “Less! I refuse to think about it. I’m a massive avoider of those sorts of things. I know it’s a bad thing to be, but what’s the point of thinking about it? It’s far too late for me to go down the gym every 10 minutes. At least, I did give up smoking, but now I’m a champion vaper.”

Best just to get on with things. Or at least take a tip on ageing from her great-grandmother, “who just went to bed and ate chocolate all day”. Not that retirement holds any appeal. Brand is lucky, she says, in that her job is not one she has to retire from. “There are still enough people to come and see me at shows, so I can do that if I want to.” Long may she reign.

Decline and Falling Over is published by Penguin (£22). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Backlash to Immigration Crackdown Creates a Challenge for Republicans

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump promised to end the chaos at the southern border. But deadly ICE shootings and high-profile raids have shaken many voters.

By Jennifer Medina and Jazmine Ulloa

President Trump returned to the White House calling for “mass deportations now,” after anger over illegal immigration drove his voters to the polls in 2024. But two years later, amid high-profile raids and deadly ICE shootings, immigration politics have been scrambled once again, creating unpredictable fault lines in the hours leading up to Election Day.

Public polling suggests that voters are now more likely to trust Democrats on immigration policy, although Republican voters remain more motivated by the issue. And while some Latino voting-rights activists worry that recent immigration raids in California and elsewhere could suppress Hispanic turnout, others are optimistic that the opposite is true in some of the most competitive congressional districts in the country.

“Republicans are really out of step with where Americans are with immigration, just like how Democrats were out of step in 2024,” said Senator Ruben Gallego, a Democrat who won in Arizona two years ago while calling for stricter immigration enforcement. “They wanted the chaos to be done, but what is happening now is not what they wanted. They are not for heavy-handed immigration forces. They are not for racial profiling; they see the sob stories.”

In the first two years of his second term, Mr. Trump has moved aggressively to overhaul the nation’s immigration system, and the southern border has largely been shut down. Attempted illegal border crossings have plummeted from a peak of nearly 250,000 in November 2023 to about 11,000 this past August.

But the administration also unleashed an enormous enforcement apparatus that has drawn widespread criticism. Large-scale raids have unfolded in Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis. Federal detention capacity has more than doubled through a network of local jail contracts, retrofitted warehouses and tent cities.

And the administration has all but dismantled pathways to asylum, reduced refugee admissions to a trickle and stripped temporary deportation protections from roughly one million migrants who entered the country during the Biden administration. At the same time, the government has pressured immigrants into self-deportation and pushed immigration judges to expedite dockets, keeping more people behind bars and deporting hundreds to countries where they have no personal ties.

At campaign events, the president has compared his record favorably to that of his predecessor. At a recent rally in Iowa, he blamed Democrats for the flood of migrants entering the country during the Biden administration and warned that it would happen again if Republicans lost the election. “It was an invasion — it was like a military invasion,” he said. “They will do it again. They’re going to open up the border.”

But his assertive approach has created a backlash among voters.

Voters in 2024 were more likely to list immigration as a top issue than in this midterm year, when economic concerns are driving the conversation even more. And immigration continues to be more of a motivating issue for Republicans than Democrats. But opposition to the Trump administration’s policies has changed the calculus significantly. In the most recent New York Times/Siena poll, half of all voters said they trusted Democrats on the issue, while 46 percent said they trusted Republicans. That is a striking reversal from just two years ago, when Mr. Trump held an 11-point advantage on immigration in the Times/Siena national poll.

Immigration has helped drive the gains that Democrats appear to be making with Hispanic voters throughout the country. While Latino voters were divided on which party to trust on immigration in 2024, they now give Democrats a 27-point lead. And about one in five Latinos said immigration was the most important issue to their vote, according to the Times/Siena poll, compared to just 6 percent in September.

The Rev. Samuel Rodriguez, who leads the National Hispanic Christian Leadership Conference, which includes thousands of churches, said Republicans had squandered a unique opportunity to make politically popular changes to immigration policies.

“They could have developed a viable solution to immigration and bring a secure border, and get rid of egregious criminals,” he said. “Instead, you’re picking up people who have been making their lives for years, and even ministers. What are we doing here? What just happened?”

The issue could help Democrats in dozens of tight races throughout the country, particularly in California, Colorado, Florida and Texas, where immigrant-heavy communities have felt the impact of the crackdown. In September, Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a television ad warning Mr. Trump that his aggressive tactics had “gone too far” and left many of his Hispanic supporters feeling “betrayed.” Like many Republicans who represent areas with a large Latino population, Ms. Salazar is in a surprisingly tight re-election campaign in a district where Mr. Trump won with a double-digit lead.

One such district sits in the heart of California’s Central Valley, where Representative David Valadao, a Republican, has repeatedly faced serious challengers since he was first elected in 2012. The district stretches across the state’s agricultural heartland. Roughly 65 percent of registered voters are Latino, and Democrats have long outnumbered Republicans.

Recent immigration raids in Mr. Valadao’s district have gripped some farmworker communities with so much fear that local markets began delivering groceries to immigrant families afraid to leave home. Local residents say the rise in traffic stops and other arrests has kept Latino workers from reporting to work and emptied Latino businesses.

Mr. Valadao has long said he would support a legal pathway for undocumented residents who have been in the country for many years and have not committed crimes. He has also urged the administration to prioritize deporting violent criminals rather than agricultural workers.

In the final days of the campaign, Mr. Valadao’s Democratic challenger, Randy Villegas, 31, a college professor and the son of Mexican immigrants, has seized on the issue of immigration, attacking Mr. Valadao for supporting legislation that tripled the budget for federal immigration enforcement. He blames Mr. Valadao for enabling a deportation campaign he says is harming agricultural workers and the economy.

“It’s shameful, it is despicable and we deserve a member of Congress who has a spine to actually stand up for our immigrant communities,” Mr. Villegas said in an interview.

In a statement, Mr. Valadao said that he has worked with both parties to “fix our broken immigration system” and that “meaningful immigration will require bipartisan cooperation.”

“I understand the concerns about enforcement activities, but based on my conversations with the administration and producers around my district, there’s no evidence that farmworkers are being targeted,” he added.

Immigration continues to be a campaign issue for Republican candidates for Congress, but Democrats in this election have increasingly used it as a line of attack, too, including in political advertising.

Democrats have produced about 320 ads focused on immigration — more than five times the number in the 2022 midterms, according to AdImpact, a media tracking firm. Republicans have created about 890, a slight uptick from four years ago.

Across competitive races in the Southwest, Andrea Flores, a lawyer and immigration policy adviser in the Obama and Biden administrations, said she had seen a slate of Democratic candidates more willing to “flip the script” by tying immigration policy to labor shortages and the battered economy.

In New Mexico, Representative Gabe Vasquez, a Democrat locked in a tight bid for a third term, has championed visas for child care providers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat who has pulled within striking distance of unseating Gov. Greg Abbott, addressed reporters from an uncompleted construction site, where she said immigrant workers did not feel safe showing up.

Still, Ms. Flores said Democrats have largely focused on attacking Republicans, rather than articulating their own policy agenda. “There is an urgent need to define what they are for on the issue because just being against ICE is not enough,” she said.

In the run-up to the election, some voting rights advocates have worried about the impact of immigration enforcement on turnout.

Although voters are by definition U. S. citizens, many fear being harassed or even detained by immigration agents, said Cesar Fierros, a spokesman for a group called Living United for Change in Arizona.

“There was a time when there was a belief that, ‘Hey, I am a citizen. I am not undocumented. I don’t have to worry about it,’” he said. “But now you are seeing U. S. citizens arrested and detained.”

But so far, early data suggests an increase in early voting turnout among Latinos, including in Texas and California.

“If this was meant as voter intimidation, it’s not working,” said Andrea Guerrero, executive director at Alliance San Diego, a legal services and voter mobilization organization. “Voting is surging in San Diego County and in California.”

Ruth Igielnik and Miriam Jordan contributed reporting.

Jennifer Medina is a Los Angeles-based political reporter for The Times, focused on political attitudes and demographic change.

Jazmine Ulloa is a national reporter covering immigration for The Times.

Iran Says It Would Reopen Strait of Hormuz in 2 Days as Part of U. S. Deal

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Iranian officials spoke of some progress in negotiating to reopen the strait, a vital oil and gas shipping lane, even as they prepare for all-out war.

By Erika Solomon and Sanam Mahoozi

Iran is prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in two days if the United States agrees to a set of demands, its foreign ministry said on Monday, after a week of intensified negotiations to avert a return to war.

But those demands, which include the Trump administration lifting sanctions on Iran and releasing billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets, appear difficult for Washington to accept.

The foreign ministry’s spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, made the comments hours after President Trump had said at a campaign rally that he might eventually decide to give Iran “the hammer” if the two sides could not reach a deal to end the war.

Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil and gas shipping in the Persian Gulf, after U. S. and Israeli forces attacked the country in February. That move roiled energy markets, and continues to shake the global economy.

American and Israeli military officials have been drawing up plans for renewed strikes on Iran after this week’s U. S. midterm elections. Iranian leaders have warned that, if the country were attacked again, its forces would expand their range of targets, and are they are now publicly considering a withdrawal from the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, which prohibits the development of a nuclear weapon.

Propelled by increasingly bellicose rhetoric from both Iran and the United States, Qatari mediators have been pushing to broker a last-ditch deal between the two countries.

In recent days, Iranian officials have signaled that those negotiations have made some progress, though Mr. Baghaei stressed that they were not at a point where Iranian negotiators were prepared to hold direct talks with their U. S. counterparts.

“If Iran’s legitimate demands are accepted and implemented, it would be possible to put the entire plan into operation within two days, restore security to the Strait of Hormuz, and initiate the negotiation process,” Mr. Baghaei told reporters on Monday. ⁠ “⁠The realization of this depends entirely on Washington’s will and decision.”

The global benchmark oil price, apparently responding to potential progress in the talks, declined about 8 percent on Monday to about $104 a barrel.

Still, conditions around the Strait of Hormuz remain dangerous. More than 35 ships were attacked in October, more than in any other month since the war began.

In September, Iran proposed a phased deal to reopen the strait, in which the warring countries would take turns to make concessions, culminating in Tehran ensuring safe passage through the strait, while Washington would lift a naval blockade on Iran’s ports.

After that initial phase, Iran proposed that the two sides could begin negotiating a comprehensive peace deal that would restart talks over its nuclear enrichment program. U. S. officials rejected this proposal, saying Iran should commit to nuclear concessions earlier.

Qatari mediators have managed to revive negotiations over the past few weeks, initially accelerating the implementation of the initial phase to five days, and more recently condensing that to two days, Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told the broadcaster Al Jazeera on Saturday.

Mr. Araghchi made no mention of nuclear concessions. In a televised interview on Saturday, one of the officials overseeing the talks, Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s national security adviser, said nuclear negotiations could begin only after Washington had met Iranian conditions.

Alongside the demands related to sanctions and frozen assets, Mr. Araghchi said in his interview that the U. S. would also have to recognize a deal between Oman and Iran for administering passage through the strait in the future.

At the same time, Mr. Rezaei said that a recent letter sent to him about negotiations from Vice President JD Vance had shown a changed tone toward Iran, which the Iranian official called a “good sign.”

Even as Gulf leaders pin their hopes on a diplomatic solution, they are “braced for the worst,” said Anwar Gargash, the diplomatic adviser to the president of the United Arab Emirates, at the Manama Dialogue security conference over the weekend. The stakes of the negotiations are particularly high for Gulf Arab countries, which were battered by Iranian drone and missile attacks in retaliation for U. S.-Israeli strikes.

“The rules of logic tell us that the Iranian stand and U. S. stand are far apart,” Mr. Gargash said at the conference in Bahrain. “If these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.”

Iranian officials have repeatedly stressed that they are suspicious the talks could unravel. In his news conference on Monday, Mr. Baghaei said that the United States and Israel had attacked Iran in June 2025 shortly after Iranian officials had held negotiations with Washington.

Mr. Trump’s current stance remains ambiguous. On Sunday, he told journalists that he had had a “good talk” with President Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel over the weekend, which included a discussion of the war.

“The only reason we’re not finished with Iran is I want to be nice — I want to try and save all those lives if I can,” he told a campaign rally in Iowa later on Sunday. “But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer.”

Adam Rasgon, Vivian Nereim and Ismaeel Naar contributed reporting

Erika Solomon is The Times’s bureau chief for Iran and Iraq.

Trump Is Playing Up Voter Fraud Prosecutions. Meet Some of the Accused.

The New York Times November 02, 2026
