The Trump administration’s campaign to identify and charge immigrants in connection with voting violations has led to fears of being jailed, or deported.

By Livia Albeck-Ripka and Jacey Fortin

Livia Albeck-Ripka reported from Los Angeles and Jacey Fortin reported from New York.

It was before dawn when Amandeep Kaur turned herself in to federal authorities in downtown Los Angeles last Monday. Wrapped in a tasseled shawl, she paced and shivered as she waited outside the courthouse.

At 6:30 a. m., two plainclothes agents rounded the corner, served Ms. Kaur her arrest warrant and walked her to an unmarked vehicle, where they lightly searched her. She would be fingerprinted and taken into custody before appearing in front of a judge that afternoon.

Ms. Kaur, a 30-year-old from India, lives with her two young children, her husband and her in-laws in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif. She speaks little English and is a legal permanent resident of the United States.

The government says in court documents that Ms. Kaur registered to vote in 2022, voted in the 2024 election — unlawfully, they say, because she is not a U. S. citizen — and then made false statements about that history on her naturalization application.

As of Friday, she was among more than 220 people across 28 states charged in connection with voting violations during President Trump’s second term — part of the administration’s far-reaching, monthslong effort to find, arrest and publicize instances of voter fraud.

In the process, people like Ms. Kaur have been caught up in a disorienting and often demeaning experience: Taken by federal agents from their homes, or ordered to turn themselves in. Portrayed as criminals by the country many of them are trying to become citizens of, with their names and faces circulating online. Forced to appear before judges, in some cases in shackles. Some people have been kept in custody for days. At least one man remains in a Texas jail.

Election officials in California and other states have condemned the government’s crackdown, saying its system for identifying suspected violators is severely flawed, based on incomplete information, and has been rife with mistakes, including targeting people who are citizens.

The backdrop to the latest round of charges is the fierce midterm battle in which Democrats are in position to retake the House and possibly the Senate. Mr. Trump has repeatedly made unsubstantiated claims that Democrats have stolen past elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally. He has called for national measures to prevent fraud that include voter identification, proof of citizenship and restrictions on mail balloting.

State audits and studies have repeatedly found that noncitizen voting is extremely rare, and there have been no instances in which their votes are known to have swayed an election.

The New York Times spent more than a week contacting people whom the administration charged in connection with violating election law. In interviews, some of the defendants and their family members cited language barriers, confusion about the voting process and unexpectedly receiving ballots in the mail as reasons for mistakenly registering or casting a vote.

Others denied the allegations completely. They said they were shocked when the authorities contacted them or showed up at their doors.

The Homeland Security Department did not respond to a request for comment. Nor did the Justice Department. It has described the arrests as part of a coordinated effort “to combat and root out fraud in U. S. elections and protect electoral integrity.”

Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, has said that “every illegal vote cancels out the vote of a lawful American citizen.”

Ms. Kaur’s husband, Kulwinder Ghotra, said that his wife, who speaks Punjabi, began receiving voter information in the mail after taking a driving test at the Department of Motor Vehicles. Believing she was eligible, he said, she voted in 2024.

“She was confused,” said Mr. Ghotra, 38. “She said there was no translation there at the voting center.”

Ms. Kaur was eventually charged with making false statements on her naturalization application — a felony that carries a maximum sentence of up to five years in federal prison, a fine, or both, and which can result in deportation. She declined to be interviewed about her case while it is pending.

Mr. Ghotra now fears that his wife could be deported. The couple has two children, ages 3 and 5.

Last week, a judge ruled that Ms. Kaur could return home in advance of her hearing this month. A translator relayed this to Ms. Kaur in Punjabi.

She was escorted from the courtroom in shackles and handcuffs.

Early on Oct. 19, federal agents banged on the door of Omar Alexander Muñoz, a 72-year-old from Belize, at his home in Commerce, Calif. They threatened to break down the door, Mr. Muñoz said in an interview.

He said the agents pulled his arms behind his back to handcuff him, injuring his shoulder and his neck, both of which he said he had recently had surgery on.

Several police cars, as well as members of the media, were stationed outside his home during the arrest, Mr. Muñoz said.

“They were positioned in a way, waiting,” he said of the reporters. “I was used to make a show of voter fraud.”

The Justice Department did not respond to questions about whether or not agents had notified the news media in advance of the arrest, or whether they had used excessive force.

Voting rights experts have called arrests of individuals like Mr. Muñoz performative stunts intended to bolster the government’s legal effort to disqualify California voters.

“This is to serve a political purpose, and that political purpose is to support the civil suit, as well as to support Donald Trump’s claims of a big problem of noncitizen voters,” said Richard Hasen, a law professor and election law expert at the University of California, Los Angeles.

“My first reaction was: These are the best cases they have?” Mr. Hasen said. “Like this guy, Omar Muñoz, like, he’s the perp? Please.”

A legal permanent resident of the United States for more than five decades, Mr. Munoz was charged with illegally registering to vote and making false statements on his citizenship application.

He maintains his innocence. In an interview with CBS News, he said he believed someone else may have used his name.

Though President Trump has made a particular example of California, charges of voter fraud have been made across more than two dozen states, including Florida, North Carolina, Pennsylvania and Texas.

Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, of Arlington, Texas, is originally from India and became a permanent legal resident in 2022.

Mr. Bhengura, 70, who speaks Punjabi, had been living in Texas with his wife, according to his brother-in-law Jay Chima. But he had an old habit of nodding along to things he did not understand in order to seem agreeable, Mr. Chima said, and “his English skills are nil.”

In September, Mr. Bhengura was charged with making false statements while registering to vote, and with casting a ballot unlawfully in 2024. He took his case to trial and pleaded not guilty; his lawyers argued that there was not enough evidence to prove that he had voted. They also worried about his ability to comprehend a fast-moving trial.

On Tuesday, a jury found Mr. Bhengura guilty of making false statements of citizenship in order to register to vote, and of voting by an alien in a federal election.

After the verdict was read, Mr. Bhengura was jailed. He remains in custody.

Nicole Knox, a lawyer for Mr. Bhengura, said she found the jailing appalling, and that she worried about what it could mean for other immigrants.

“It creates basically a blank check for further indictments of similarly situated people with innocent intent,” she said.

Jamil Ahmad, 51, of Philadelphia, came to the U. S. from Pakistan about a decade ago and claimed asylum. He is now a United States citizen. But in November 2024, he still had his green card. At the time, he said in an interview, get-out-the-vote campaigners were contacting him by mail, by phone and in person, encouraging him to register.

Mr. Ahmad reasoned that if were not allowed to cast a ballot, then the government would not let him. And he considered it his duty to vote, he said. He helped his wife, Nighat Jamil, a 47-year-old permanent legal resident, to register alongside him.

“I was thinking that, if I’m eligible, then they will accept the form,” he said. “If I’m not eligible, they will send me the form back.”

What came in the mail was not a rejection, but a ballot. Mr. Ahmad voted for President Trump. Ms. Jamil, whose English skills are more limited than her husband’s, said that she trusted him to fill out her ballot.

In September, Mr. Ahmad was charged with voting as an alien in a federal election. The authorities came to his house to question him, he said, which spiked his stress levels. But after a couple of weeks, Mr. Ahmad thought it made sense to take responsibility for what had happened.

“When I read all the things,” he said, “now I understand that this is a crime.”

He pleaded guilty last month and is scheduled to be sentenced in January.

Ms. Jamil was also charged with the same voting misdemeanor. She has a court hearing scheduled for this month and is nervous, she said, because she is not a citizen and could be at risk of deportation.

That makes Mr. Ahmad feel sick with guilt, and concerned for his four children.

“I’m just worried,” he said. “How I can look after them if they deport my wife?”

Kirsten Noyes and Seamus Hughes contributed research. Sameen Amin contributed translation.

Livia Albeck-Ripka is a Times reporter based in Los Angeles, covering breaking news, California and other subjects.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.

By Mark Arsenault

A federal judge granted Harvard University’s motion to dismiss a Trump administration lawsuit that sought to force the school to turn over admissions documents for a government discrimination investigation.

The administration sued Harvard in February, accusing the university of trying to stymie a federal review of the school’s admissions procedures by withholding documents that the government wanted — among them, application essays written by individual students.

The school portrayed the lawsuit as “part of the Trump administration’s ongoing campaign against Harvard” to try to force it into negotiations. The school has said that it has complied with federal law in its admissions processes.

Harvard did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday. Trump officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

How a Beleaguered U. S. Cyber Agency Retreated From Election Security Work

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

Protecting the vote was once considered among the top priorities of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Now it barely mentions the issue.

By Dustin Volz and Julian E. Barnes

The reporters cover cybersecurity and intelligence and are based in Washington.

Two years ago, the government agency at the forefront of election security did what it had done for every federal election cycle since 2018.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency set up a digital and physical war room, to quickly swap insights and intelligence with state and local officials; updated reporters every few hours on problems occurring nationwide; and sought to educate the public about foreign disinformation campaigns and the resiliency of the United States’ voting process.

But on Tuesday the agency, established by President Trump in his first term, will be largely absent from the action, current and former CISA officials say, weakening the federal government’s ability to help states respond to problems ranging from routine vote-machine disruptions to online hoaxes to bad actors looking to undermine public confidence in the vote. Instead, it is expected to offer light assistance to state and local election officials, many of whom fear the federal government is more likely to meddle with election results than to help safeguard them. There will be no scheduled briefings with reporters, an agency spokesman confirmed on Monday.

“The posture seems like the bare minimum,” said Geoff Hale, a former top election security official at CISA. Such an approach to election security, he said, was not well suited to identifying problems that cut across multiple voting jurisdictions or “the type of national security concerns that once drove the mission.”

It is a remarkable retreat from the agency’s history as a loud and visible presence around Election Day across both the first Trump and Biden administrations.

CISA, the cyber wing of the Department of Homeland Security, was a lead federal partner for states on election security efforts after the 2016 election, sharing cybersecurity best practices and intelligence about foreign intentions around elections. The agency’s leadership and election security advisers painstakingly worked to build trusted relationships with Republican, Democratic and nonpartisan state and local officials, eventually smoothing out concerns among many of them worried about federal intervention in elections, which the Constitution says are overseen by individual states.

But Mr. Trump developed disdain for the agency, and for the government’s election security work generally. Its director at the time, Christopher Krebs, validated the integrity of the 2020 election, prompting the president to fire him.

During Mr. Trump’s second term, the agency has been largely rudderless, with no Senate-confirmed leader. It has continued to be sidelined on elections, even as Mr. Trump gave a prime-time address this summer in which he exaggerated claims about election vulnerabilities and vowed to fix security issues.

Much of its work on election security was gutted as the administration systematically dismantled the expertise built up at the agency. Staff reductions and budget cuts hit deeper than at other offices within the Department of Homeland Security or the broader federal government — CISA shed about a third of its work force, which stood at 3,400 in January 2025. In February last year, the administration put more than a dozen CISA election security workers on leave as part of an investigation into its election work, a move that had a chilling effect on the 100 or so people in the division, former officials said.

While CISA has recently hired some new personnel, the jobs are not for election security positions, current and former officials said.

Other federal agencies have also downsized their election security work, including the F. B. I. and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. But CISA, as the public-facing arm of the federal government’s election protection efforts, has made cuts that state and local officials have felt the most.

Among other changes, the agency ended the voluntary cybersecurity reviews it had offered to state and local jurisdictions for election systems. In some locations, though, they continued if local officials requested generic cybersecurity reviews for a courthouse or other state building that housed election tabulation machines, instead of specifically requesting help for an election.

And the regular flow of intelligence warnings, prepared by spy agencies and passed to local officials by CISA, slowed to a trickle, according to election experts.

In a statement, a CISA spokesman said it was “fully equipped and prepared to address any national security cyber threats that face our nation,” and described the agency as “stronger than ever” despite the staff reductions.

“Our regional teams assist partners across the country by assessing risks, helping entities strengthen their defenses and resilience, and responding promptly to threats,” the spokesman said. “As CISA has routinely done for previous elections, the agency has activated an incident coordination group before and on Election Day to support election officials and maintain a unified operational picture.”

CISA is treating the midterm elections as a “one-day hurricane,” said a current official at the agency, who was granted anonymity to speak freely. In practice, that means that regional personnel are expected to be on hand to lend help to states as requested on cybersecurity or physical security issues as they arise. But there is no coordinated national war room effort as there has been during every election cycle since 2018, the official said.

The lack of briefings to the news media will leave a vacuum of reliable federal information on Election Day, former officials and election experts said.

“They don’t have the expertise anymore,” said Mr. Hale, now a visiting fellow on election security at the Center for Democracy & Technology. “But they were a value add amid the fog of an election.”

Officials from the agency note that since Mr. Trump took office, their regional teams have conducted 700 engagements — including planning events, training sessions, and cyber and physical security assessments — with state, local and federal partners. The agency, officials said, continues to pass on warnings and provide technical guidance.

Former officials and election experts said that there was a low bar for what qualified as an “engagement.” Regardless, they added, the figure was low given the number of election jurisdictions nationwide, which some estimates put between 8,000 and 10,000.

Internally, employees acknowledge that little has been done to help states ahead of the midterms, current and former agency officials said. Election experts and local officials say that much of the engagement that took place this year was not helpful for this election, but could potentially be useful for the 2028 presidential election.

In 2020, during the first Trump term, the agency released its election security plan that February. This year, it was issued in late September. It contained minimal information that was new or helpful, election experts said.

In some ways, CISA’s help may be less needed today than in the past. States have improved their election security efforts considerably since revelations of Russian interference operations emerged a decade ago. They also have better protocols today than before Russia sought to interfere in the 2016 election.

But the federal government has returned to its posture before the 2016 cycle, former CISA officials said, no longer regularly sharing intelligence with states about foreign threats or convening election officials to address local and state issues as they arose.

“While the federal government may be back to its 2016 understanding of elections, states aren’t there — they are better postured to defend themselves,” Mr. Hale said. “There are more paper ballots than ever. There are more controls than ever. But that means that the one area that’s at its weakest is the cyberthreat information sharing, the understanding of adversaries and sharing of information about their plans and intentions.”

A recent interview with Nick Andersen, who is serving as both the acting director of CISA and its deputy director, underscored the agency’s rapid shift in approach under the second Trump administration.

Mr. Andersen, appearing on a podcast late last month to discuss the agency’s new cyber strategy, spoke for 10 minutes about its focus on protecting U. S. critical infrastructure. He discussed many aspects of CISA’s mission, including partnerships with the private sector, improving national resiliency to physical and cyber threats, and the integrity of essential services.

He made no mention of the election.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

A 31,000-Mile Walk Ends in England, at Mom’s House

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Karl Bushby arrived in Hull, England, on Monday after spending 28 years crossing four continents on foot.

By Amanda Holpuch

Where does a 31,000-mile walk end?

For Karl Bushby, it was his mother’s house in Hull, a port city on the east coast of England. He had walked around the globe for 28 years.

Mr. Bushby, 56, spoke to a crowd in the city center on Monday before he strolled the final miles to see his mother, Angela Bushby, who had decorated her yard with Union Jack bunting and a banner welcoming her boy.

It had been decades since Mr. Bushby was in his hometown. He began his walk in Punta Arenas, Chile, in November 1998, heading north to the Bering Strait, which he crossed on foot in March 2006. He continued across Asia and Europe.

Along the way, he traversed some of the world’s harshest landscapes, like the jungle of the Darién Gap. He was arrested and deported, and he got lost.

He had self-imposed rules for the walk, which included that he would not set foot in Britain until his journey concluded. This made it difficult to see his son, and his son’s daughter. She is 12, and Mr. Bushby had not met her before Monday.

Another rule was that Mr. Bushby would not use a mode of transport, like a car, a boat or a plane, to travel. So, in order to conclude his journey, he had to swim across the English Channel in October.

He made it to England, and arrived Monday in Hull with his main companion: a modified golf trolley that he has used to haul camping supplies, clothing, toiletries, food and water.

The documentarian Werner Herzog was there to welcome Mr. Bushby and his trolley. Last week, Mr. Bushby said on social media that Mr. Herzog would be making a documentary about him.

At a news conference on Monday, Mr. Bushby said he would be kept busy for the next year with the documentary and a book he is planning to write.

First, though, he had to process what it meant to be back in Hull.

“It’s difficult to explain how all that felt today,” Mr. Bushby said. “It’s all still one great big, blurry mess at the moment in my head.”

Amanda Holpuch covers breaking news and other topics.

A 20-Year-Old Was One Pilot of the Jet That Plunged to Earth in Florida

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Supported by

Nathalia Filgueiras received a pilot’s license at 17, had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and was the co-pilot on Sunday, her mother said in an interview.

By David OvalleJacey Fortin and Karoun Demirjian

One of the pilots of a private jet that plummeted to the ground on Sunday afternoon in Florida, killing all nine people on board, was a 20-year-old aviator named Nathalia Filgueiras, her mother said on Monday.

Ms. Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, Fla., had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and received her pilot’s license at 17, according to her mother, Camila Corteleti. She said her daughter had worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale, and was co-pilot of Sunday’s flight.

The other pilot on the jet has not been identified, and it’s not known who was at the controls when the plane began to fall.

Ms. Corteleti said her daughter had been passionate about flying since childhood, a love forged soaring the skies with her father, who is a recreational pilot. She recalled that her daughter, as a child, used to enjoy going to the Boca Raton Airport to watch planes taking off and landing, and she announced when she was about 12 that she wanted to be a pilot.

“She loved the freedom,” Ms. Corteleti said. “It was completely different seeing the world from the top.”

Three years ago, Ms. Filgueiras, then a senior in high school, was interviewed by TV news reporters, because she had gotten her private pilot’s license even before her driver’s license. “I like being different than everyone,” she told CBS12, a news outlet based in South Florida.

Efforts to reach Upper Jets were not immediately successful.

The company’s plane, a Learjet 60, which had been traveling from Texas to the Bahamas, crashed down in a residential area of Palm Beach County, Fla., leaving a smoldering crater and wreckage in the street.

The authorities said that everyone on the plane had died, but did not identify them. Officials said it did not appear that any people on the ground had been injured.

Thomas B. Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, told reporters at a Monday afternoon news conference in Florida that investigators had not yet recovered a cockpit voice recorder, and that they could not yet say whether one was on the plane.

The agency has just begun documenting the crash scene, which will take several days, said Timothy W. Monville, an investigator with the board. “The biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway,” he said.

In the moments before the plane crashed, a pilot — the authorities have not confirmed whether it was Ms. Filgueiras — radioed air traffic controllers. She said that the plane was facing rain, and “light, clear ice that is manageable, and moderate turbulence,” according to archived communications with air traffic controllers in Miami.

The woman asked whether the plane could climb to 37,000 feet, but, soon after, she desperately declared mayday, a life-threatening emergency. The woman screamed into the radio that the plane was descending at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute. “We’re going to crash into the ground,” she said.

Dr. Robert Joslin, an aviation expert and associate professor at Embry-Riddle Aeronautical University in Florida, said in an interview that a two-person cockpit typically has a pilot flying and a pilot monitoring, or P. F. and P. M. — positions commonly described as pilot and co-pilot.

It is not uncommon for young aviators to serve as pilot monitors on small jets, he said, so that they can log flight hours and move onto bigger aircraft.

Given that Ms. Filgueiras seems to have been handling radio communications, she was almost certainly the pilot monitoring, Dr. Joslin said. Her work probably involved not only communications but also keeping a close eye on the cockpit’s many instruments and gauges, while the pilot flying would have had more physical control over the aircraft.

Jared Isaacman, the administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, wrote on social media on Monday that it was too early to speculate on what might have gone wrong.

Mr. Isaacman said that Ms. Filgueiras “was doing her job, communicating with A. T. C. right to the end in a terrifying situation.”

“She likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die,” he said.

Karoun Demirjian contributed reporting.

Jacey Fortin covers a wide range of subjects for The Times, including extreme weather, court cases and state politics across the country.

Do Animals Grieve?

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Loren Elliott for The New York Times

Supported by

The feeling of existential loss was long thought to be uniquely human. But studies of coyotes, cockatoos and other creatures are prompting some scientists to reconsider.

By Emily Anthes

Coyotes are not obvious romantics. Their habit of stalking across the landscape alone has earned them a reputation as solitary creatures — and not particularly popular ones, with a public image that ranges from troublesome nuisance to dangerous predator.

But they are deeply loyal mates. They remain with their partners for life, grooming each other, sharing food and raising pups together. “Basically, until death do us part,” said Sara Freeman, a neuroscientist at Utah State University.

In her airy, third-floor laboratory, Dr. Freeman is trying to understand how coyote couples forge these bonds — and what happens when they are broken.

“This is a widowed brain,” she said, pulling a few foil-wrapped packages from an ultracold freezer one morning in August. Each held a block of brain tissue, collected from a female coyote who had outlived her mate.

A student began shaving the frozen tissue into paper-thin slices, using the tip of a small paintbrush to nudge each translucent cross-section onto a glass slide. Later, the researchers would examine the samples, looking for neurological signs of “what we would call a grief state,” Dr. Freeman said.

The study remains in early stages, and it could take years to find clear answers. But the project is one of many in the young field of comparative thanatology, an interdisciplinary effort to unpack how animals respond to — and what they might understand about — death.

Evocative anecdotes abound. In 1972, Jane Goodall watched as a chimp named Flint stopped eating and socializing after the death of his mother, Flo; he died, weeks later, near the spot where her body had once lain. In 2003, African elephants were seen repeatedly returning to the body of a fallen matriarch, periodically prodding her with their trunks. In 2018, an orca named Tahlequah spent at least 17 days swimming with the body of her dead calf.

But whether animals experience grief — a complex, often long-lasting psychological and biological response to loss — remains an open question. “It’s definitely one of those great mysteries,” said Jennifer Vonk, a comparative cognitive psychologist at Oakland University. “And a challenge for scientists.”

Animal deaths are often unpredictable and unseen, especially in the wild. And grief is a complex and loaded concept; it’s easy to project our human experiences onto other creatures and impossible to truly get inside their heads.

Scientists are trying anyway. “The field is ripe for development,” said André Gonçalves, a comparative cognitive scientist at the Indianapolis Zoological Society. “I mean, mortality is kind of a big deal, right?”

For decades, many scientists maintained that grief was unique to humans. Researchers who dared to suggest otherwise, armed with anecdotes about animals like Flint, were accused of committing the sin of anthropomorphism — viewing animals through a human-centered lens — and of venturing beyond the available data.

In 2008, an elderly chimpanzee named Pansy unwittingly provided compelling new data. When she died at a British wildlife park, two overhead cameras captured the reactions of her three chimpanzee companions. In the minutes before Pansy died, the other chimps gently groomed and caressed her.

After Pansy took her last breaths, her daughter spent hours beside her body. The other adult female spent an unusually long time grooming her own son. All three chimps slept fitfully that night. And when they awoke, they picked some stray bits of straw from Pansy’s body, then watched quietly as keepers carried her away.

“The chimpanzees seemed to know that this was a momentous event,” said James Anderson, a primatologist at Kyoto University.

In 2010, Dr. Anderson and his colleagues published a detailed analysis of the footage, noting that the behaviors of the surviving chimps were “strikingly reminiscent of human responses to peaceful death.”

“We propose that chimpanzees’ awareness of death has been underestimated,” they added.

The Pansy paper seemed to embolden other researchers to write up their own observations of animal responses to death. Soon, scientists were designing new research projects and looking for patterns in the growing pile of case studies.

“It kind of started snowballing,” said Susana Monsó, a philosopher of animal minds at the National University of Distance Education in Madrid and the author of “Playing Possum: How Animals Understand Death.”

There is no magic formula for determining whether an animal’s behavior qualifies as grief, said Barbara J. King, an anthropologist at William & Mary and the author of “How Animals Grieve.” But changes in daily routines and “species-specific signals of deep sorrow” are among the indicators that animals might be in mourning, Dr. King said.

Many studies document behaviors that seem to fit the bill. Apes, monkeys, dolphins and whales sometimes carry the corpses of their young for days or weeks. Some bereaved macaque mothers become isolated and withdrawn, receiving less grooming and initiating fewer hugs. Giraffes stand vigil over fallen calves; elephants touch the bones of their dead. Dogs, cats and horses sometimes seem to lose interest in food after the death of animal (or human) companions, owners have reported.

Whether these behaviors are signs of sorrow is open to interpretation, and reports from animal caretakers are not always reliable. (Bereaved pet owners might project their own grief onto their surviving animals.) But to Dr. King, there are more than enough credible reports to be convincing. “Grief is not a ‘human’ behavior, by which I mean it’s not a human-only behavior,” she said.

Other scientists are more circumspect. “I would really like there to be strong evidence of grief,” said Alecia Carter, an evolutionary anthropologist at University College London. “But I just personally haven’t found very much.”

Even a behavior like clinging to a corpse is not necessarily easy to interpret. In a 2021 meta-analysis, Dr. Carter and her colleagues found that primate mothers were more likely to carry infants who had died from “nontraumatic” causes, like disease, than from accidents or attacks, which often leave more obvious injuries. The behavior was also more common among young mothers than older ones.

One possible explanation? Primate mothers are most likely to carry dead infants when they don’t fully recognize that they are dead. That’s just a hypothesis, and even Dr. Carter doesn’t find it to be entirely convincing. But it highlights the need to be cautious when drawing conclusions about what’s driving animal behavior.

While anthropologists and zoologists document animal behavior, neuroscientists are peering into the brain. Many are focused on monogamous species that form strong pair bonds, like prairie voles and California mice, simulating death by permanently separating animals from their mates.

This kind of romantic rupture can produce signs of anxiety and what scientists call behavioral despair. After losing their partners, male prairie voles are quicker to abandon their attempts to escape from cylinders full of water, for example. Such losses also activate the brain’s stress circuits and disrupts the signaling pathways for oxytocin, a hormone that facilitates bonding. In a small early analysis of three widowed coyotes, Dr. Freeman of Utah State found that changes to the brain’s stress pathways might begin within days and last for over a year.

Breaking individual bonds can have effects distinct from those of general isolation. One recent study found that after losing a mate, California mice showed signs of heightened brain inflammation. Un-bonded mice housed alone did not.

“An animal that has never had a partner is biologically different from an animal that had a partner and lost their relationship,” said Erica Glasper, a behavioral neuroscientist at Ohio State University who led the research.

Some of these findings have tantalizing parallels in humans. For example, losing a spouse seems to promote inflammation in people, an effect that becomes more pronounced as grief severity increases.

Still, Dr. Glasper is reluctant to say that the mice are in mourning. “Our data tell us that the loss does matter to the animal,” she said. “It can’t really tell us how they feel. We can’t ask the mouse whether it’s longing for its partner.”

That’s a critical question, said Zoe Donaldson, a behavioral neuroscientist at the University of Colorado Boulder. “Yearning is what differentiates grief from depression,” she said.

Some emerging research, from Dr. Donaldson and others, suggests that voles might yearn for missing mates. Dopamine, which plays a crucial role in motivation, seems to drive a vole’s desire for its partner. The hormone spikes when voles are seeking out their mates or anticipating reuniting with them. And several studies suggest that a five- to seven-day separation may increase a vole’s motivation to reunite with its partner and amplify dopamine signaling in the brain.

Dr. Donaldson, who said she had initially been dismissive of the idea that the monogamous rodents could mourn, now believes that prairie voles experience “something akin to grief.”

While scientists tend to be cautious, the public has embraced the idea of animal grief. In a survey of 1,000 Australian adults, 90 percent said that some animals could grieve and 23 percent said that all of them could. Among those who believed that animals could mourn, 18 percent attributed grief to ants; 10 percent to prawns.

“People have incredibly intense emotions around this when I talk about my research,” Dr. Donaldson said. “Like, ‘I can’t believe you’re taking away their partners.’”

Animals don’t need to understand abstract concepts like nonexistence in order to know something important about death, some experts argue.

Dr. Monsó, the philosopher of animal minds, has outlined a “minimal concept of death,” which requires understanding just two essential concepts: nonfunctionality, or the idea that dead animals don’t do things that living ones do, and irreversibility, “which is the idea that unlike asleep individuals, dead individuals don’t go back to doing things,” she said.

In a new study, Dr. Monsó and her colleagues found that Goffin’s cockatoos, brainy birds that are known to be talented tool users, could distinguish between permanently broken, or “dead,” tools and those that were only temporarily out of commission.

The findings suggest that the birds may have “some of the cognitive prerequisites” for understanding death, Dr. Monsó said. But even if they don’t, she added, animals don’t necessarily need to understand death in order to feel grief.

Dr. Gonçalves of the Indianapolis Zoological Society agreed. Three-year-olds don’t fully comprehend death, he noted, but few people would question whether they’re capable of mourning a dead parent. “We readily attribute them with grief,” he said.

In some ways, the debate over animal grief has become a semantic one. The loss of a close companion can cause emotional distress in animals, scientists agreed. At issue was whether that distress could be called grief.

“There’s part of me, as an animal behaviorist, that definitely hesitates a little bit,” Dr. Freeman said. “You can’t just say animals grieve and then not stand behind it with data.”

But there’s plenty of reason to believe that animals can mourn, she said, and as the data come in, she would rather err in the direction of assuming that their sorrow is real: “It offers the opportunity to give them credit, perhaps, for a richer lived experience than we often ascribe to wild animals.”

Anecdotes have their limits, but they also have real power — and they’ve played a huge role in opening our minds to the reality of animal grief. So what have you seen in your own lives, whether it's a pet responding to the loss of a companion or an encounter in the wild? Let’s add to the growing list of observations.

Emily Anthes is a science reporter, writing primarily about animal health and science. She also covered the coronavirus pandemic.

Judge Throws Out Charges Against Former F. B. I. Officials

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

The magistrate judge, Zia M. Faruqui, said the case was a rushed, political prosecution ordered by the White House intended to affect the midterm elections.

By Alan Feuer

Reporting from Federal District Court in Washington

A federal magistrate judge on Monday threw out charges against two former F. B. I. intelligence officials accused of lying to Congress, excoriating prosecutors for what he described as a failure of one of their most basic responsibilities: showing there was any probable cause that crimes had been committed in the first place.

In an emotional, hourlong address from the bench in Federal District Court in Washington, the magistrate judge, Zia M. Faruqui, said that the case against the former officials — Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides — was a rushed, political prosecution ordered by the White House intended to affect the upcoming midterm elections. Two weeks ago, the administration charged the former officials with falsely minimizing their work on investigations involving Hunter Biden, the son of the former president.

Judge Faruqui blasted the U. S. attorney’s office in Washington for how it handled the case, admonishing prosecutors for trying to avoid some of the fundamental checks and balances of the criminal justice system. At the same time, he apologized directly to Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides for having been “dragged through this process” of being charged by the same federal government they had served for decades.

“I am deeply troubled by what happened here in this case,” Judge Faruqui said. “What has transpired here cannot be described as anything other than weaponization.”

The dismissal of the charges was the Justice Department’s latest failure to follow through on President Trump’s relentless demands to take revenge against a long list of people who have run afoul of him. In recent months, both judges and grand juries have repeatedly rejected the department’s attempts to prosecute the president’s enemies in a growing — and humiliating — series of legal defeats.

Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides drew the president’s ire because of their work on the F. B. I.’s Foreign Influence Task Force, a group created after Russia interfered in the 2016 election. The task force was designed to help intelligence agencies monitor clandestine efforts by foreign governments to manipulate American politics and in the weeks before the 2020 election it raised concerns that reports about Hunter Biden — especially those concerning a laptop that he left behind at a computer repair shop — may have been influenced by a Russian disinformation campaign.

From the outset, the case against them was a particularly bitter one, embodying a battle that has raged for nearly two years between the F. B. I.’s current leadership and the scores of agents who have been purged from the bureau because of their supposed disloyalty to Mr. Trump.

That rancor was on full display in court on Monday as several former F. B. I. agents — some fired by the bureau’s director, Kash Patel — showed up to cheer the dismissal of the case. Among those in the gallery were Brian Driscoll, the former acting director of the F. B. I.; Dave Sundberg, the former agent in charge of the bureau’s Washington field office; and Steven Jensen, another longtime F. B. I. leader.

Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides were charged in a complaint last month with making false statements during testimony they gave in 2023 to the House Judiciary Committee about the roles they had played in the bureau’s contentious investigations of the younger Mr. Biden and his laptop. But during his speech, Judge Faruqui dismantled almost every aspect of the government’s case. He pointed out that most of the false statements the two defendants were charged with making were not actually false, that none of the false statements were made knowingly and that none of them had any material effect on the congressional investigation which they were called upon to assist.

“That is not probable cause,” he said over and over.

Ms. Floris’s legal team hailed the dismissal of the case in a statement on Monday.

“The charges brought under the clearly discredited authority of the Department of Justice should never have been brought in the first place,” the statement said. “And while Nikki should never have had to endure this disgraceful public attack, we hope the courts continue to be a refuge for all citizens unlawfully targeted by the Trump administration.”

In a statement, lawyers for Mr. Benavides denounced the government’s efforts: “The government’s attempt to tarnish his distinguished reputation for a political headline ahead of the midterm elections is inexcusable.”

The statement added, “The government should heed the judge’s decision and drop this case immediately.”

Judge Faruqui was allowed to weigh in on the viability of the case because prosecutors chose to charge Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides through a criminal complaint, not an indictment. Complaints require a judge to make a finding of probable cause whereas indictments require only a majority vote by a panel of grand jurors and do not require a judge’s approval.

But federal prosecutors in Washington have failed so often over the past two years to secure indictments from grand juries that they have grown wary of the panels — especially in politicized cases involving Mr. Trump’s opponents. While their complaint against Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides is dead, prosecutors could try to resuscitate the charges by asking a grand jury to approve them.

Judge Faruqui, who once worked as a prosecutor in the office that brought the charges, said it was clear to him that his former colleagues were worried about taking this case in particular to the grand jury given how often they had failed to obtain indictments.

“It is self-evident that the U. S. attorney’s office is avoiding taking this case to the grand jury,” he said, “and that is understandable given their poor record there lately, but it is also unbelievable.”

The judge left almost no part of the government’s efforts to prosecute Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides unscathed. He pointed to its politicized origins, saying that Mr. Patel had personally assigned the inquiry to the F. B. I.’s Kansas City field office one day after Mr. Trump, during a prime-time address, criticized bureau intelligence officials for supposedly suppressing evidence that China had interfered in the 2020 election.

Mr. Patel went so far as to specify the charges — conspiracy and obstruction — he wanted the agents in Kansas City to investigate. But when the agents failed to find any evidence to support those allegations, they quickly pivoted to examining the congressional testimony Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides had given the House committee and comparing it to hundreds of thousands of internal F. B. I. communications looking for discrepancies.

Judge Faruqui noted that one of the agents assigned to the case had testified last week that the investigation was widely viewed inside the Kansas City office as a “witch hunt.” The judge also said that the case had been conducted so hurriedly that the original complaint was riddled with factual errors.

The judge expressed incredulity that an investigation personally ordered by the president and directly overseen by the F. B. I.’s director — who often checked in with the case agents by video conference — could have been handled in such a slipshod manner.

“It’s preposterous,” he said, “but not illogical given the timeline.”

That timeline was directly connected to the midterm elections, Judge Faruqui said, adding that he could find no other reason the charges were brought in a rush last month other than to make a splash before voters went to the polls.

“There was simply no other event on the calendar except one — the midterms,” he said. “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend that I cannot read a calendar.”

In a moment of levity, Judge Faruqui said he would never have expected to still be discussing Hunter Biden and his laptop in late 2026, adding that the subject was clearly an obsession for Mr. Trump and his congressional allies.

But he concluded his address on a somber note, asserting that the case had badly damaged the reputation of the F. B. I., greatly chilled Congress’s ability to get honest testimony from witnesses and further eroded confidence in the Justice Department.

He then apologized to Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides.

“I am sorry you have been dragged through this process,” he said. “I am sorry everyone has dragged through this process. But this is where we are.”

Alan Feuer is a reporter for The Times who covers the effects President Trump has had on the courts, the Justice Department and the broader rule of law.

Justice Kagan Sounds an Alarm About the Court

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Jesse Wegman

Mr. Wegman, a contributing Opinion writer, is a senior fellow at the Brennan Center for Justice.

Like a lot of Americans, I’ve grown accustomed to Supreme Court justices speaking out much more frequently and informally than they once did. Yet still there was more than one moment in a public conversation Elena Kagan had at Catholic University last month when I almost couldn’t believe what I was hearing.

The justices like to say that their opinions speak for themselves. In the old days, they nurtured the mystique of their delicate yet elevated position in government, rarely if ever revealing their own feelings about the law, American politics or life in general. Anyone who wanted to know what a justice really thought, they claimed, would do best simply to read their rulings.

That is no longer true. Today’s bench is among the most voluble in the court’s history — the justices seem constantly to be writing books, giving speeches, engaging with interviewers and, increasingly, complaining about the institution they serve and (sometimes) the colleagues they serve with.

Even by that new standard, Justice Kagan’s comments, which came during an hour-plus sit-down interview at Catholic University’s law school, broke the judicial omertà, both in what she said explicitly about her conservative counterparts’ blasé attitude toward American democracy and in what she appeared to say about the dangerously compromised state of the court in 2026.

The Catholic University law professor J. Joel Alicea, who interviewed Justice Kagan, started the conversation by asking her about rulings involving partisan gerrymandering, voting rights and money in politics, all of which were decided on party-line votes with her and the other Democratic appointees in the minority.

“The court got it wrong” in each of these cases, Justice Kagan said, because of a “lack of appropriate concern or understanding of the consequences of their decisions.” She pointed to the Republican-appointed majority’s evisceration of the Voting Rights Act in April, which was followed almost immediately by a mad scramble in states across the South to pass new, more partisan gerrymanders aimed at erasing Black lawmakers’ districts.

Protecting Black political participation and representation was precisely what the Voting Rights Act was enacted to do, she noted. By eliminating the last meaningful tool of that landmark law, she explained, “the court kind of said, ‘Oh, well.’” Whether that was meant in the sense of “we don’t care if Black political representation plummets” or in the sense of “it won’t plummet,” Justice Kagan concluded, “the court has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of their rulings on how the political system works, and has created a democracy that does not work as well as it should.”

This wasn’t the first time she has leveled such sweeping criticisms; you can find similar charges in her dissenting opinions in that and other democracy-related cases, in which she skewered her right-wing colleagues for misunderstanding the law and disregarding Americans’ democratic rights.

But Justice Kagan was offering this critique off the bench, in public — where the justices know their words carry a special significance, particularly before the midterms. Even more surprising, of all the Democratic appointees, if not all nine justices, Justice Kagan has a reputation as the most restrained and institutionalist.

At a judicial conference in July, Justice Kagan took pains to defend her conservative counterparts against accusations that they were acting as a rubber stamp for the Trump administration. So it was that much more remarkable to hear her admit, just a few months later, such wide-ranging frustrations with her fellow justices.

And she wasn’t done: “This court is deeply conservative, and in that way very different from the court I joined 16 years ago.” That court, she added, “was by no means liberal” — it still had a 5-4 conservative majority and had only months earlier decided Citizens United v. F. E. C., which transformed the role of money in politics (and in which Justice Kagan, then serving as President Obama’s solicitor general, had argued the losing side). Still, as recently as 2017, “nobody in America thought the court was in the pocket of any one group or any one party or any one anything,” she said. “The court had a kind of legitimacy. And when the court has a kind of legitimacy of that kind, it helps to create a stable country.”

Her implication, of course, is that today’s court, dominated by a right-wing supermajority that rules consistently in favor of a longstanding conservative agenda, lacks that “kind of legitimacy” — about as serious a charge as a sitting justice can make.

Justice Kagan had one more dig, which verged on the personal. Reflecting on the role of originalism in the court’s jurisprudence, she said, “I’ve never thought originalism really works,” adding that the “cartwheels” originalists perform to reach their preferred outcomes are “almost embarrassing.” In sum, she said, “the whole project is kind of misconceived, and it’s not a very good match with the Constitution we have.”

Originalism has been the coin of the conservative judicial realm for decades and is currently ascendant at the Supreme Court; as Justice Kagan said ruefully at her own confirmation hearings, “We are all originalists.” Calling it “misconceived” and its practitioners “embarrassing” may sound relatively mild to ears accustomed to the crude invective of the Trump era, but it suggests that the interpersonal conflicts on the bench aren’t getting resolved anytime soon.

I would go so far as to infer a deeper message in Justice Kagan’s remarks: When taken together, her critiques of her colleagues — their disregard for democratic rights, their undermining of the court’s legitimacy and their “misconceived” commitment to originalism — offer a coherent case for reforming the court.

It goes something like this: The conservative majority has been arrogating outsize power to itself over the past several years, claiming the authority to decide many of the most contested questions of American legal and political life, while Congress has stood idly by. Even when the court rules that it has no power to act, as it did in the partisan gerrymandering case, it has “deleterious effects” on democracy, as Justice Kagan pointed out. (That ruling has also disproportionately benefited Republican political interests, which goes to her point about legitimacy.)

Next, pair the court’s arrogation of political power with the fact that the right-wing justices apparently consider themselves accountable to no one. As Justice Samuel Alito wrongly claimed about Congress in 2023, “No provision in the Constitution gives them the authority to regulate the Supreme Court — period.”

Finally, consider this in the broader context of judicial life tenure, a functionally impossible-to-amend Constitution and — to Justice Kagan’s point about originalism — a majority in thrall to a theory of constitutional interpretation that privileges the supposed consensus of people living more than two centuries ago over the values and wishes of those alive today.

Put it all together, and the American people have no way to push the Constitution in a more democratic direction. No way to stop six justices from deciding that protecting democratic rights like voting — “just about the most important thing that the court does,” as Justice Kagan described it at Catholic University — is no longer necessary.

The court’s profoundly antidemocratic attitude was summed up neatly by Chief Justice John Roberts, who said in a 2009 interview: “The most important thing for the public to understand is that we are not a political branch of government. They don’t elect us. If they don’t like what we’re doing, it’s more or less just too bad.”

The chief justice offered one remedy: impeachment followed by conviction in the Senate. However, as he also noted, that has never happened in American history. Impeaching even a single justice would be an enormous lift.

There is a better and easier solution, and Justice Kagan’s critiques last month point directly to it: major court reform imposed by Congress.

Structural failures demand structural repairs. Whether these repairs take the form of term limits, an expanded bench, binding ethics rules, restrictions of the court’s jurisdiction or other measures, they are the only way for the American people, through their elected representatives, to reclaim power over a court gone rogue.

Is this what Justice Kagan was saying, implicitly, in her talk at Catholic University? I can’t be certain, but I’m comfortable speculating.

In this moment of rock-bottom public confidence in the court, Justice Kagan was not unaware that she was speaking outside of the formal boundaries of court decisions, and thus challenging the public appearance of judicial comity. Indeed this may be Kagan’s restraint showing up after all: With her comments, she is ringing alarm bells about the seriousness of problems at the court.

And while the justices may have concluded that they are the final word in interpreting the Constitution, no one gave them power over how we interpret their own words.

Source photographs by Michael Lee and PhotoPlus Magazine/Getty Images

Russia Senses Opportunity in Polish Political Turmoil

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

After its sometime allies were ousted in elections in Hungary and Serbia, Moscow has seized on Poland’s constitutional standoff in its effort to weaken Europe’s support for Ukraine.

By Andrew Higgins

Reporting from Warsaw

When Poland’s centrist government sent the riot police late on Friday to seal off the country’s Constitutional Tribunal amid a long standoff over control of the court, its right-wing enemies accused it of staging a criminal “coup d’état.”

Now, Russia has jumped in, too, fanning claims of a putsch by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and amplifying attacks on Poland’s pro-European government by hard-right politicians at home and abroad.

Mr. Tusk, long reviled by Moscow because of his strong support for Ukraine, sent police officers to the court after right-wing protesters gathered outside to denounce the suspension of its chief justice, an ally of Poland’s former governing party, Law and Justice.

Dmitri Medvedev, a former Russian president who is now vice chairman of the Kremlin’s security council and a close ally of President Vladimir V. Putin, declared on Sunday that “a constitutional coup is underway in Poland.”

Claims of a coup at the Constitutional Tribunal, the focus of a decade-long political struggle over the Polish judiciary, have dominated attacks in recent days on Mr. Tusk by his right-wing enemies at home and Kremlin-friendly European politicians like Marine Le Pen of France, Nigel Farage of Britain and Geert Wilders of the Netherlands.

Right-wing allies of the suspended chief justice, Bogdan Swieczkowski, who over the weekend still controlled the tribunal’s social media account, accused their rivals of “committing the crime” of a putsch, a charge quickly taken up by a swarm of commentators on X, Telegram and internet bulletin boards.

Referring in a speech over the weekend to often false claims on social media of violence and police brutality at the court, Mr. Tusk said, “They are using an army of Russian bots on the internet.”

Russia and Europe’s E. U.-skeptic hard right seem eager to inflame Polish tensions in the hope of weakening Poland’s staunchly pro-Ukraine and pro-European Union government at a time when Moscow is working hard to undermine Europe’s support for Ukraine.

Those efforts suffered setbacks with the election defeat in April of Prime Minister Viktor Orban of Hungary, a longtime opponent of helping Ukraine; and of Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s longtime leader, on Oct. 25. Mr. Vucic had resisted imposing sanctions on Russia and met regularly with Mr. Putin, even as he turned a blind eye to the sale of large quantities of Serbian weapons and ammunition to Ukraine.

The victors in Serbia’s recent election, a largely leaderless and diverse new movement called Student List, Students Win, say there will be no sharp turn away from friendly relations with Russia. But in a sign that the mood in Belgrade may be shifting, the Serbian Central Bank announced on Saturday that it was shutting down Alta Bank, a lender that Russian citizens and companies had used to transfer funds to and from Russia.

The prosecutor’s office for organized crime said on Monday it had arrested the bank’s Croatia-born Serbian owner and two executives in connection with an investigation into the illegal removal of nearly $400 million from the bank’s vault.

Poland stands at the opposite end of the spectrum from Serbia in relation to Russia and has been a frequent target of abuse, disinformation campaigns and sabotage operations by Moscow.

Maria Zakharova, the Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman, said on Sunday in a lengthy post on Telegram that Poland faced “collapse and tragedy” akin to the 2014 political crisis in Ukraine that led to the downfall of President Viktor F. Yanukovych.

Mr. Yanukovych fled to Russia in February 2014 after months of street protests against him in Kyiv, opening the way for a new government that Russia immediately denounced as dominated by Nazi nationalists, a false claim used by Mr. Putin to justify his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Mr. Tusk’s government, the foreign ministry spokeswoman said, was struggling “to steer away from a bloody downward spiral and back into a legal framework.”

There has been no bloodshed at the Polish court, only minor scuffles between police officers and a small group of protesters who support Law and Justice, a hard-right nationalist party.

Russian officials and propaganda outlets have frequently amplified the accusations of European nationalists and far-left groups of brutal repression by mainstream political forces, cheering on the Alternative for Germany party as well as rioters in France and Albania.

Mr. Tusk, in his speech over the weekend defending the deployment of riot police officers outside the court, said of the widespread accusations by Polish right-wing politicians of a coup: “It’s no coincidence they are finding support among pro-Russian forces worldwide.”

Accusing Polish officials of hypocrisy, Ms. Zakharova said the standoff at Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal “is essentially the very same thing they supported and blessed among their Ukrainian neighbors 12 years ago.”

Mr. Medvedev, the former Russian president, also compared Poland’s fracas over the court to events in Ukraine, claiming on X that “liberals — protégés of Brussels-backed Tusk — are hounding the conservatives from the Law and Justice party” and that “the method used is exactly the same as in neo-Nazi Ukraine.”

The dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal dates back a decade to when Law and Justice came to power in 2015 and refused to seat justices already appointed by Parliament, naming its own right-wing judges instead. Years later, Europe’s highest court, the European Court of Justice, ruled this illegal and declared the tribunal’s decision invalid.

After Law and Justice lost an election in 2023, a new coalition government led by Mr. Tusk sought to undo what it saw as the previous administration’s degradation of judicial independence but was blocked by the president, an ally of Law and Justice’s who has used his largely ceremonial powers to prevent new judges from being sworn in.

The current president, Karol Nawrocki, a nationalist former historian elected last year and, like his predecessor, an ally of the previous governing party, has kept five judges appointed by Parliament from taking their seats on the bench by refusing to attend their swearing-in ceremonies.

Under Polish law, the president has no veto power over appointments to the Constitutional Tribunal, but judges are supposed to be sworn in during ceremonies “before the president.”

These new judges, who took their oaths in Parliament while declaring they were doing so “before the president,” on Friday entered the court, and one of them, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, announced the suspension of the chief justice, Mr. Swieczkowski, an ally of Mr. Nawrocki’s who insists the new judges are impostors because they have not been sworn in personally by the president.

This prompted Mr. Nawrocki, who was flying to Senegal at the time, to turn around his plane midair, rush back to Warsaw and push his way through the police cordon around the court. He scuffled with the new judges, denouncing them as illegitimate.

Alisa Dogramadzieva contributed reporting from Belgrade, Serbia.

Andrew Higgins is the East and Central Europe bureau chief for The Times based in Warsaw.

They Tried Kratom for Its Health Benefits, Then They Became Addicted

The New York Times November 02, 2026

U. S. Health Policy

Advertisement

Supported by

Some say they were introduced to the drug through wellness podcasts, free samples at gyms or fitness influencers.

By Olivia Tauber

Kratom, long used by people seeking relief from addiction to prescription opioids and alcohol, is increasingly being pitched as a wellness product that purports to raise energy, sharpen focus and enhance athletic performance.

Some makers of kratom, a substance that is derived from the leaves of a tropical tree and often sold in the form of drinks, powder or capsules, have distributed free samples at gyms. Others have sponsored sporting events or trumpeted the product’s benefits with the help of social media influencers and wellness podcasts.

What this marketing often fails to acknowledge is the potential for kratom to lead to addiction, liver injury, seizures and in some cases, fatal overdoses.

The Food and Drug Administration has not approved kratom products for any medical use. Federal officials have moved to temporarily ban on products with high levels of a synthetic version of kratom known as 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH. They also announced plans earlier this year to ban a semi-synthetic form of kratom called mitragynine pseudoindoxyl, or M. G. P. I., but they agreed to allow it at certain levels after industry lobbying.

Some states have banned kratom outright or restricted sales to minors. But in many parts of the country, the drug remains widely available in gas stations, smoke shops and online.

Doctors are especially concerned about the growing number of synthetic kratom products which can be far more potent than natural kratom. M. G. P. I., which is an opioid, has been linked to at least 48 fatal overdoses. But even products marketed as whole leaf or natural can contain compounds like M. G. P. I., and carry a risk of addiction, experts said.

When Hilary Tesluck, 31, first tried kratom, she was looking for an alternative to the prescription medication she took for anxiety. To Ms. Tesluck, kratom sounded like a “life hack” worth trying, similar to the vitamins and supplements she took every day. Initially, she felt like it eased her anxiety and depression.

“I would praise kratom and share it with everyone I knew,” she said.

After about a year and a half of what she considered moderate use, she began taking kratom in larger doses and more frequently. When she realized the drug seemed to suppress her appetite, she began taking even more, to lose weight. At her peak use, Ms. Tesluck was consuming up to 100 capsules a day.

She often became severely nauseous after taking it. “I would throw up some of my dose and then take more immediately, just because I didn’t want to waste anything,” Ms. Tesluck said. She began falling asleep unexpectedly while working from home, episodes she attributed to the high doses of kratom.

It was only when she ran out during a snowstorm that she realized she had become addicted. Ms. Tesluck woke the next morning drenched in sweat. Her muscles ached and she felt anxious. “Now I know I can’t miss a dose,” she recalled thinking.

While estimates vary, some studies suggest between 29 and 40 percent of regular users of kratom become dependent, as was the case for Ms. Tesluck, who now works for a nonprofit focused on kratom addiction. Experts said they were concerned that many people trying kratom based on its wellness claims do not fully understand how dangerous it can be.

“The public deserves accurate, nuanced information rather than messaging driven primarily by commercial incentives,” said Dr. Cornel Stanciu, the director of addiction services at New Hampshire Hospital.

Kratom brands have used a number of wellness-focused tactics to promote their products. One brand, MIT45, has sponsored the men’s division of the International Fitness and Bodybuilding Federation, in a partnership described as having the potential to “transform the fitness industry,” and “enrich the experience for athletes.” The company also previously paid individual athletes to promote its products, Ryan Niddel, its chief executive officer, said.

MIT45 continues to sell its products at gyms and through other health and wellness channels, Mr. Niddel said.

When asked about safety concerns, Mr. Niddel maintained that the company’s products posed little risk when consumed according to its serving and frequency recommendations, adding that sponsored athletes had been instructed to avoid health claims. “We think it has a place in the market, but that place isn’t for everybody and that place isn’t in high quantities for long periods of time,” he said.

Another brand, Mitra-9, has recruited mixed martial arts fighters, wrestlers and sobriety content creators for a social media campaign promoting its products. Kingdom Kratom, which markets its products specifically for workouts, sells kratom sample packs that its website suggests customers test “across a training week.”

One popular brand, Feel Free, has drawn particular scrutiny for its marketing tactics, which have included distributing free samples through partnerships with university athletic programs and an Instagram campaign for using the hashtag #alcoholalternative. (That campaign was the subject of a class-action lawsuit that ended in an $8.75 million settlement.)

The company, like other kratom makers, has also promoted its product on podcasts. Jasmine Adeoye first heard about kratom on an episode of The Skinny Confidential Him & Her Show, now known as The Bossticks. Michael Bosstick, the co-host of the podcast, called kratom a “magical elixir.”

Ms. Adeoye, 31, said at first she drank Feel Free only occasionally, on the weekends. But as a stressful remote job left her feeling anxious and isolated, she started drinking more.

“It feels very, very safe at first,” she said, adding: “It very quickly turns on you.”

Within a year, Ms. Adeoye said, she was drinking two, two-ounce bottles a day, sometimes back-to-back. (Feel Free’s serving size is half a bottle, and the company warns against consuming more than one bottle in 24 hours, because it can be “habit-forming.”)

Ms. Adeoye maxed out two credit cards to support her habit, she said. Her sleep deteriorated, and she developed heart palpitations that would wake her up at night. She kept her addiction to herself.

“Who’s going to believe me if I’m addicted to a wellness tonic?” she recalled thinking. “You start to believe there’s something wrong with you when you become addicted,” she said.

In response to questions about Feel Free’s marketing, Aaron Henninger, the chief marketing officer of its parent company, Botanic Tonics, said the company is “continuing to invest in research to better understand our products and their effects.”

He added that Feel Free “will continue to prioritize the safety and well-being of our customers above all else.” The company now clearly identifies kratom as an ingredient in its products’ labeling and advises people with a history of substance abuse not to use it.

Dr. Stanciu and other experts noted that people who have previously struggled with alcohol or other drugs may be especially vulnerable to kratom addiction. He added that targeted marketing through podcasts, influencers and wellness branding gives consumers a false sense of safety, especially when audiences include young people or those with a history of substance abuse.

That was the case for Jason Ellis, a podcast host, former professional skateboarder and mixed martial artist. Mr. Ellis first learned about kratom through friends in the fight community, who described it as something relaxing — “kind of like a painkiller, but herbal,” he recalled.

In 2023, Mr. Ellis, who had spoken openly on his podcast about his history of misusing alcohol and painkillers, received a message from Jerry W. Ross, the founder of Feel Free, he said. Mr. Ross offered him free cases of his company’s products, along with a cut of purchases made through a listener discount code, in exchange for promoting the drinks, according to Mr. Ellis. (Mr. Ross did not respond to a request for comment.)

Mr. Ellis took the deal, and tried the products himself. Within about six months, he was drinking up to three bottles a day. He recalled a time when his child called him while he was using kratom, hoping to talk. “I’m thinking, when can we get off the phone so that I can get high again?” he said.

He and others described attempting to quit kratom, only to relapse or struggle with difficult withdrawal symptoms, like sweating, chills and muscle aches — like “the flu, but worse,” Ms. Tesluck said.

She tried several times to quit, going so far as to seek treatment at a detox program. She sometimes went weeks without kratom, only to return to it when she began feeling depressed.

“I would cry all day long,” said Ms. Tesluck, When she finally was able to quit, she said, she experienced a mental fog that persisted for months.

Ms. Tesluck said she continues to hear from people who were introduced to kratom through free samples offered at gyms or on social media. She is concerned that the problem could become even worse if more potent products gain traction.

“Companies are coming out with new derivative products that are even stronger,” she said. “It’s not slowing down.”

Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Intervene in California Ballot Case

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Latest polls

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

In an emergency application, administration lawyers asked the justices to immediately order California to set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to require that California set aside 20,000 mail-in ballots that the administration claims have been provided to noncitizens.

The emergency application to the justices came after a divided federal appeals court rejected the administration’s arguments that California officials should impound the ballots for further scrutiny.

Legal experts have been skeptical of the Trump administration’s arguments in the case. Filing just one day before the midterm elections may forestall a ruling in the case — and a potential loss for the administration — until after Election Day.

The request requires the Supreme Court to consider how much power the federal government has to order states to make last-minute changes to their vote-counting procedures. Under the Constitution, states have responsibility for administering elections. The Justice Department has claimed that it is empowered by a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to cast ballots.

In their emergency application, lawyers for the administration urged the justices to grant what they called a “modest remedy,” requiring California to separate ballots of “citizens and suspected noncitizens.” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote that such an order by the court “would not cancel any vote but would allow time to verify the eligibility of suspected noncitizens.”

The legal challenge to 20,000 California ballots is part of a broader effort by the administration to argue that the elections could be marred by illegal votes by noncitizens. The effort comes as polls show Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers of Congress and as President Trump has sought to cast doubt on the validity of the vote, despite little evidence of widespread problems with illegal voting. California officials have said the voter list provided by the Trump administration is filled with errors.

As the lawsuit has wound through the lower courts, the administration has also threatened criminal charges over claims of noncitizens voting, including charging 28 people with violating federal election laws and subpoenaing county election workers in California.

The Justice Department sent the list of 20,000 names to Los Angeles County elections officials in October, claiming that those ballots should be separated because the names had been flagged through a government process as potential noncitizens. Officials have been vague about exactly how the list was prepared, and county officials have said that the list appeared to include people with addresses throughout California. Only 7,035 names on the list sent to Los Angeles were listed with addresses in Los Angeles County. Officials confirmed others were born in the United States and were citizens.

Shortly after, the Justice Department sued to stop the counting of mail-in ballots sent to people on the list until their citizenship could be verified.

On Friday, a divided three-judge panel on a federal appeals court rejected arguments by the Justice Department to segregate the contested ballots, finding that the administration had overstepped its bounds by interfering with the state’s role in setting its election rules. The panel also cited a principle repeatedly upheld by the Supreme Court that federal courts should avoid ordering changes to how ballots are counted too close to an election.

That same panel of federal judges had already rejected an appeal in the same case earlier in the week, declining to leapfrog a trial judge.

That judge, David O. Carter, then sided with California officials, writing that the federal government’s request could “wreak havoc” on state election administration and “create a chilling effect on election workers and voters alike.”

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.
