The company went on a deal spree with tech giants, former crypto miners and others to gain computing power to further its artificial intelligence ambitions.

Credit... Illustration by Mark Harris; Photographs by Thea Traff for The New York Times, AJ Mast for The New York Times, Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times, Getty Images

Supported by

By Sri Muppidi and Kalley Huang

Reporting from San Francisco

Late last year, Anthropic’s executives were in a bind. Their company, which was growing like a weed, was running out of computing power for artificial intelligence.

The amount of computing power that was needed became a “cone of uncertainty,” Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, said at The New York Times’s DealBook Summit in December. “Because the cone is so wide,” he added, “it’s hard to avoid making a mistake.”

The realization sent Anthropic on an all-out effort to obtain more computing power. In the ensuing months, the San Francisco company embarked on a deal spree, according to 14 people with knowledge of the A. I. lab, investors and industry experts.

Anthropic has since signed dozens of contracts with former cryptocurrency miners, data center start-ups, chipmakers and tech giants like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX to secure enough computing power. It hired experts in data centers, which are the enormous computing sites powering A. I., and bought data center equipment to speed up construction. It met with developers and explored converting old coal plants and factories into data centers. And it considered deals for tiny amounts of computing power that could add up to what it needs.

“Anthropic is gobbling up a lot of the capacity,” said Erik Bernhardsson, the chief executive of Modal, a New York company that sells computing power.

Anthropic’s pursuit of computing power, some details of which have not been previously reported, is critical as it tries to lead in A. I. and conduct what could be the largest-ever initial public offering this month. The company needs computing power to develop cutting-edge A. I. models and to deliver products, like the Claude chatbot, to businesses and consumers. The resource is so vital that Anthropic spent more than 10 pages of its public offering prospectus detailing the stakes.

“Our ability to remain at the frontier of A. I. capabilities is substantially dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads,” the company wrote.

In total, Anthropic has committed a whopping $895.4 billion through 2045 to computing power and chip deals that it largely cannot back out of, according to its prospectus. This year, it is expected to have more than 3.5 gigawatts of computing power, two people with knowledge of its plans said, or enough electricity to power all the homes in Chicago. Next year, it aims to double that amount, the people said.

But its voracious demands are expensive, intensifying Anthropic’s need to go public in an offering that could raise $100 billion. It is also raising debt financing, including $63 billion last week, from Wall Street banks and private credit firms. Even so, Anthropic has warned that it may need to seek additional financing sooner than anticipated.

While other A. I. companies also need computing power, giants like Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta have deep pockets and credit histories for buying chips and building data centers. Younger companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have to rely on others for computing power.

Anthropic declined to comment on the record before its I. P. O.

After Anthropic was founded in 2021, it turned to Amazon and Google, which agreed to invest a combined $6 billion in the start-up in 2023, for computing power. The company then spent much of that money on Amazon’s and Google’s cloud computing services.

Tom Brown, Anthropic’s chief compute officer, spearheaded both deals, two people with knowledge of the company said. He also led efforts to diversify beyond Nvidia’s A. I. chips and use chips from Amazon, Google and Advanced Micro Devices, for more options.

Finding enough computing power is “very clearly the bottleneck for all of our progress,” Mr. Brown said at a Group of 20 event in September. “We’re in a huge shortage of the power and labor needed to support the demand for A. I.,” he said.

Last year, Anthropic’s A. I. coding tool, Claude Code, became a hit. But as it became popular, the company lacked computing power to meet demand and had to limit free use of its products and raise prices for some of them.

So Anthropic embarked on its deal spree. It has committed $121.3 billion to computing power from Google, $110 billion with Amazon, $44.9 billion with Microsoft and $120.5 billion with SpaceX through 2036, according to its prospectus.

Anthropic also started working with “neoclouds,” companies that provide computing power, including a $50 billion deal with one called Fluidstack and a $41.3 billion deal with another, Lambda. And it is working with former crypto miners like TeraWulf and Hut 8 to construct the data centers.

Unlike Amazon and Microsoft, which are backlogged with demand for their computing power, neoclouds and former crypto miners have access to land and power for data centers and can bring computing power online sooner.

For even more speed, Anthropic is helping to design the data centers that other companies will build and operate. It has added construction and supply chain experts, three people with knowledge of its plans said, and is buying chips directly from Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom for the computing sites. It is also buying cooling systems and other equipment for the chips so data center operators can install the components faster, two people said.

“We operate as one team,” said Asher Genoot, Hut 8’s chief executive.

Starting last year, Anthropic met with developers in Texas, Indiana and other states about building data centers, according to four people with knowledge of its plans. It has asked some developers about their permits and connection to the power grid, two of those people said.

The efforts have faced hurdles. In one instance, Fluidstack pushed back against some Anthropic data center designs over concerns about power fluctuations that could cut off electricity and damage equipment, before reaching a solution, two people familiar with the situation said.

In another instance, TeraWulf, which is building a data center for Anthropic in upstate New York, was competing for electricians with the owners of the Buffalo Bills’ football stadium. Anthropic and TeraWulf ultimately asked the local electricians’ union for names of traveling electricians from other areas, even though it would make the project more expensive, TeraWulf’s chief executive, Paul Prager, said.

Anthropic has started considering sites with at least 200 megawatts, or enough electricity to power about 140,000 U. S. homes, according to three people familiar with the plans. That is less power than the company originally wanted but a faster way to get what it needs. It has since become open to data centers as small as 50 megawatts and would supplement the sites with power from batteries and natural gas, the three people said.

John Tough, a managing partner of Energize Capital, which invests in data center technology, said Anthropic did not control the pipelines of computing power, so it might have to settle for building “gigawatts, megawatts at a time.”

“The next best thing is to scavenge the world to figure out where there’s power lines,” he said.

Sri Muppidi is a business and technology reporter for The Times and DealBook, covering artificial intelligence. Contact her securely on Signal: @srimuppidi.13.

Kalley Huang is a Times reporter in San Francisco, covering Apple and the technology industry.

He Wants to Be One With Nature. But He Can’t Quit Instagram.

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Once, Robin Greenfield aspired to wealth. Now, he has no home and eats from the earth. He chronicles it all on social media, but does the persona match the man?

Once, Robin Greenfield aspired to wealth. Now, he has no home and eats from the earth. He chronicles it all on social media, but does the persona match the man?

Robin Greenfield in Prospect Park, Brooklyn, where he foraged wild foods for future meals. Credit...

Supported by

By Hilary Howard

Visuals by Lexi Parra

About 80 New Yorkers gathered in Prospect Park, Brooklyn, to watch a gaunt, barefoot man hug an oak tree during a foraging walk.

“This tree produces in the realm of millions of calories of food,” said Robin Greenfield, a social media influencer known for his outlandish and risky stunts to reduce food waste.

Greenfield’s gambit this year was to survive only from foods he had found in the wild. He would not rely on grocery stores, garden produce, farm products, cooking staples like butter or olive oil, or foraged foods others might share with him. The Brooklyn gathering, in late July, was day No. 292.

Reduced to a sinewy waif, running low on carbs and fats, Greenfield had calories on the brain. He had used up all of his wild rice and was down to half a gallon of hickory oil and about four pounds (7,000 calories) of acorn flour.

He was also struggling with energy levels and a low social battery. After a three-hour interview with me in Prospect Park, he stumbled into a thicket of trees, drained from talking. He’d had enough of the media-friendly facade.

Once a poster boy for capitalism who was determined to become a millionaire by his 30th birthday, Greenfield remade himself more than 10 years ago into an environmental stuntman, dumpster diving and stuffing bags full of trash and affixing them to his body to raise awareness about our ravaged planet.

“Food is the central way we’re impacting the earth,” said Greenfield, a 40-year-old who presents like a millennial Mr. Rogers (if he had a California surfer’s drawl).

At first, he kept his apartment and a few changes of clothes. But gradually and methodically, Greenfield embraced asceticism and dedicated himself to it full-time. He let go of his possessions, as well as his connections to the government and commercial society.

He has no phone, car, driver’s license, passport, health insurance, property, bank accounts or credit cards. He wears biodegradable clothing and has not paid taxes or taken pharmaceuticals for more than a decade. He lives under the poverty level, and said he has no romantic or sexual attachments. He brushes his teeth with a twig.

And he carries his poop around in a bucket, refusing to rely on the flush toilet system, which he calls destructive and ineffective (composting toilets can be difficult to find on the road). He brought the bucket with him that afternoon in Brooklyn.

“OK, this is too much,” murmured one woman in the crowd.

Social media is his one remaining vice. It is both the megaphone for his earth-friendly messaging and his Achilles’ heel. It’s hard, after all, to be a purist or an anti-corporate stalwart when counting “likes.”

He still owns a laptop and digital camera, necessary for his chronicling and communication. He and those who volunteer in the effort shoot his videos, which get edited by workers at a nonprofit he started. He doesn’t make money from his social media accounts, he said.

He no longer flies. So when he travels, he hitches a ride with someone he knows or takes a bus or train.

Pinpointing what drove a once-aspiring rich guy to a now-aspiring nature monk is a murky undertaking. According to Greenfield and those closest to him, his transformation arose from a combination of family history, personal compulsion and the way his brain works.

“All data leads to me losing my mind,” Greenfield said. He likens his practices to those of wandering sadhus, holy men who take vows of poverty and celibacy to pursue spiritual freedom in India.

But as the sadhus know, the path to spiritual freedom is often uneven. Few things are more natural than interpersonal conflict, and Greenfield has seen his share. He has posted videos in which he describes — and says he regrets — behavior as a young adult involving what he believes were sexual and financial misdeeds. Even he acknowledges that sometimes his most formidable opponent is not the food industrial complex, but his own complex nature.

“I have a tone,” he said.

Greenfield’s parents, part of the Hare Krishna movement, moved from Oregon to Northern Wisconsin in the 1980s, with back-to-the-land aspirations. But they split up, and Greenfield grew up on welfare in a cluttered duplex “with paint chipping off the walls,” he said.

“I was not into my lifestyle growing up,” he said. “I Febrezed everything. I had the American Eagle clothes.”

He developed a keen interest in money and structure, working in fast food and as a lifeguard and becoming an Eagle Scout. He saw financial independence and goal-setting as ways to gain social acceptance and love.

“I shined the wheels of my car every Sunday,” he said. “My food came from Walmart. I went to McDonald’s.”

Though he partied while at the University of Wisconsin–La Crosse, sometimes getting blackout drunk, he said, he remained focused on success, selling educational books door to door over summer breaks, working up to 90 hours a week.

After graduating, Greenfield traveled through Southeast Asia and Africa. It was a turning point, according to several friends. He was exposed to global poverty and off-the-grid living that made his childhood look comfy by comparison, they said.

Greenfield moved to San Diego and started a business, selling advertising in grocery stores. The year he was 25, the business pulled in $250,000 in revenue, he said.

But he also began to read books and watch documentaries about the same commercial food system that was making him rich. “The Story of Stuff,” a short film by the anti-consumerism activist Annie Leonard, left a particularly strong impact.

“I learned that the reason I was doing most of what I was doing was because corporations had large advertising budgets, and they had convinced me that I needed to do these things in order to be a loved member of society,” Greenfield said.

“The way that I was living was basically a lie.”

He wrote a list of 100 changes he wanted to make in his life — some of them the sorts of shifts many people aspire to, like shopping with reusable bags and switching to LED lightbulbs — and hung it up in his kitchen, with plans to incorporate one each week.

Around this time, Greenfield met Cheryl Davies, a student of Eastern medicine who would figure prominently in his evolution. The guy was goofy, Davies said, but his curiosity and sense of play charmed her.

“He had this big story about how he was in Africa by himself, and he was wearing these colorful bracelets,” Davies recalled. Once, she and her roommates were cooking herbs and he grabbed a mouthful.

“And we’re like, ‘You’re not supposed to eat that,’” Davies said. “And he’s like, ‘I’m going to try everything.’”

By then, Greenfield had accomplished the 100 goals on his list, including the more exteme ones, like getting rid of his credit cards and cellphone and undergoing a vasectomy. But he’d also kept going, not showering for a year (bathing instead in natural bodies of water and the occasional leaky fire hydrant), starting to run barefoot and finishing a 4,700-mile sustainable bike ride across the United States.

“I managed to use just 160 gallons of water, create a mere two pounds of trash, plug into only five outlets, not turn on a single light switch and consume 280 pounds of food from grocery store dumpsters,” he wrote on his website.

Soon, he was living in a 50-square-foot, solar-powered home, having dissolved his company and buried his earnings, in the form of gold and silver, in his yard. He would dig up the treasure to finance his early eco-adventures, which Davies gamely joined.

But as Davies reached her mid-30s, she grew tired of the physically demanding lifestyle, and of being a sidekick to Greenfield’s agenda. Plus, her friends and family had wearied of his uncompromising nature.

“They didn’t want to deal with Robin composting in the kitchen, or not flushing the toilet,” she said. “I was always the person in the middle.”

During a yearlong challenge in which Greenfield was living from a garden he’d started in Florida, Davies left for Italy, and is married there, with two children. Greenfield dated a few more people before committing to celibacy.

They are still friends. “She was one of my greatest teachers,” Greenfield said. As for Davies: “Robin taught me how to be free.”

After Davies left, Greenfield tried to expand his fledgling nonprofit, which focused on planting fruit trees and helping gardeners. But he found that working with people and managing their expectations was not his strong suit.

“He’s always had intense determination,” said Myrna Greenfield, his aunt. Ryan Sandberg, who sits on the board of the nonprofit, said Greenfield would sometimes drive away co-workers who lacked his priorities.

Tanja Vidovic, a public radio producer and host in Florida at the time, thought Greenfield’s involvement with community gardens dovetailed perfectly with the ethos of the show “Sustainable Living.” When she reached out for an interview, one of Greenfield’s colleagues told her that a local program wasn’t worth his time. “It kind of put a sour taste in my mouth,” she said.

Increasingly, Greenfield felt compelled to retreat and reconnect with himself. Loud music bothered him. So did too much chatter. In 2020, when he moved his operations to Asheville, N. C., he began to believe he was probably on the autism spectrum, like other close family members, Greenfield said.

“I read the description of Asperger’s, and I was like, wow, this is such a clear description of my own mind and how I function,” he said. He never got an official diagnosis.

His focus and discipline had supercharged his naturalist agenda, winning him more than two million followers on social media. But in the real world, he struggled to work with others.

Greenfield hired an expert in nonviolent communication, a practice that helps people relate to each other through compassion.

The practice, which encourages self-repair and transparency, inspired him to post videos about his past transgressions. In one, he spoke of taking advantage of women sexually while in college and in his early 20s, including what he described as nonconsensual touching, having sex blackout drunk and letting his friends watch him with a woman through a peephole. Two women working on a documentary about him stepped away from the project when they learned about his past.

“I am a product of a sexist, broken society,” Greenfield said. The raunchy 1999 movie “American Pie” was his playbook as a young man, he said. An important way to heal from this culture, he stressed, was to talk truthfully about these issues, something he aims to do with young people, perhaps on college campuses, in the future.

Vidovic, the journalist in Florida, had already deleted Greenfield from her social media feed after watching a video he’d posted in 2024 about walking down a closed road naked. She thought it was an affront to women and it made her uncomfortable. When the confessional videos emerged, she was not surprised, she said.

“He just loves the attention,” she said. “I think he’s a covert narcissist.”

Greenfield said that his truth-telling videos and his naked jaunts — there was more than one — were simply part of his “strategy to have nothing to hide.”

Awkward communications remain an issue for Greenfield, who spent his foraging year teaching the skills to others across the country.

In June, he offended a group of women in California who had picked him up in a car to look for mushrooms. He was expecting just one person, he told them curtly, announcing that he did not like surprises, recalled a woman who spoke on the condition of anonymity because she is part of a tight-knit foraging community where Greenfield is revered. The difference between the mild-mannered online persona — an amalgam of Henry David Thoreau and the Dude — and the aggravated guy in the back seat was upsetting, she said.

New York’s screeching car alarms, fast-talking pedestrians and Bluetooth speakers blasting reggaeton can be a lot for anyone, but especially for a nature monk who has a hard time with people. Greenfield kept a smile this summer, but one could sometimes glimpse how hard he worked at managing the stress and exhaustion behind it. The self-negotiating seemed like a part of who he was, like yoga teachers fighting their own anxiety to summon a spirited “namaste.”

The day before Greenfield’s Brooklyn event, he met a group of foragers inside the New York Botanical Garden in the Bronx. When a security guard kicked the group out, Greenfield’s smile shifted to a grimace. I watched him struggle to keep the peace and control his irritation.

As the group left, the guard told Greenfield he could not be barefoot. He took a deep breath and his shoulders tensed. But he reached into his bag, took out his moccasins, slipped them on and pointed out a sassafras tree to the foragers while they walked.

Later, crouching by a sewer grate, he said, “Within 10 feet of this spot, I count about eight plants that are edible.” Greenfield the sadhu was back. Soon the group was chewing on wood sorrel. One woman said it tasted like Sour Patch Kids.

During Greenfield’s week in New York, he had to balance his foraging guru status with a growing desperation for some peace. The journalist Kiri Blakeley, who put him up in her home, caught a glimpse of his moodiness while trying to vacuum his room. When the noise annoyed Greenfield, he sharply asked her to leave.

“I was thinking, I am not your maid, you are not in a hotel,” she said. She told Greenfield that if he spoke to her again like that, she would kick him out. He apologized.

Sophia Moskalenko, a psychologist who studies extreme behavior, said: “There’s so much effort that goes into an extreme lifestyle that it encompasses absolutely everything. You want the persona to be true, but you’re doing performance art, and it’s exhausting.”

At Blakeley’s apartment, Greenfield made stew for lunch. It had acorn flour, hen of the woods mushrooms, lambsquarters (a wild green he had found in Brooklyn the day before), elderberries, applesauce, a little hickory oil and maple syrup, and some green powder made from the leaves of a basswood tree.

It was hearty and nutty, sweet and salty. You could taste the berries.

“Six different trees are in this meal,” he said. “I will say that eating from the trees changes you at a core level.”

After a fortunate stop in Minnesota, where Greenfield gathered 25 pounds of nuts (about 13,000 calories) from an oak tree prematurely dropping acorns, he returned in the early fall to the woods of Wisconsin, where he lives in a sauna with a wood-burning stove, which a friend is letting him use for now, rent-free. There, he was able to harvest wild rice, fruit and fish, more than enough to see him through his wild food challenge, which ended in October.

These days, Greenfield is reconsidering his online presence. This winter will be a trial run: He will log off for three months while he canoes around Florida.

But that doesn’t mean he will quit technology, and the social friction it can bring, for good. “One day I will get there,” he said.

But not quite yet.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

To understand why Robin Greenfield radically simplified his life, I turned to Britt Wray, a climate change and mental health expert. People are increasingly undergoing what she calls "climate awakenings" — moments when normal psychological defenses against global warming crumble, prompting a sudden impulse to align daily actions with their values.

Hilary Howard is a Times reporter covering how the New York City region is adapting to climate change and other environmental challenges.

Lexi Parra is a photojournalist for The Times, based in New York. She is a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

The Fine (and Not So Fine) Art of Conceding an Election Defeat

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Latest polls

Senate

House

Governor

Pres. approval

Advertisement

Supported by

Rejecting President Trump’s election denial playbook, nationalist leaders in Serbia and Hungary opted for an orderly retreat.

By Andrew Higgins

Andrew Higgins reported from Belgrade, Serbia, and Budapest, Hungary, during elections in both countries this year.

They curried favor with President Trump and, following his lead, promoted conspiracy theories about the “deep state” and shadowy foreign forces working to oust them.

But when the time came, and the tide of voting went against them, the longtime leaders of Serbia and Hungary both stepped back from following the American president down the path of denying election defeat.

The quick acceptance of defeat in Serbia’s Oct. 25 general election by Aleksandar Vucic and, six months earlier, by Prime Minister Viktor Orban of Hungary, left Mr. Trump, who is still insisting that he won the 2020 presidential election, an outlier rather than a trendsetter in defying basic electoral arithmetic.

The concessions by even like-minded strongmen highlighted the gulf separating Mr. Trump’s denialism from the acceptance of reality. They also underlined yet again the question that looms over the most fiercely contested congressional races on Tuesday about whether the losers, from either party, will concede or challenge the balloting.

In Brazil’s recent presidential election, held on the same day as Serbia’s, Flávio Bolsonaro, the losing Trump-backed candidate, cried foul and demanded that the vote be annulled. But he fled to the United States instead of trying to mobilize his supporters to overturn the numbers, as his father, Jair, did after his own defeat in 2022 and Mr. Trump did two years earlier.

Other strongmen have taken a more Trumpian approach, like Nicolás Maduro, who was declared winner in a tainted election in 2024 and ruled Venezuela until United States forces plucked him from power this year.

So after years of running down democratic norms, the ready acceptance of defeat in Hungary and Serbia was not to be taken for granted. People close to the process said that the decisions were influenced, among other factors, by the fact that both leaders are angling for a return to power and that they lost so decisively that there was little room to manipulate the results.

Mr. Vucic, the master of a seemingly invincible political machine that dominated Serbia from 2012, carped on election night about “nonstop lying” by his foes and claimed that he had been “toppled” by foreign enemies, including “the American deep state — the one opposed to President Trump.”

Yet, to the surprise of both opponents and allies, Mr. Vucic prefaced his complaints with a simple statement: “It is clear that we have lost these elections.”

Christopher R. Hill, a veteran American diplomat who served as ambassador to Serbia under President Biden and assistant secretary of state under President George W. Bush, said of Mr. Vucic’s swift concession speech: “There is no way he would have ‘pulled a Trump.’ No way at all.”

“He knew he lost and lost big and wanted to get out ahead of the process,” Mr. Hill said, noting that his victorious opponents in a newly formed political bloc called “Student List-Students Win” have such divergent views that they could have trouble hanging together. This, he said, encouraged Mr. Vucic to believe “I’ll be back.”

Mr. Orban, too, believed that he would be back, using his concession speech after an April 12 election to try to rally his shellshocked Fidesz party for future battles. “We are not giving up,” he said. “Never, never, never.”

“From our point of view, it is simple: We are democrats,” said Balazs Orban, Mr. Orban’s former political director and his party’s campaign manager for the April election it lost. “Our system only works if it has the support of the people. If we lose that support, even if there was election interference, our first task is to win it back,” he added.

Ana Brnabic, a close ally of Mr. Vucic’s serving as Serbia’s interim president, said that the election results “came as an enormous surprise. I accept them fully.” Many Serbs, she said, “will come to regret this choice” and vote differently in the future.

In contrast to the United States, where executive powers vested in the president give the White House wide leeway to declare its own reality, real power in Europe rests with Parliament and a prime minister named by the party with the most seats rather than a leader ensconced in office for a fixed term.

And European prime ministers, no matter how firm their grip at home on party machinery, the security forces, electoral commissions and other state institutions, are constrained in what they can say and do by foreign governments and foreign investors.

Hungary is a member of the European Union, which crimped Mr. Orban’s room for maneuver by tying tens of billions of euros in grants and loans to his acceptance of basic democratic norms. Serbia, though still outside the bloc and stalled in its halfhearted efforts to join, also depends heavily on E. U. funds and investment from Germany and other European countries.

“It is pretty obvious that the international pressure on Vucic was too high to resist,” said Milan Protic, an opposition-aligned historian and former mayor of Belgrade, the Serbian capital.

Still, he said, as the first results came in “it was pretty evident that Vucic and allies were ready to preserve power by using force.” Armed security forces and burly young men dressed in black and carrying baseball bats poured into the center of Belgrade on election night in support of Mr. Vucic.

But then, he added, “something happened that made him change his mind.”

Spasoje Vulevic, the former head of Serbia’s anti-terrorist unit, who was dismissed by Mr. Vucic last year, said in an interview that he was in touch with contacts in the security forces throughout the evening and feared violent resistance to a likely opposition victory.

Foreign pressure, particularly from the European Union, he said, “played an important role in Vucic’s decision not to resort to force and to concede defeat so quickly.”

Andreas Schieder, an Austrian member of the European Parliament who led the legislature’s election monitoring mission in Belgrade, said there had been a “completely weird atmosphere” around the central electoral commission in Belgrade in the early evening, with streetlights all turned off and “streets blocked by heavily armed policemen.”

Informer, a zealously pro-Vucic media group comprising print and television outlets, reported shortly after the polls closed that the governing party had won 54 percent of the vote, giving it a decisive victory. (In reality, it had won only 39 percent, far behind the Student List’s 52 percent.)

Mr. Schieder said “international pressure” helped persuade Mr. Vucic not to even think of following Mr. Trump’s example. “At the end it was too clear a result. He could not play with it,” the European legislator said. “If it had been more narrow, he could have tried something.”

Mr. Vucic, responding to media reports of foreign intervention to persuade him to accept the landslide against him, last week denied that he had spoken to any foreign officials until late on election night, long after he had conceded. His first caller, he said, was Mr. Orban, at 11:15 p. m.

Mr. Vucic said he had been encouraged by early results from villages showing his party “winning everywhere” but, after watching the tide turn as results came in from Belgrade and other cities, decided that it “made no sense” not to accept defeat.

“There was tension among the people, and everyone was nervous. It is the responsibility of serious people, of statesmen, to calm tensions in the country. It is their responsibility to come out and do what needs to be done,” he told a news conference two days after the vote.

For Ivan Krastev, chairman of the Center for Liberal Strategies in Sofia, Bulgaria, and a permanent fellow at the Institute for Human Sciences in Vienna, the main reason that Mr. Vucic and Mr. Orban bowed out of a fight was simple arithmetic.

“The margin was big and, unlike in the case of Trump, the enthusiasm of their support was limited,” he said. “They had been in power for a very long time and even their supporters wanted some change.”

“The other reason they did not act Trump,” he said, “is Trump. They knew that he is a guarantee for their personal security,” once out of power, much as he did by offering haven to Flávio Bolsonaro.

On Saturday, six days after his defeat, Mr. Vucic hosted Mr. Orban at his father’s house near Belgrade. “Yes, we both recently lost elections but we did not lose our dignity, our pride and our faith,” Mr. Vucic said, standing next to the defeated Hungarian leader.

“We’ll come back,” he added.

Alisa Dogramadzieva contributed reporting from Belgrade.

Andrew Higgins is the East and Central Europe bureau chief for The Times based in Warsaw.

What to Know About the Florida Plane Crash That Killed 9

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

A small jet plummeted to the ground on Sunday, exploding into a fireball and killing everyone on board. The authorities did not immediately release information about the victims.

By Bernard MokamChristina MoralesGeorgia Gee and David Ovalle

David Ovalle reported from the site of the plane crash in Palm Beach County, Fla.

The authorities are investigating why a private jet carrying nine people plunged from the sky on Sunday afternoon, falling at a rate of 20,000 feet per minute before crashing into a roadway outside Palm Beach, Fla.

Everyone on board was killed, the authorities said. They have not released information about the victims. One of the pilots was a 20-year-old aviator named Nathalia Filgueiras, according to her mother, Camila Corteleti.

The plane, a Learjet 60, was traveling from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed in a residential area, showering the neighborhood in debris and forcing the authorities to evacuate hundreds of residents.

Here’s what we know.

Radio traffic between the pilot and air traffic control in Miami indicated that the plane was encountering “light, clear ice that is manageable” on Sunday afternoon, as well as “moderate turbulence.”

The pilot asked if she could climb to 37,000 feet, presumably to fly above the turbulent air. But moments later, she declared “mayday” to air traffic controllers, indicating a life-threatening emergency.

The plane was “descending 20,000 feet per minute,” she screamed.

“We’re going to crash into the ground,” she added.

At a news conference on Sunday, Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida said that footage of the crash, captured on dashboard cameras, showed what “looked like a missile going down.”

The Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board said they would be investigating. The N. T. S. B. has scheduled a news conference for Monday.

Local officials said on Sunday that they were evacuating about 600 residents in the small community of trailer homes near the impact zone, where smoldering chunks of metal ignited small fires.

No one on the ground was injured, officials said.

Ms. Filgueiras, of Boca Raton, Fla., had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time and earned her pilot’s license at 17, Ms. Corteleti said. She said her daughter had worked for Upper Jets, a private charter firm based in Fort Lauderdale.

The cause of the crash was not immediately clear. Aviation safety experts were studying clues such as the plane’s rapid loss of altitude and the pilot’s mention of ice.

The pilot was indicating that the “plane was uncontrollable,” said Steven Arroyo, a retired United Airlines captain who listened to an audio recording of the pilot’s conversation with air traffic controllers.

Mary Schiavo, an aviation lawyer and former inspector general for the Transportation Department, said that ice buildup on a plane’s wings could disrupt airflow and reduce lift. That could be consistent with how the plane dropped from the sky so suddenly.

“Icing can be so severe it can overcome and stall the plane,” said Ms. Schiavo, who reviewed publicly available flight data and videos posted on social media.

“That is a plane not descending, but a plane falling,” she said.

Esteban Ruiz, a resident of the trailer home community near the crash site, said he had been relaxing on Sunday afternoon when he heard a loud noise.

“I thought maybe it was lightning,” he said, adding that he also heard what he thought was rain pelting his roof. It was actually metal debris from the plane or its impact. Mr. Ruiz said he rushed outside and saw a chaotic scene and a crater in the ground.

Stephanie Platts, who also lived near the crash site, said she had been sitting on her patio with family members when she heard what sounded like a car crash. Ms. Platts said her mobile home caught on fire, caused by flying debris.

Neighbors tried to help her put out the flames. She said she saw human remains scattered around her.

“Everything was engulfed in flames,” Ms. Platts said, “and then after the flames, was like rain of metal.”

Bernard Mokam covers breaking news.

Christina Morales is a national reporter for The Times.

The Big Change Coming in U. S.-China Relations in the Age of A. I.

The New York Times November 02, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Thomas L. Friedman

By Thomas L. Friedman

Opinion Columnist

At Beijing Capital International Airport, it is now required after landing to send carry-on bags through a scanner before leaving the arrivals building. As I approached the scanner belt with my bags, though, I saw a sign that I had never encountered before: Any passenger carrying a drone has to remove and declare it. A Chinese security officer pointed directly to the sign to confirm that I had no drones in my bag. I shook my head no. I don’t usually travel with a drone.

That sign was not the only new thing I saw on this trip. It was one of many. Having traveled to China regularly since the early 1990s, I found this journey totally different for a very specific reason: It was my first visit to China in the full-blown age of artificial intelligence.

As I end nine days in the country, having visited Beijing and Xiong’an as well as China’s tech hubs in Hangzhou, Ningbo and Shenzhen, it is very clear to me that the A. I. era is already reshaping the geopolitical and geoeconomic relationships between the United States and China in ways that are actually pulling our two countries closer together geopolitically, while exacerbating our trade differences.

How so? Let’s go back to that drone sign at the Beijing airport. What is it telling us? It is telling us that while the United States and China are still economic and strategic rivals jostling for advantage, they both realize that there is now an intruder into their two-superpower marriage: the superempowered bad actor.

I’m not talking about Chinese democracy advocates. I’m talking about agents of chaos — fraudsters, drug dealers, human traffickers, the kind of hackers who just stole $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance. I’m talking about bad individuals and small teams that can now arm themselves with off-the-shelf drones or A. I.-powered cyberweapons to wield the destructive force of a superpower all by themselves. And I am talking, even more important, about both American and Chinese A. I. models that are demonstrating greater and greater capacities to go rogue and become agents of mass disruption as they become increasingly self-directing, self-improving and self-preserving.

Both countries are just beginning to wrestle with the mind shift this requires in how they relate to each other — even as they continue to reflexively take the opposite sides on wars from Gaza to Ukraine to Iran. A Chinese blogger friend put it to me candidly over dinner in Beijing last week: “We still have real differences over issues like Taiwan. But sometimes the U. S. and China don’t know what they are fighting about anymore,” he said. “It’s just a habit.”

Well, it’s an obsolete habit that both nations must unlearn, and quickly, in the age of artificial intelligence, when global stability will increasingly require mutually assured collaboration between the world’s two A. I. superpowers.

To be sure, our definition of disorder is often not the same as China’s. Any regulatory system embraced by the United States needs to protect democratic values, free expression and peaceful protest. China is unlikely to have any of those in its regulatory scheme. But a lot of overlap remains between our self-interests, which lies in preventing artificial intelligence from causing violent harm — to infrastructure, to individuals, to countries and even to our species. That is the kind of disorder that Washington and Beijing should be able to agree needs controlling. We need these basic rules more than ever because the next steps for A. I. involve, literally, walking — as in robots.

I saw a demonstration at an A. I. robotics exhibition in Beijing where a Chinese humanoid robot replaced its own battery pack, lodged in its back. It just took a couple of minutes. As I stared at it doing this maneuver, I wondered: What happens when it also has autonomous intelligence?

While the need for more collaboration against those trying to get the worst of their A. I. technologies may push Beijing and Washington closer together over time geopolitically, in geoeconomics the opposite is likely to happen.

That is because A. I. is simultaneously superempowering something else: China’s manufacturing juggernaut. As of 2024, China already made almost a third of all manufactured goods sold in the world. What I saw on this trip, visiting some of China’s most advanced car companies and telecom manufacturers, is that A. I. is intensifying their efficiency and competitiveness even more.

You can see it in trade statistics. China’s trade surplus in 2025 — exports over imports — was a staggering $1.19 trillion. That was a 20 percent increase from the year before. This year it is expected to grow to $1.3 trillion — a trade imbalance out of line with global economic output not seen by any country since the end of World War II, when the United States was the only major industrial economy standing!

Trust me, you have not seen anything yet.

Because while American companies are burning through billions investing in frontier A. I. models that are so advanced they’re humbling the best mathematicians, Chinese companies are focused on deploying cheap, “good enough,” open-weight A. I. models that could make its large lead in advanced manufacturing simply unbeatable. To put it differently, America is spending vast sums on frontier A. I. models that are already so powerful the latest versions are too dangerous to be released. China, by contrast, starts the A. I. era with such a dominant base of advance manufacturing facilities, it can reap immediate and broad gains from its smaller “good enough” A. I. models.

When you combine this with China’s cowboy capitalism — scores of companies fiercely competing in every sector of the domestic economy — you get a pace of progress that is downright scary in some industries. At the Beijing Robot Industrial Park, where I saw that robot swapping out its own battery pack, another exhibit impressed me even more.

It was two humanoid robots standing side by side. They were built by different Chinese companies to compete in the Beijing E-Town Humanoid Robot Half-Marathon race — 21 kilometers, or 13.1 miles. The first robot runner, which had a gold medal on a ribbon draped around its neck, won the 2025 race in two hours, 40 minutes and 42 seconds. The second robot runner, also sporting a gold ribbon, won the same race in April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds, beating what was then the human world record, 57 minutes and 20 seconds, held by Jacob Kiplimo.

In a single year, Chinese advances in embodied artificial intelligence produced a robot marathon runner faster than the fastest human ever recorded. My Chinese guide pointed at the two robots and said: “Last year, this year. Next year — we’ll see.”

We certainly will. Other than that, folks … nothing to worry about here.

What follows is what I gleaned from dozens of conversations and company visits in China on how the age of A. I. is reshaping China and China-U. S. relations.

Let me start with some good news.

Six months ago, if you asked pretty much any A. I. expert if China and America would ever get together and agree on a set of guidelines to control their now increasingly dangerous A. I. models, the answer you would get is, “No way, no how” — with a special emphasis that China would never agree to such a thing. Think again.

Right now, I would say that Beijing may actually be more eager to discuss A. I. guardrails than President Trump, who told the United Nations in September that the United States “rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control” A. I. — a theme he repeated after his summit with President Xi Jinping days later. Trump to the world: America’s frontier A. I. models are in the lead and I won’t collar them. Full stop. Get lost.

At the opening session of the 2026 Global Governance Forum in Xiong’an, I had a discussion with Wang Yi, the Chinese foreign minister and Politburo member, and John Thornton, co-chair of the Asia Society board of trustees. I was struck by Wang’s clear message in support of multilateral A. I. safeguards.

As Wang put it to us: The “leading nations in A. I., China and the United States, have both the capability and the responsibility to jointly develop and manage A. I. effectively, ensuring its development remains under human control and benefits the people. We must not only mitigate risks but also cooperate to jointly discuss globally applicable rules and standards” to make sure A. I.’s development stays under human control and for the benefit of people.

Of course, China, like the United States, is building A. I. tools to enhance weapons to fight abroad and improve every tool in its domestic surveillance kit to control dissent at home. But Beijing also knows — as that no-drones-in-your-luggage sign at the airport indicated — that A. I. is a two-edged sword and can be used by a lot of bad actors. That is why when you talk to U. S. administration officials about what the Chinese are doing with us behind the scenes, you’ll get a complex answer.

These officials have no illusions that Beijing would like to see more guardrails on America’s frontier models, because the United States is in the lead. But they will also tell you that China’s law enforcement agencies lately have become much more cooperative with their U. S. counterparts on combating cybercrime, fraud and money laundering — all of which A. I. is rapidly enhancing. The Chinese know that the open-weight A. I. models being distributed by Chinese companies are easier for software developers, including those that are bad actors, to adapt to specific, targeted applications than Silicon Valley’s frontier models.

But don’t take my word for it. In September, the Chinese Communist Party’s top intelligence official, Chen Yixin, head of the Ministry of State Security, wrote in the journal China Cyberspace that emerging A. I. technologies were “directly threatening” China’s political, institutional and ideological security. Chen added: “Various hostile forces and individuals with ulterior motives abuse generative artificial intelligence technologies” to create rumors, spread misinformation and “incite confrontational sentiments at low cost and in large quantities.”

Read those words: at low cost and in large quantities.

Chen’s government has the world’s largest state-run facial recognition surveillance system, which can pluck a single person out of a huge crowd — what I call “the big acting small.” What Chen was saying is that he also knows that A. I. is a dual-use technology that is enabling the small to now act big. That is the essence of the huge change in the geophysics of the world — the spread of cheap, precision technologies, like drones and cyber-hacking tools, that are now supercharged by A. I. That new superempowered actor can be another nation or a single foreigner or one of your own citizens. Either way, it’s a big new problem in need of a big new answer.

Which is why I was not surprised that while I was in China last week the government issued a draft of A. I. rules that would give the governing Communist Party new powers to track or restrict exports of some advanced Chinese systems. Why now? Maybe because, as The Times reported on Oct. 14, A. I. agents attributed to tests being run by the Chinese tech giant Tencent recently went rogue and tried to “bypass anti-robot protections on websites,” among other shenanigans. Yup, the Chinese have the same problems with their biggest A. I. models as we do, even if they are six months to a year behind in their capabilities.

So, I am going to go out on a limb here: In the coming year, China and America will be seriously exploring collaborative controls on A. I. models. Because, as America’s frontier models reach the point of training themselves 100 percent through recursive self-improvement (without human direction) and as China’s open-weight models that learn off ours through distillation get strengthened in their wake, I predict that 2027 will be the year when both countries fully grasp what an amazing opportunity A. I. is for humanity — and what an unprecedented threat it is to humanity.

This collaboration will be tricky for America. Because, unlike the U. S. government, the Chinese government of President Xi is worried not only about A. I.’s empowering criminals at home, but also about political opponents. Managing that complexity is precisely what makes U. S.-China relations in the age of A. I. different.

Given all of these competing pulls, it may not be possible for the United States and China to come up with a shared system of A. I. guardrails as much as they might need to — at least not without a perfect A. I. storm. That is, a large-scale A. I.-driven event that is big enough to frighten both countries into collaborating on effective controls — but not so big as to end the world.

I repeat: 2027 could be that year. Let’s hope the storm is perfect.

Now let’s look at how A. I. is reshaping economic relations between China and the United States and the rest of the world. Every time I visit China, I come away more struck than from the trip before by the stark contrast in its economy. If China were a person, it would have the upper body of an Olympic weight lifter — rippling with muscles that represent its export-driven advanced manufacturing economy — and the lower body of an Olympic skier who just crashed into a mogul, broke his leg and can now only hobble on a crutch.

That lower body represents a domestic Chinese economy that is still so weakened by the explosion of its large, quarter-century-long housing bubble — which ravaged its middle class and left hundreds of millions of people with mortgages that are underwater or with wiped-out savings — that many Chinese are holding tight to every yuan they can. The frenzied overbuilding of high-rise apartments with cheap money in the early 2000s got so crazy that, as the Times Beijing bureau chief, Keith Bradsher, wrote in February 2025, China now has “abundant housing for the country’s 1.4 billion people and enough empty apartments for another 300 million people.” Put another way, Bradsher said this past spring, China has enough empty apartments to house almost every person in America, which has a population of about 350 million.

In short, China is an export giant and domestic consumption invalid. Unfortunately, the government, instead of injecting money into the domestic economy through improved pension programs, is doubling down on subsidies to build up its global lead in advanced manufacturing — and telling Chinese consumers to suck it up.

Therein lies a huge problem for the global economy at the dawn of the A. I. revolution. Because what I saw on this trip is that the Olympic weight lifter part of the Chinese economy is now guzzling down protein shakes labeled A. I. and is becoming an even more dominating competitor in every advanced manufacturing realm — from socks to robots.

Sure, American, European, Japanese and Korean manufacturers are also benefitting from A. I. enhancements. The problem is that China has so much more installed advanced manufacturing and therefore is going to reap outsized gains. Come along with me on my whirlwind tour of some major Chinese advanced manufacturers.

On my visit to Alibaba headquarters in Hangzhou, Xiong Xiong, chief of staff to Alibaba’s co-founder and chairman, Joe Tsai, pointed out to me that in Formula 1 racing, you rarely overtake your competition on the straightaways. “You win in the turns,” he said, “because in the turns it is not how fast you go, it is how daring you are — how fast you brake and how you respond to my braking — and do you have the stability to control your car at high speed.”

Well, one day we may look back at the years 2019 to 2023 as one of those turns and China came out of it now leading the pack on the straightaway. Two things happened in that period: Covid-19 and A. I. both exploded around the world. Because of Covid, virtually all American students and many American business executives left China. I was also not able to make my own annual trips.

Here is one example of what happened while we were sleeping.

When I visited China, before Covid, Xiaomi was a smartphone company. When I came back in 2023, it was also an electric car company. It put four wheels on its phone. But it didn’t stop there. When I visited its almost entirely roboticized car factory on the outskirts of Beijing last Monday, I found Xiaomi was a superconnected, A. I.-enabled E. V. company. My hosts noted how Xiaomi’s self-developed “multi-material performance simulation system” uses A. I. to quickly figure out what the company believes is the optimal alloy formula — from 10.16 million possibilities — to produce what it called “a perfect combination” of strength, resilience, stability and low carbon footprint for its newest vehicle bodies.

Trump hates electric cars. What he has never understood is that China’s hypercompetitive E. V. industry birthed a powerful, deeply integrated supply chain of advanced battery technology, robotics, material science and, now, A. I. Today, any Chinese inventor or entrepreneur looking to manufacture absolutely anything can seamlessly leverage this hyper-efficient, foundational ecosystem to innovate better, faster and cheaper than most any global competitor. Global manufacturers used to say you had to be in China “to sell to China.” Now they say, you have to be in China and have access to its supply chains “to sell to the world.”

You want to make shoes with electric rollers and flashing lights that sing the Chinese national anthem on the left shoe and the American national anthem on the right shoe? Someone here will have the parts and tools for you to do it in 24 hours.

In Ningbo, I visited the Geely electric vehicle manufacturing plant. I watched an engineer use the company’s latest charging station to power up a car from Geely’s newest A. I. luxury E. V. brand, called the Lynk & Co, in eight-plus minutes with a charge that will last some 500 miles. That is not a typo — that is almost like filling up a tank of gas. “In the future, we intend to improve it further,” the Geely demonstration engineer laconically told me. Yes, I thought, I am sure you will.

In Shenzhen, I toured Huawei Technologies’ assembly line for its newest Mate 90 smartphones. Zha Jun, who oversees Huawei’s research and development, explained that this line used to have 86 workers per shift — doing mostly manual inspections — and the rest of the work force was robots. It recently shrunk that number down to nine people by turning to A. I.-enabled image recognition systems.

When I asked what kind of data center it used to run the A. I. systems, Zha said: “We have no need for a data center. Huawei can get all the A. I. benefits it needs for these kinds of manufacturing improvements using our own open-weight, domain-specific A. I. models with less than one billion parameters.” Those are the ones with circuitry that amounts to the size of a small suitcase. (Parameters are a measure of the connections and weights that an A. I. model uses to process information and are used as a general proxy for its complexity and capacity to learn.) These small A. I. models, Zha added, were “good enough” to make big improvements in manufacturing.

“Good enough” A. I. was a phrase I heard at a lot of factories on this trip. It describes the improvements to businesses produced by the less-than-frontier A. I. models.

“China and the U. S. are taking different directions when it comes to A. I.,” Ren Zhengfei, Huawei’s founder and chief executive, explained to me over tea at Huawei’s research campus in Shenzhen, one of many technology hubs where the company employs some 110,000 researchers, many of them engineers and scientists with advanced degrees. In the United States, Ren said, A. I. research revolves around “what does it mean to be human these days and what is the meaning of the world, and of God? In China, A. I. research is more practical” and is being deployed in big industries, like steel.

“China produces one billion tons of steel a year,” Ren said, “so if that industry can achieve a 1 percent improvement by using A. I. to increase the efficiency in how it mixes the various chemicals that go into every single steel-making furnace,” the additional profits generated for a single furnace will exceed 10 million yuan ($1.5 million) per year. In the past, China was not a world leader in medicine. With the help of A. I., China is now able to strikingly accelerate its ability “to discover and produce new drugs” by rapidly testing different molecular combinations.

He concluded: “That is why we call A. I. in the U. S. ‘Socrates A. I.’ and we name our approach ‘Lu Ban A. I.’” Lu Ban was a legendary ancient Chinese master carpenter and engineer.

Now add one more increasingly important factor: rare earths, which in the age of A. I. will be more important than ever — not only for manufacturing but for running all the chips that go into every data center as well.

My traveling partner on this trip has been Keith Bradsher, who will soon be coming out with a book, “The Race for Rare Earths: Why China Is Winning the Contest for the World’s Most Critical Resources.” The book traces how decade by decade, the United States and Europe lost their early leadership to China in these vital metals that go into cars, drones, wind turbines, fighter jets, smartphones, missiles, lasers, A. I. chips and practically every other high-tech invention you can think of over the past 40 years, including most consumer electronics.

In 1964, Deng Xiaoping, later to become China’s paramount leader, visited the world’s biggest rare-earth deposit, in northern China. In 1973, he began planning for China’s rise in rare-earth technologies, and by the early 1990s he foresaw the geopolitical power of China’s tightening grip on rare earths, declaring: “The Middle East has oil. China has rare earths.”

The United States and Europe are only now restarting a rare-earth industry — from the mines to the manufactured magnets — but will need at least five years and probably 10 to catch up, according to Bradsher’s book, which suggests ways to speed up the recovery. Meanwhile, Beijing has wielded its almost total control over the world’s supply of crucial rare earths to force the Trump administration and European Union to back down repeatedly on tariffs and to put heavy pressure on Japan not to support Taiwan.

You add it all up and China’s dominance in global manufacturing is extraordinary. Jens Eskelund, the head of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, citing information from members, told me that 90 percent of global manufactured goods move in containers. The percentage of global container exports by China rose from 31.8 percent in 2019 to 37.5 percent in 2025, he said. “The rolling three-month average for the most recent months is now 40 percent,” he said. The reason? China’s manufacturing output rose 5.3 percent during the first eight months of this year, he said. (Meanwhile, China’s domestic retail sales increased only 0.4 percent year on year in August, he pointed out.)

In 2019, China exported about 2.5 containers to Europe for every container shipped in the opposite direction, Eskelund told me. During the first eight months of 2026, the ratio widened to six containers moving from China to Europe for every one container moving from Europe to China.

“I tell the Chinese: ‘Guys, trade becomes inherently volatile if you cannot point to value creation for both sides,’” Eskelund added. “China actually understands the world’s concerns. For China, though, the question is: Why should we accommodate these concerns when the world has not put up any serious resistance?”

It is a good question. And one that prompts me to leave this trip with some free advice to China and America from someone who believes the world will be a more prosperous and stable place if people in both countries thrive.

To China: You are going too far too fast too alone, and in the process you are creating too many economic relationships with too many developed and developing countries that are not win-win but win-lose. As a result of your domestic economic weakness, combined with your huge advantage in homegrown engineering talent, unparalleled manufacturing supply chains, the unrivaled work ethic of your people and your high savings rate plowed into the world’s best transportation and electricity infrastructure, China just can’t stop itself from making everything for everyone.

I don’t know when, I don’t how, but the rest of the world will not let that happen — not when robots and A. I. are also creating steadily more worker layoffs. China is courting a real backlash. As Eskelund bluntly put it to me: “There is now a real risk we get into a trade war. We are not going to tolerate a world where China makes everything, and we just give museum tours.”

To my fellow Americans (and our E. U. allies): China is not going to slow down in manufacturing as a favor to anyone. If we want to influence China’s geopolitics and geoeconomics in the age of A. I., we have to create the economic competitiveness that would compel it to do so. That requires the United States to be as serious as the people here are.

In my view, the Chinese today are getting the best out of a bad system of government — by thinking long-term and executing on a plan to align their country with the economic trends of the 21st century.

But one of the weaknesses of China’s system has been on dramatic display lately: the sudden disappearance and arrests of senior officials accused of corruption — so many that it could start to slow down the whole system here, if high-level bureaucrats fear making spending decisions that could land them in jail. Or as one Chinese economist put it to me, quoting a Chinese proverb: “If the water is too clear, there will be no fish.”

And America? By doing no long-term thinking, appointing incompetent cabinet secretaries and having each new administration undo major initiatives of the previous one — like on clean energy — we’re getting the worst out of a good system.

Just look around. Republicans are spending more than $200 million to elect a terrible man — an impeached Texas attorney general, Ken Paxton — to be Texas’ next senator. Trump is savaging America’s scientific research budget and driving away the most talented foreigners who want to come to America to work, study and invent. Trump gutted the electric car industry in favor of gas guzzlers, while Democrats did not think it was a bad idea to leave our southern border porous, which helped to get Trump re-elected.

The only way we will restore some balance to the economic relationship between China and America (and between China and Europe) is not by begging Beijing but by rebuilding our leverage — by being serious again about our governance, by making cost-competitive products and by planning beyond next week and then executing on those plans.

I know just what to call this strategy — I saw it on a red baseball cap the other day: “Make America Great Again.”

If only we could start electing people who knew how.

I'm curious about the impact of robotics and AI on Chinese employment, especially given the real estate value collapse.

"And America? By doing no long-term thinking, appointing incompetent cabinet secretaries and having each new administration undo major initiatives of the previous one — like on clean energy — we’re getting the worst out of a good system."If it is a "good system", why has the system generated such a long list of awful results? Isn't it the right time to think what the problems with the system are and how to fix them, rather than simply wish for all the bad things to go away?!

AI is rewriting the definition of national power in real time. China is building factories, robots, energy systems and supply chains while America exhausts itself fighting culture wars. America has everything it needs to lead the next century, except perhaps the political fortitude to stop fighting over the last one.

Thomas L. Friedman is the foreign affairs Opinion columnist. He joined the paper in 1981 and has won three Pulitzer Prizes. He is the author of seven books, including “From Beirut to Jerusalem,” which won the National Book Award. @tomfriedman • Facebook

Can You Afford to Watch TV?

The New York Times November 02, 2026

What to Watch

Advertisement

Supported by

Critic’s notebook

The streaming era has provided viewers a lot of great things to watch. But it comes at a price.

By James Poniewozik

James Poniewozik is the chief television critic for The New York Times. He spent much of the ’80s adjusting the cable box to tune in the scrambled signal for HBO, which his parents didn’t pay for.

A little over a month ago, “American Hostage” premiered. The series, about a real-life armed standoff at an Indiana mortgage office in 1977, is one of those out-of-nowhere surprises I love to discover as a TV critic. It has committed performances from Jon Hamm and Giovanni Ribisi and eerily timely things to say about the frustrations of the powerless with the powerful.

You should watch it if you can. Which you probably can’t, unless you reach into your wallet, one more time.

See, “American Hostage” is on MGM+. What is MGM+? Good question! It’s a streaming service, descended from the premium channel Epix. (What is Epix? No time for that!) More saliently, it is $7.99 a month. That is, it’s $7.99 on top of the endlessly scrolling list of subscriptions you probably already have.

(Note: With many of the plans I discuss here, there are multiple pricing options — monthly or annual, with or without ads, bundled this way and that way. You may want a calculator.)

TV critics are not traditionally in the habit of considering price when they decide what to cover. This isn’t restaurant criticism. But lately TV consumption has begun to feel like high-end dining, with no limit of upcharges and price hikes and caviar supplements sending the tab to the heavens.

This is frustrating for consumers in inflationary times. But it’s also not great for the art, or at least for the experience and conversation around it. It creates yet another division of haves, choosing from a vast menu in media’s first class, and have-nots, missing out in steerage. It turns a medium that was once universal, if frustrating, into one that is increasingly inaccessible, if often excellent. “American Hostage” is good. But is it $7.99-a-month good? Is any show?

Once, TV was free — well, save for the investment in a set and an antenna and your precious time watching ads. Everyone had access to the same air and the same shows. I was born in the rabbit-ears era of TV, and I will not romanticize it as having been better. But like so many aspects of life “improved” by technology, it was less complicated.

This changed with the popularization of cable. “The Sopranos” helped turn HBO from an occasional domestic luxury (or motel-room amenity) into a cultural must-have. Increasingly, the TV worth watching and talking about was something you had to pay for. And then pay a little more. Cable channels proliferated, and the cable bundle — smushing together the channels you watched with the many you didn’t — got fatter and fatter.

Oversqueezed media consumers wished it could be different. If only you could pick and choose which platforms you subscribed to! Somewhere on Wall Street, a finger curled on a monkey’s paw, and the streaming business was born.

Now, if you had an internet connection (another fee, unless your neighbor’s Wi-Fi password hygiene was lax), you could choose your services à la carte: Netflix, Hulu, Amazon, Peacock. Disney+, Paramount+, AMC+. YouTube TV and YouTube Premium. Dropout, for comedy. Shudder, for horror. Crunchyroll, for anime. Want to follow pro sports? You may want a second job.

I am familiar with all of these because my work requires that I be able to watch anything that runs anywhere. Someday when I retire, dismantling my monthly media commitments will resemble unwinding the assets of a bankrupt Fortune 500 corporation.

At the same time, I am writing for people who are weighing another subscription against gas and groceries. And we all exist in an economy that is increasingly built around subscriptions for damn near everything, as discussed in a recent episode of “Last Week Tonight With John Oliver.” (HBO Max, starting at $10.99/month with ads.)

Sure, $7.99 is cheaper than a matinee movie ticket where I live, let alone a Broadway show or concert. But is it worth it for you? How would I know? As a critic, I know what is worthwhile, and the streaming era has created more spaces for the worthwhile to flourish.

The best of the art form is now scattered across a lot of walled gardens whose walls get a little higher every year. At this point, the rate of announcements you receive for streaming price increases — which are outstripping inflation — rivals the texts from candidates asking for donations. (PBS, despite its funding challenges, looks like a better deal every day.)

So the medium that used to be a pop-culture lingua franca becomes a Tower of Babel. The stories you experience and the references you get are determined by the purchase decisions you’ve made. A terrific show — say, last year’s “Hal & Harper” on Mubi — can languish on an obscure service, its audience curtailed before it even premieres.

And a population already fragmented by tastes, demographics and subcultures becomes further subdivided by economics. You can go rogue and share streaming passwords. You can create a system of reminders to drop various platforms. Or you can just give up, pick a service or two, and pray the algorithm gives you something good.

What’s good this year? There’s the new “East of Eden” on Netflix ($8.99 a month with ads, $19.99 without, $26.99 in 4K). There’s my favorite new series of the year, “Widow’s Bay” on Apple TV ($14.99 a month ad-free — or “free,” I guess, if you buy qualifying Apple products every three months for eternity). There’s a great new installment of FX’s “The Lowdown,” which streams on Hulu ($12.49 with ads, or part of an array of bundles as lengthy as the instructions for a tax return).

There’s also “Cupertino,” a new legal drama about the tech industry that I enjoyed more the longer it went on — and which blessedly airs on CBS, one of those old broadcast networks whose signal still flies magically through the air and can be gathered by an antenna.

Don’t have an antenna? There are plenty of streaming services with a “live TV” feature. It’ll cost you.

We would love to hear your thoughts about the costs of streaming TV. Fill out the form below, and we may contact you for an upcoming story. We will not publish or share your contact information outside the Times newsroom, and we will not publish any part of your submission without contacting you first.

James Poniewozik is the chief TV critic for The Times. He writes reviews and essays with an emphasis on television as it reflects a changing culture and politics.
